POST /api/v1/auth/register and PUT /api/v1/auth/profile answer 400 with {"error_code": "USERNAME_INVALID", "message": "A username cannot contain @: the sign-in reads it as an email address"} in detail: the message is USERNAME_RESERVED_MESSAGE, and the code that of the service's refusal, which register_user() raises as the RegistrationError USERNAME_INVALID (listed in _REGISTRATION_REFUSALS) and the profile route answers (Refusals with a code). The command line prints that message after ❌ and exits with 1. A LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_USERNAME with an @ raises the AdminBootstrapConfigError ADMIN_USERNAME_INVALID, whose message names the variable and the @, and stops the start (The Initial Administrator): the administrator signs in with LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_EMAIL anyway. The registration card refuses the @ before sending; the card and the Profile tab word the server's refusal in the user's language, with auth.validation.usernameNoAt (Registration errors, ProfileTab).
  2. No email address that is another account's username, A–Z case aside (the fold of SQLite's lower(), decision P18): user_service.address_is_a_username(), called by create_user() and, for an address that changes, by update_profile() — so registration, the Profile's change of address, ./dev.py user create and ./dev.py user set-email. The answer is the one of an address already registered: 400 Email already registered, a plain string, and on the command line the same message after ❌. An account may take its own username as its address (other_than).
  3. The lookup reads an address first. An identifier holding @ is the account whose email it is, in any A–Z case (get_user_by_email()); only when no account has that address, the account whose username is exactly that string, a legacy name. Without @ it is a username only, compared exactly as before (get_user_by_username()), never an address. Whichever row was written first, no username stands in front of another account's address.

Usernames written before lot A-21a keep their @: nothing renames them. Their accounts sign in with their address, as every account has one, and with that exact name while no account has it as its address. A rename follows rule 1. Usernames are still compared exactly as written, capitals included. The administrator's side: «Usernames with an @» in Users & Invitations.

The length of a new username (lot A-46). _new_username_refusal() checks the @ first, then the length: 3 to 50 characters (USERNAME_MIN_LENGTH and USERNAME_MAX_LENGTH in backend/app/config/accounts.py, which LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_USERNAME follows too). Registration and the Profile refuse another length before the service, with the 422 of their request schemas (AuthRegisterRequest, UpdateProfileRequest); ./dev.py user create had no such check, and now stops with ❌ A username must be 3 to 50 characters long (USERNAME_LENGTH_MESSAGE), exit 1, writing nothing. Over HTTP the 422 must stay first: the app words USERNAME_INVALID as the rule of the @ (auth.validation.usernameNoAt). A name an account keeps is never checked again: one of 2 or 51 characters, which user create could write before lot A-46, stays as it is, and ./dev.py user set-email still finds the account by it.

Refusals with a code (lot A-47). create_user() and update_profile() answer (None, error) on a refusal, error a user_service.AccountError: a str subclass holding the message as before, so a caller that prints or compares it keeps working, with a code. USERNAME_INVALID for a new username against its rules, the @ or the length; USERNAME_TAKEN; EMAIL_TAKEN, an address registered or another account's username; USER_NOT_FOUND, from update_profile(). register_user() and PUT /api/v1/auth/profile branch on the code, never on the wording: USERNAME_INVALID becomes the RegistrationError USERNAME_INVALID, or the profile's 400 with that error_code; any other refusal keeps its plain-string 400, through the RegistrationError ACCOUNT_EXISTS for registration (not in _REGISTRATION_REFUSALS). An AccountError survives copy.copy, copy.deepcopy and pickle with its code: its __getnewargs__() hands back the code with the message, where str's own would give the message alone and AccountError.__new__() would raise TypeError (UNAME-032).

Tests: ./dev.py test services username-rules (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_username_rules.py: the @ refused by user create and in LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_USERNAME, and nothing else of the character set; an address that is a username, in any A–Z case, refused by register_user(), user set-email and user create; a legacy name left as it is; UNAME-020 to UNAME-023, lot A-46: a length of 2 or 51 refused by user create, create_user() and update_profile(), 3 and 50 taken, a legacy name of either length kept; UNAME-030 and UNAME-031, lot A-47: the code of every refusal, the message unchanged, and register_user() deciding on the code once the message is reworded; UNAME-032: an AccountError copied, deep-copied and pickled keeps its code), ./dev.py test services username-lookup (test_username_lookup.py: an address finds its owner before a legacy name written like it, in both orders of the rows; the exact legacy fallback; without @ a username only, exact) and ./dev.py test api username-rules (backend/test_scripts/test_api/test_username_rules_api.py, in-process: the registration, profile and login routes, workstream E's scenes; UNAME-API-12 to UNAME-API-14: both routes deciding on the code, the answer of the @ as before, and a length still refused with 422 first); for the app, ./dev.py test front-utility core-unit (registrationErrors.test.ts) and ./dev.py test front-utility component-unit (RegisterCard.test.ts, tabs/ProfileTab.test.ts).

docs.title: 🗝️ JWT Secret
docs.text:
Tokens are signed with HS256 and one key per process, _JWT_SECRET in backend/app/services/accounts/auth_service.py, resolved once when that module is imported:

  • configured_jwt_secret() (backend/app/config/platform.py) returns env_secret("JWT_SECRET"): the JWT_SECRET variable when it is not blank, otherwise the content of the file named by JWT_SECRET_FILE (Secrets from Files), otherwise None. An empty or blank JWT_SECRET counts as not set: a stray space is never used as a key. Neither variable is a field of the Pydantic Settings: both are read from the process environment only.
  • With None, the process falls back to its own secrets.token_urlsafe(64), so every start makes a new key and signs every user out. This default is deliberate: keeping sessions across restarts is opt-in.
  • A JWT_SECRET_FILE that cannot give its secret raises SecretFileError during that import. main.py imports the API router, which imports auth_service.py, so the server does not start.

⚙️ Multi-worker support

Uvicorn starts its workers with spawn on every platform (uvicorn/_subprocess.py): each worker re-imports all modules and resolves the key on its own. With nothing shared, each worker would make its own key, and a token signed by one would fail on the others. Before launching Uvicorn, _ensure_shared_jwt_secret() in dev.py makes sure that every worker finds the same key:

  1. a non-blank JWT_SECRET is kept as it is, and wins over JWT_SECRET_FILE;
  2. otherwise, with a non-blank JWT_SECRET_FILE, nothing is generated and nothing is removed: every worker reads the same file, and a blank JWT_SECRET beside it is harmless, since the server ignores it;
  3. otherwise a fresh secrets.token_urlsafe(64) goes into JWT_SECRET, shared by every worker of that run.
  • dev.py loads .env into the environment first; values already set in the shell win.
  • The Docker image starts a single uvicorn worker (CMD in the Dockerfile) and receives .env through the env_file: of Compose: without JWT_SECRET or JWT_SECRET_FILE, every container start invalidates all sessions.
  • The administrator's side is Keep Users Signed In After a Restart.

docs.title: ⏰ Token Expiration
docs.text:
• Configurable via Global Settings: session_ttl_hours (default: 24 hours)
  • Read each time a session cookie is issued — at login, at the setup of the initial administrator, and when a password or email change re-issues it — it sets both the token's exp and the cookie's max_age (24 hours when the setting cannot be read): a new value applies to the cookies issued after it
  • After expiration, the user must log in again
  • There is no token refresh mechanism — a new login is required. The only cookies issued without a login are the ones a password change or an email change sends back to the device that made it (Session Revocation), and the one that signs in the initial administrator once its setup link is spent (The Initial Administrator)

docs.title: 🚪 Logout
docs.text:
• Frontend calls POST /auth/logout which clears the session cookie
  • No server-side blacklist — logout leaves the session version alone: a copy of the token remains technically valid until it expires, or until the account's sessions are ended (Session Revocation)
  • This is acceptable for a self-hosted application with short TTL: a user who fears a copied cookie changes the password, which ends every other session of the account

docs.title: 🔁 Session Revocation
docs.text:
Each account has a session generation, users.session_version (0 on a new account), and each session cookie carries the generation it was issued at, the sv claim. Raising the account's version ends every session issued before it, on every device, at its next request. There is still no session store: the check compares one integer column of the user row that get_current_user() already loads on every request.

await user_service.end_sessions(session, user) (backend/app/services/accounts/user_service.py) raises the version by one in SQL, in the caller's transaction, and does not commit: the caller commits it with the change that asks for it. Seven changes call it:

Change Entry point Sessions ended Password change POST /api/v1/auth/change-password (PasswordChangeModal, Profile tab) Every other session of the account: the same response sets a new cookie at the new version, so the device that made the change stays signed in Email change PUT /api/v1/auth/profile with a new email and the right current_password (Profile tab) → user_service.update_profile(): see Changing the Email; ./dev.py user set-email → the same function From the Profile tab, every other session of the account, as for a password change: the same response sets a new cookie; from the command line, all of them Password reset ./dev.py user reset → user_service.reset_password(); a reset link spent by POST /api/v1/auth/password-reset → user_service.complete_password_reset() All of them Deactivation ./dev.py user deactivate → user_service.set_user_active(…, False); PATCH /api/v1/users/{user_id} with is_active: false → user_service.update_user_status() All of them: a later activation does not bring them back Demotion ./dev.py user demote → user_service.set_user_admin(…, False); PATCH /api/v1/users/{user_id} with is_superuser: false → user_service.update_user_status() All of them Sign-out by an administrator POST /api/v1/users/{user_id}/sessions/revoke All of them Setup of the initial administrator A setup link spent by POST /api/v1/auth/setup → bootstrap_admin_service.complete_admin_setup() All of them, though an account waiting for its setup has none: the same response sets a new cookie at the new version, which signs the administrator in

One increment in SQL (lot A8a, backlog A-34, from workstream E's security review). end_sessions() used to add one to the object's own copy (user.session_version += 1): two requests that loaded the same account before either committed — the user changing the password, which re-issues the device's cookie at the new version, and an administrator's «sign out everywhere» — both stored v+1, so the cookie re-issued between them survived the second. It now runs one Core statement on the session's own connection (await session.connection()), UPDATE users SET session_version = session_version + 1 WHERE id = :id RETURNING session_version, and sets the returned value on the object with set_committed_value(): two such requests raise the version by two.

  • Core, not an ORM update(User), which would autoflush first. Nothing is flushed or refreshed: a field the caller already changed, such as a new hash, stays pending for the caller's commit, neither written early nor lost.
  • The version alone does not mark the object changed: it is set as committed, since the statement already wrote it in the transaction. After the caller's commit the object still holds it (the request's session keeps its objects, expire_on_commit=False), so the cookie that change-password re-issues carries the new version.
  • The nine call sites — six in user_service, the change-password route, revoke_account_sessions() in backend/app/api/v1/users.py and complete_admin_setup() in bootstrap_admin_service.py — await it with their own session. A call written in the old shape, end_sessions(user), fails at once with a TypeError.

Activation, promotion, logout and every refused operation leave the version alone: a new password that misses a password rule, wherever it is chosen; a wrong current password, or a new password equal to it, on change-password; a missing or wrong current password, or an address or a username already taken, on PUT /auth/profile; an unknown user; the last active administrator; already an admin or not an admin; the demotion of the initial administrator waiting for its setup (lot A-43, The Setup Link's Lifecycle); a cancellation of its setup link refused with SETUP_COMPLETED (lot A-51); a reset or setup link that is not valid, a link refused because its account was set up before included. So do issuing a reset or setup link, which ends nothing until it is spent, a PATCH whose values equal the current ones, and a profile change that changes no email (a new username, or the stored email sent again, as written or in another A–Z case).

Since lot A-27, the password change, an email change and ./dev.py user reset also revoke the account's live reset links, whoever issued them, in the commit of the change, with token_service.revoke_tokens(…, purpose=AccountTokenPurpose.PASSWORD_RESET) as issuing and spending a link already did: no other purpose (invitations and email-verification links stay; the account's setup links follow their own rule since lot A7b-2, retired by the new password and revoked by the new address: see Revocation), and nothing for a refused change, the same address in another A–Z case or a username alone; what it revokes is logged as Account tokens revoked (count, user_id, purpose), with no address. Otherwise whoever reads the mailbox — the old one, after an email change — could ask for a link through «forgot password» before the change and spend it after, within its 30 minutes (security review of workstream E, E6.9).

A restore sets the version of every account at once, without end_sessions(). The first start on a restored backup (Restoring a Backup), in its step restore-commit, gives every account of the restored database the same version, through sqlite3: max(R, A + 1, B + 1), where R is the restore time in milliseconds, A the largest version of the restored database and B the largest of the database of before (.restore/previous/sqlite/app.db, opened read-only; 0 when it cannot be read or holds no account, as on a new installation). With a clock that is right the value is R: a time, not a counter, which a later end_sessions() still raises by one. Why a time (decision 40): JWT_SECRET is not in the backup and a restore does not change it, so where it is configured a cookie issued before the restore keeps a valid signature. The restored database is another history, where an account's id and version can be those of such a cookie, issued by the database of before or by one an earlier restore replaced; the time is above every version a counter reaches in any of them. The max only matters when the clock is behind a stored value. The value is recorded in the restore's state (session_version). Code: _close_the_way_in() in backend/app/services/platform/instance_backup/apply.py.

  • The token. create_jwt_token(user_id, ttl_hours, session_version) (backend/app/services/accounts/auth_service.py) writes sub (the user id, as a string), sv, iat and exp. decode_jwt_token() returns SessionClaims(user_id, session_version), or None for a token that is expired or badly signed, that has no numeric sub, or whose sv is not an integer — a boolean included: true is not version 1.
  • Cookies issued before session versions. A token without sv is session version 0, the starting value of every account: the upgrade signs nobody out, and the first raise of an account's version ends those cookies like any other.
  • The check. get_current_user() (backend/app/api/v1/auth.py) keeps its checks of the account (User not found, User account is disabled), then refuses a token whose version differs from the account's, behind or ahead, with 401 Session expired or invalid: the answer to an invalid token, so nothing tells the holder why. While an account is deactivated, its cookies get User account is disabled first.
  • The re-issued cookie. Login, password change, email change and the setup of the initial administrator set the cookie through one helper, _issue_session_cookie(): a JWT at the account's current version, lasting session_ttl_hours (24 hours when the setting cannot be read), with the same name and attributes as the login cookie, so the browser replaces the old cookie instead of keeping both.

A request in flight during a password or email change

A request the same device sent with its old cookie, and that reaches the server after the change is committed, gets 401. The frontend's 401 interceptor (frontend/src/lib/api/zodios-client.ts) sends it to the login page (from any page but / and the anonymous pages of a link: A 401 on a Link Page), where the new cookie signs it straight back in. The race is benign, and the code does not try to close it.

Tests: ./dev.py test services session-version (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_session_version.py: the token, the check, the command-line callers and the refusals, in-process; its contract 5, rewritten in lot A8a (A-34): end_sessions() a coroutine function of (session, user), its increment in the caller's transaction at once and committed by the caller only (a fresh connection still reads the old version, a rollback leaves it there), a field set before it left pending for the caller's commit, and two requests that loaded the account before either committed raising the version by two, the cookie re-issued between them refused; its contract 7, the live reset links revoked by reset_password() and by a real address change in update_profile(), the account's setup link retired by the first and revoked by the second (lot A7b-2), every other link left as it was), ./dev.py test api session-revocation (backend/test_scripts/test_api/test_session_revocation_api.py: the password change over HTTP, with two devices and a second account; REVOKE-003 to REVOKE-007, an administrator's reset link revoked by a password or an address change, kept by the own address in other A–Z capitals and by a refused change), and, for the administrator API and the reset links, ./dev.py test api users-admin and ./dev.py test api registration. The email change has its own tests: see Changing the Email. The restore's version: ./dev.py test services backup-apply (the clock behind, a restore on top of another, then a password change that adds one, through the helper of contract 5, _end_sessions_of()).

docs.title: ✉️ Changing the Email
docs.text:
An account's email is a way into it: a password-reset link sent to that address lets whoever reads it choose the password. PUT /api/v1/auth/profile used to change the email on the session cookie alone, so with the self-service «forgot password» (open since lot E4) a moment inside someone else's session — an XSS, a stolen cookie, a computer left unlocked — would become a permanent takeover: change the email, ask for a reset, choose the password (security review of lot E3, rated medium). Since lot A6e (release 1.3), an email change asks for the current password and ends the account's other sessions. No other route changes an account's email; on the server, ./dev.py user set-email does, through the same user_service.update_profile() and without a password (Command-Line Tools, «Change the Email Address of an Account»).

  • What counts as an email change. An email in the body that is another address than the stored one, compared regardless of A–Z case with user_service.same_email(), in the route and in user_service.update_profile() alike (developer decision P18, see USER). A username-only change, or the stored email sent again, needs no password, as before, and a current_password sent beside it is not checked. The stored email in another A–Z case is treated the same way (decision C5): it is the same address, so only its stored form changes — email_verified_at stays, no session ends, no cookie is set. Letters outside A–Z compare as written: Émile@example.com and émile@example.com are two different addresses, and changing one into the other is an email change.
  • The body. UpdateProfileRequest (backend/app/schemas/auth.py) has an optional current_password of at least one character: an empty string is refused with 422.
  • Checked first. The route (update_profile() in backend/app/api/v1/auth.py) checks the password before anything else, uniqueness included, so whoever lacks it cannot probe which addresses are registered. Only the failed sign-in limit comes before, and past it refuses with 429 without checking the password. bcrypt runs in a worker thread (asyncio.to_thread(verify_password, …)), as for the password change.
  • The sessions. user_service.update_profile() calls end_sessions(), revokes the account's live reset links (Session Revocation) and sets users.email_verified_at back to NULL (the new address is not verified, and no flow of release 1.3 verifies a changed one), in the commit of the new address. The route then sets a new session cookie through _issue_session_cookie(), as change-password does: the device that made the change carries on, and every other session gets 401 at its next request. A username-only change ends no session, nor does a refused one.
  • The notice. After a change of address, the route queues workstream E's email_changed_work() with the address read before the change: a notice to that address, after the answer, showing nothing of the new one (decision N62) (An Email Address Changes). It changes neither the answer nor the cookie; with email off, nothing is sent.
  • The log. Neither the route nor user_service.update_profile() writes an address: Profile updated and User profile updated carry user_id, username and email_changed, true only when the address changed (lot A7c, workstream E's rule: no address in any log).
Answer detail When 400 {"error_code": "CURRENT_PASSWORD_REQUIRED", "message": …} An email change without current_password, left out or null 429 {"error_code": "TOO_MANY_ATTEMPTS", "message": …}, with Retry-After An email change with a current_password, while the account's username or the request's address is past the failed sign-in limit: the password is not checked, nothing is written 400 {"error_code": "CURRENT_PASSWORD_INVALID", "message": …} A wrong current_password. Nothing is written, the failure counts toward the failed sign-in limit under the account's username, and the warning Email change refused: wrong current password goes to the log with user_id 400 {"error_code": "USERNAME_INVALID", "message": …} A new username holding @ (rule 1, lot A-21a): the name the account already has is not checked again. After the password when the email changes too. Nothing is written. The route answers the code of the service's refusal, never its wording (Refusals with a code, lot A-47); a length outside 3–50 never gets here, the 422 below comes first 400 Email already registered or Username already taken, plain strings as before, the service's code (EMAIL_TAKEN, USERNAME_TAKEN) left out The password was right, or not needed, but the address belongs to another account, in any A–Z case, or is another account's username, in any A–Z case too (rule 2, lot A-21a), or the name belongs to another account, compared exactly. Nothing is written 422 Validation errors An empty current_password, an invalid email, a username outside 3–50 characters 200 — The change is committed. After an email change, the answer sets the new session cookie, and the log has Email changed, other sessions ended (user_id)

Since lot A8a, a wrong current password here counts toward the failed sign-in limit, under the account's username, as on the password change.

The Profile tab asks for the password in the email row; the user's side is Profile, section «Changing Your Email».

Tests: ./dev.py test api profile (backend/test_scripts/test_api/test_profile_api.py, PROF-010 to PROF-022: the refusals, the taken address not revealed without the password, the sessions with two devices, the username-only and same-email guards, the own address and another account's in another A–Z case, and no address in the log of the route, in-process), ./dev.py test services user-profile (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_user_profile.py, TestUpdateProfileEmailVerification: email_verified_at; UPROF-001 and UPROF-002: no address in the service's log), ./dev.py test services email-case (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_email_case.py: the A–Z rule on the service, the index and the lookups), and for the tab ./dev.py test front-utility component-unit (tabs/ProfileTab.test.ts) and ./dev.py test front-utility settings (frontend/e2e/settings.spec.ts, its «A6e» block).

docs.title: 🔏 Password Rules
docs.text:
The rules a new password must meet are written once, in backend/app/services/accounts/password_policy.py (decision 37, lot A6c, release 1.3), and every way of choosing a password applies them. Before, they were written twice and disagreed: validate_password() in scripts/user_cli.py used Python's str.isupper(), str.islower(), str.isdigit() and a fixed list of ASCII symbols, PasswordStrength.svelte ASCII regular expressions and another list, and the API asked only for 8 characters (min_length=8 in the request schemas).

  • The rules. PASSWORD_RULES, in this order: min_length (value MIN_LENGTH, 8), uppercase, lowercase, digit, special. failed_rules(password) returns the codes of the rules a password misses, in that order; an empty list means it meets them all.
  • Unicode classes. Each class is a Unicode general category (unicodedata.category()): an uppercase letter is Lu, a lowercase one Ll, a digit Nd; a symbol, for special, is any character that is neither a letter (L*), nor a number (N*), nor whitespace. The length counts characters, that is code points. So É is an uppercase letter and é a lowercase one, ٣ (Arabic-Indic three) a digit, € and _ symbols; a space is not a symbol, and ² is a number (No) but not a digit, so it meets neither digit nor special.
  • Stored passwords stay valid. The login never checks the rules: they apply only when a new password is chosen, so an account whose password predates them keeps signing in with it.

Each entry point checks the new password first, as soon as the request body is valid (and, for change-password, the session and the failed sign-in limit):

Entry point Checked before POST /api/v1/auth/register The registration mode, the invitation, the user limit, a username holding @ (Which Account an Identifier Names), and whether the username or the email is taken; for the first account of an empty instance too. A refused registration spends no invitation POST /api/v1/auth/change-password The current password, and the rule that the new one must differ from it POST /api/v1/auth/password-reset (reset links) The link's token: with a weak password the link is not even read, so a valid link stays valid POST /api/v1/auth/setup (setup link of the initial administrator) The link's token, likewise ./dev.py user create, ./dev.py user reset Anything in the database, the username included: validate_password() in scripts/user_cli.py is a thin wrapper over failed_rules()
  • The refusal. The four routes call _refuse_weak_password() (backend/app/api/v1/auth.py), which answers 400 with {"error_code": "PASSWORD_TOO_WEAK", "message": "The password does not meet the password rules", "rules": […]} in detail, rules being the codes missed, in the rules' order. Nothing is written: a refused change or reset leaves the password, the session version and the sessions as they were. The command line prints ❌ Password does not meet security requirements:, then one line per rule missed that starts with its code (_RULE_MESSAGES), such as min_length: the password must be at least 8 characters long, and exits with 1.
  • The schemas. AuthRegisterRequest.password, ChangePasswordRequest.new_password, PasswordResetRequest.new_password and AdminSetupRequest.new_password (backend/app/schemas/auth.py) only require a non-empty string (min_length=1): an empty password is still a 422 of the request validation, not PASSWORD_TOO_WEAK. The length is the policy's rule.
  • Published to the app. password_rules_public() is the list GET /api/v1/system/instance publishes as accounts.password_rules, [{code, value}] (PasswordRuleRead), value being null for every rule but min_length (Public instance configuration). The app draws and checks that list under every new-password field, with the same classes (\p{Lu}, \p{Ll}, \p{Nd}, a symbol [^\p{L}\p{N}\s], the length in code points) in frontend/src/lib/features/auth/passwordRules.ts (PasswordStrength), so a rule changed here reaches the interface without a change of its own. A code the app does not know is not checked there: the server decides.
  • Other passwords, the same rules (lot B4). failed_rules(password, rules=…) and password_rules_public(rules=…) take a list made from these rules instead of PASSWORD_RULES, which they read at each call when rules is None, the default, so a change here reaches every list made from them; without rules, both answer as before. rules_with_minimum_length(n, rules=None) gives those rules with a minimum length of at least n characters: raised, never lowered, the other rules and their order kept (ValueError for n below 1). The password of a secure backup takes the accounts' rules with at least 12 characters (archive_password_rules(), ARCHIVE_PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH, in backend/app/services/platform/instance_backup/secure.py, decision P12): GET /backup/instance/options publishes them in the same [{code, value}] shape (InstanceBackupOptions), and the Backup tab draws them with PasswordStrength through its rules prop, which replaces the instance configuration's list.

Tests: ./dev.py test services password-policy (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_password_policy.py, POLICY-000 to POLICY-006: the published list, the order of failed_rules(), the Unicode classes, the length in code points; B4-RULES-01 to B4-RULES-09: rules= and rules_with_minimum_length()); ./dev.py test api auth (test_api/test_auth_api.py, REG-004, CHPWD-005 and PWD-001 to PWD-008: registration and password change, the new password checked before the current one, a login that never checks); ./dev.py test api registration (test_api/test_registration_api.py, RESET-004, RESET-006, RESET-007 and RULES-001 to RULES-003: the reset link and the invitation left unspent, the order of the checks, the first account, the accounts block); ./dev.py test api admin-setup (test_api/test_admin_setup_api.py, SETUP-006, SETUP-007 and SETUP-011: the setup link left unspent, the password read before the token); ./dev.py test utils dev-cli-image (test_utilities/test_dev_cli_image.py, IMG-031 to IMG-031d: validate_password(), then user create and user reset on a copy of the image's files). The app's half: ./dev.py test front-utility core-unit (passwordRules.test.ts) and ./dev.py test front-utility component-unit (PasswordStrength.test.ts).

docs.title: 🚦 Failed Sign-in Limit
docs.text:
Since lot A8a (release 1.3, F15, decision D-A5), the sign-in counts its failures and stops checking passwords once there are too many, so a password can no longer be guessed at the pace bcrypt allows. The module is backend/app/services/accounts/login_throttle.py. It counts with workstream E's sliding-window limiter (backend/app/utils/runtime/rate_window.py), and keys the address its callers pass with workstream H's client_rate_key() (The Client's Address): at the routes of auth.py, rate_limit_address(request), None behind a local proxy nobody trusts (decision N70), where only the identifier's limit applies.

Limiter Key Limit LOGIN_BY_IDENTIFIER identifier_key(identifier): what was typed in the identifier field, stripped, with A–Z folded and nothing else (user_service.email_fold(), decision P18), whether an account matches it or not. " Alice ", "ALICE" and "alice" share one key; "Émile" and "émile" do not 10 failures in 15 minutes (WINDOW_SECONDS) LOGIN_BY_ADDRESS client_rate_key(address): an IPv4 address whole, an IPv6 one by its /64 50 failures in 15 minutes Function Contract refusal(identifier, address) -> RateDecision \| None None while both limits allow one more failure; otherwise the refusing decision (allowed false, remaining 0), the longer retry_after when both refuse. It only looks (peek()): no call counts. Without an address (None: rate_limit_address() gives it behind a proxy nobody trusts, client_address() for a connection without one) only the identifier's limit applies record_failure(identifier, address) One failure in each limit (hit()), the address's only with an address record_success(identifier) Forgets the identifier's failures (reset()); the address keeps its own identifier_key(identifier) The identifier's key, as above

The functions read the two limiters from the module when they run, so a test puts limiters of its own in their place (monkeypatch.setattr). Four checks of a password call them: three routes of backend/app/api/v1/auth.py, with the address rate_limit_address(http_request) gives, and workstream E's «send the link again» (resend_verification() in backend/app/services/email/verification.py, for POST /email/verification/resend), with the same rate_limit_address(request), which its route in backend/app/api/v1/email.py reads (lot E-13).

Route Before the password is checked A wrong password The right password POST /auth/login _refuse_too_many_failures(request.username, address), before the account is looked up record_failure(request.username, address), then 401 Invalid credentials, an unknown identifier included record_success(request.username), once the cookie is set. The 403s of an inactive account, ACCOUNT_DISABLED and EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED, which only the right password gets, neither count nor reset POST /auth/change-password _refuse_too_many_failures(current_user.username, address), before _refuse_weak_password() record_failure(current_user.username, address), then 400 Current password is incorrect record_success(current_user.username) PUT /auth/profile, when the email changes _refuse_too_many_failures(current_user.username, address), after the 400 CURRENT_PASSWORD_REQUIRED record_failure(current_user.username, address), then 400 CURRENT_PASSWORD_INVALID record_success(current_user.username) POST /email/verification/resend refusal(identifier, address), identifier being the body's username as typed, after E's per-address counter (delivery.ADDRESS_BUDGET, shared with the registrations and «forgot password») and before the account is looked up: EmailRateLimitedError with its wait record_failure(identifier, address), then 401 Invalid credentials, an unknown identifier included record_success(identifier), as soon as the password is checked, before the account's state is read: whatever follows resets, the 409 EMAIL_VERIFICATION_NOT_NEEDED of an active account and the 403 ACCOUNT_DISABLED included
  • The refusal. _refuse_too_many_failures() answers 429 with {"error_code": "TOO_MANY_ATTEMPTS", "message": "Too many failed attempts: try again later"} in detail and Retry-After, the wait of refusal() in whole seconds, rounded up, at least 1. No bcrypt runs and, at the sign-in, no account is looked up: the same answer, at the same cost, whether an account matches or not. It writes no log line of its own. The resend answers with its other limits' 429 instead, EMAIL_RATE_LIMITED with retry_after in detail and the same Retry-After header, so its page words it as it words them.
  • A refused attempt is not counted: it never reaches record_failure(), so knocking does not push the unlock away, and Retry-After seconds later the right password signs in.
  • One account, two keys. The identifier counts as typed: an account's username and its email are two keys, so alternating them gives about 20 guesses per account every 15 minutes, still under the address's 50.
  • The other checks of the current password count under the account's username, the key of a sign-in typed with it, and under the address rate_limit_address() gives, as at the sign-in: 10 wrong current passwords also lock the sign-in by username, and failed sign-ins by username lock the password change and the email change. Deleting one's own account (DELETE /auth/users/me) asks for no password: nothing to limit.
  • Not limited, on purpose (the coordinator's decision, backlog A-41): a wrong token of an invitation, reset or setup link (tokens/inspect, password-reset, setup, an invite_token at the registration). The tokens LibreFolio draws are 256 random bits (Single-use Account Tokens), out of reach of guessing, and a limit per address would refuse every user behind one NAT. «Forgot password» checks no password and keeps workstream E's own limits (A Forgotten Password).
  • «Send the link again» shares the sign-in's counts (lot A8a; the coordinator's decision, reviewed by workstream E). It checks the sign-in's credentials without a session, so with only E's per-address limit it was a way to try passwords past the identifier's limit. It now counts under the sign-in's own two keys, the identifier as typed and the address, both ways: wrong passwords at the resend lock the sign-in, and failed sign-ins refuse the resend before its password is checked. Unlike the sign-in, whose 403s neither count nor reset, the right password resets the identifier at once, as the password change and the email change do. E's own limits stay (Sending the Link Again); delivery.ADDRESS_BUDGET is only looked at first, and counts the email that goes, never a try. Its address is the rate_limit_address() its route reads since lot E-13, as at the sign-in: behind a local proxy nobody trusts neither delivery.ADDRESS_BUDGET nor the sign-in's address count the request, and the resend and the sign-in share the identifier's count alone.
  • The switch. login_limit_enabled() (backend/app/config/accounts.py) reads LIBREFOLIO_LOGIN_LIMIT at each call, through login_limit_value(): the value as set, stripped, or None when it is unset or blank. Unset, blank or on in any case, on; off in any case, off, and then refusal() answers None and record_failure() records nothing. Any other value, 1, true and yes included, raises ValueError naming the variable and the stripped value: LIBREFOLIO_LOGIN_LIMIT='maybe': expected on or off. log_configuration_audit() calls it right after admin_bootstrap_config(), so such a value stops the start; while the limit is off, every start logs the warning of the check accounts.login_limit (Configuration Checks).
  • The test lanes run with it off: their suites sign in wrongly on purpose, from one address, against shared accounts. dev.py server --test sets LIBREFOLIO_LOGIN_LIMIT=off in the environment of the lane's server, after configure_test_runtime() has dropped every LIBREFOLIO_* of .env and of the shell: the lane's server always runs with the limit off (Test lanes and the instance's configuration). backend/test_scripts/conftest.py sets it in every pytest process too, since the in-process apps of many test files share one process and its two limiters. It sets it at import with os.environ.setdefault() (a value already in that process's environment wins), and an autouse fixture puts that value back before each test that no longer has it: configure_test_runtime(), which setup_test_database() reaches when a test module is imported, removes it at collection. The limit's own tests turn it on, or remove it, with monkeypatch after that fixture, on limiters of their own.
  • Per process, in memory. A restart forgets every count, and with N worker processes (dev.py server --workers N) each keeps its own, so the limits are N times these; the Docker image runs one worker. Each limiter holds at most 10,000 keys (the limiter's max_keys): a new key beyond them evicts the key with the fewest failures still in the window, the one used or regrouped longest ago among them (The Sliding-Window Limiter, lot E-14). So a spray of fresh identifiers, one failure each, never pushes out an identifier with more failures, locked or one short of the lock, and behind a proxy nobody trusts no limit per address slows such a spray. To push out an identifier with n failures, every other key must hold n failures too: about 90,000 failures within 15 minutes buy 9 more guesses. The eviction of decision N70 (the first key not full among the 32 least recently used) spared only locked identifiers: one stopped a failure short of the lock went for 10,000 fresh ones, as with plain least-recently-used eviction.
  • Behind a reverse proxy the address must be the visitor's (The Client's Address). Behind one that LibreFolio does not trust, every visitor has the proxy's address: counted together, 50 failures from anyone, at about one a second, would refuse every sign-in through it, the right password included (security review R13-SEC6). So the three routes of auth.py pass rate_limit_address() (decision N70): None, decided per request, for a request from a local peer that carries a forwarding header neither uvicorn nor LIBREFOLIO_CLIENT_IP_HEADER applied (Behind a Proxy Nobody Trusts), which is then counted and refused by its identifier alone. None is no key here: the limiter would count it like any other, so refusal() and record_failure() leave the address out rather than count every «no address» together. The warning logged once per process, UNTRUSTED_PROXY_SUMMARY, and the notes behind the check platform.client_address are workstream H's: both come from forwarded_by_untrusted_proxy(), which rate_limit_address() calls.
  • A public peer's forwarding headers change nothing: a client on the internet cannot switch its own limit per address off by adding one. Behind a proxy on a public address that LibreFolio does not trust (a CDN left unconfigured), every visitor still shares its address and its 50 failures, until FORWARDED_ALLOW_IPS or LIBREFOLIO_CLIENT_IP_HEADER gives LibreFolio the visitor's.

The login page already turns any 429 of the sign-in into auth.tooManyAttempts (loginErrorKey() in frontend/src/lib/stores/app/auth.ts, see LoginCard), and the verification notice words the resend's EMAIL_RATE_LIMITED with the minutes to wait, as before (resendFailureMessage(), In the Frontend). Since lot A8b (C11), the password-change modal and the Profile tab word it too, as settings.tooManyPasswordAttempts (Too many wrong passwords: wait a few minutes and try again.): the modal for a 429 whose detail.error_code is TOO_MANY_ATTEMPTS, keeping its three fields; the tab for that code, published as data-error-code, keeping the new address and the typed password (ProfileTab). While the limit is off, the «Security» tab of Settings › Administration lists the warning of accounts.login_limit and counts it in its badge. The administrator's side is Configuration, section «Failed Sign-ins».

Tests: ./dev.py test services login-throttle (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_login_throttle.py: the two limits on an injected clock, the A–Z key, the IPv6 /64, no address and no shared count of «no address», a refusal not counted, a success that forgets the identifier only, the longer wait, the switch off), ./dev.py test services accounts-checks (test_services/test_accounts_checks.py: login_limit_enabled() on, off and invalid, the check accounts.login_limit in CONFIG_CHECKS, the startup audit stopping on an invalid value before it logs any check, the import orders in fresh interpreters), ./dev.py test api login-throttle (test_api/test_login_throttle_api.py: pure, in-process apps on private SQLite files, the limit turned on with limiters of its own on a fake clock: the 429 with an exact Retry-After before any bcrypt, the same for an unknown identifier, per address, the password change and the email change under the account's username, the switch; «send the link again»: wrong resends lock the sign-in, failed sign-ins refuse the resend before its password, the right password at the resend resets the identifier, a wrong resend counts on the address; GET /security/checks; and, behind a local proxy nobody trusts (N70, section 8, TestUntrustedLocalProxy, LT-API-20…25): from lan, loopback and CGNAT (vpn) peers forwarding X-Forwarded-For, Forwarded or X-Real-IP, fifty failures lock nobody else out while the identifier's lock holds; a public peer with the same headers, and a local peer without them, keep the lock per address; at each of the three routes, a wrong password through the proxy counts on the identifier alone, and an address its own failures locked refuses its direct requests but not those the proxy forwards), ./dev.py test utils rate-window (RWL-024: a locked identifier stays locked through 1,000 fresh ones, see The Sliding-Window Limiter), and ./dev.py test api security-checks (test_api/test_security_checks_api.py, on the lane's server, where accounts.login_limit is a warning since the lane runs with the limit off). The frontend's words for the limit: ./dev.py test front-utility component-unit (PasswordChangeModal.test.ts and tabs/ProfileTab.test.ts, both under frontend/src/lib/features/settings/).

  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \

docs.title: 📄 Secrets from Files
docs.text:
Every secret of LibreFolio is read by env_secret(name) in backend/app/config/__init__.py: today JWT_SECRET, LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY, LIBREFOLIO_WEB_LINK_FINDER_API_KEY, LIBREFOLIO_SMTP_PASSWORD, LIBREFOLIO_BACKUP_DOWNLOAD_TOKEN, LIBREFOLIO_WAKE_TOKEN, LIBREFOLIO_PANEL_STATUS_TOKEN, LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN, and every variable of the plugin settings, secret or not (plugin_setting_env() in backend/app/config/plugins.py: the derived LIBREFOLIO_PLUGIN_* names and the aliases of secret fields, see Plugin Settings). In this order:

  1. NAME, when not blank, is the secret as written, spaces included;
  2. otherwise NAME_FILE, when not blank, is the path of a file that holds it, as Docker and Kubernetes mount their secrets (/run/secrets/…). ~ is expanded, and a relative path starts from the project root. The secret is the file's text without a leading UTF-8 byte order mark, which some Windows editors add, and without its trailing line breaks (decode("utf-8-sig").rstrip("\r\n")): any other space counts;
  3. otherwise there is no secret: None.

Blank means empty or whitespace only: a value that str.strip() empties counts as not set, so a stray space is never used as a key.

read_secret_file() raises SecretFileError when the file is missing, cannot be read, is larger than 64 KiB (SECRET_FILE_MAX_BYTES), is not UTF-8 text or is empty or blank (… is empty or blank). The message names the variable and the path, never the content. Like every variable outside the Settings class, both forms come from the process environment only, never from .env directly: ./dev.py and the env_file: of Compose put .env there. For messages, env_secret_origin(name) names the source without reading the file: NAME, NAME_FILE (<path>) or None (configured_jwt_secret_origin() and configured_instance_key_origin() in platform.py).

The caller decides what a SecretFileError means. A broken JWT_SECRET_FILE or LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY_FILE stops the start (JWT Secret, Configuration Checks), and so does a broken LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN_FILE: admin_bootstrap_config() reads it in the startup audit, whatever the other variables of the initial administrator. A broken LIBREFOLIO_WEB_LINK_FINDER_API_KEY_FILE does not: web_link_finder_api_key() in backend/app/config/plugins.py reads it only when a search builds the apikey engine, and _build_engine() in backend/app/services/assets/web_link_finder.py then logs web_link_finder: <error>; disabling and returns no engine, so that search finds no links. Nor does a broken LIBREFOLIO_SMTP_PASSWORD_FILE: email is optional, so email_config_state() turns it off instead, with the problem SMTP_PASSWORD_UNREADABLE, which is logged at startup and shown to administrators in Settings › Administration › Email (Email Service). Nor does an unusable LIBREFOLIO_BACKUP_DOWNLOAD_TOKEN: backup_download_token() in backend/app/config/backup.py reads it for the startup checks (check_panel_token(), backup.panel_token: one error line in the start log, never a stop; Configuration Checks of the Backup) and at each call of the hosting panel's routes, so the server starts anyway. Besides the SecretFileError of a broken _FILE, it raises BackupConfigError for a token with anything but visible ASCII characters, spaces included (BACKUP_DOWNLOAD_TOKEN_NOT_VISIBLE_ASCII), or shorter than 32 characters (BACKUP_DOWNLOAD_TOKEN_TOO_SHORT). The hosting panel's access, panel_access(PanelScope.BACKUP) (The Hosting Panel's Access), turns either into 503 with the code backup_panel_unavailable, on every panel route, and logs one error line per refused call, The hosting panel's backup token cannot be used: its routes refuse every request, whose error names the variable, and the path of a file, never the token. Nor does an unusable LIBREFOLIO_WAKE_TOKEN or LIBREFOLIO_PANEL_STATUS_TOKEN: wake_token() in backend/app/config/sleep_wake.py and panel_status_token() in backend/app/config/hosting_panel.py follow the rules of the backup token, with SleepWakeConfigError and HostingPanelConfigError (WAKE_TOKEN_… and PANEL_STATUS_TOKEN_…, _NOT_VISIBLE_ASCII or _TOO_SHORT). The startup check platform.hosting_panel reads both (Configuration Checks), and panel_access() reads each at every call of its route, POST /system/wake-sync or GET /panel/status, which then answers 503 with the code wake_unavailable or panel_status_unavailable. Nor does a _FILE of a plugin setting that cannot give its value: the field gets the problem invalid_env, and the plugin is not configured until the variable is fixed (Plugin Settings).

When NAME and NAME_FILE are both set, neither blank, NAME wins. secrets_set_twice() lists those names for the configuration checks. It covers JWT_SECRET and every LIBREFOLIO_* variable, so a new secret named LIBREFOLIO_* and read with env_secret() needs no list to update.

Test lanes never inherit the secrets that make the instance trust a session or decrypt its data. configure_test_runtime() in scripts/cli_base.py, which every test entry point goes through (dev.py test, and dev.py server --test, which the webServer of Playwright also runs), removes JWT_SECRET, JWT_SECRET_FILE, LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY and LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY_FILE (INSTANCE_TRUST_SECRETS in backend/app/config/__init__.py) from its environment, whether they come from the shell or from .env. A test lane therefore signs sessions with a key made for its run and derives keys from an instance key generated in its own data directory.

docs.title: Test lanes and the instance's configuration
docs.text:
The same rule covers the rest of the instance's configuration: a test lane runs on the defaults, so a setting of the developer's install (a mail server, the managed profile, an instance block, account limits) can neither reach the tests nor change their outcome.

  • configure_test_runtime() removes, whatever their origin (.env, loaded by pipenv run before dev.py starts, or the shell): every variable .env.example documents (documented_instance_variables()), every LIBREFOLIO_* name in the environment and the secrets above. Keys of .env that are not LibreFolio's (a proxy, PYTHONPATH) stay.
  • It keeps only what kept_in_a_test_lane() keeps: TEST_LANE_KEEPS (the two ports, the production data directory it must stay away from, HOST, the log level, LF_APP_VERSION frozen by a release job for its gallery, and Playwright's LIBREFOLIO_SERVER_WORKERS) and every LIBREFOLIO_TEST_* name, the runner's and the tests' own (data directory, mode, the lane's readiness token, startup timeout).
  • In test mode Settings does not read .env at all (settings_customise_sources), so a setting removed from the environment does not come back from the file.
  • A new variable is covered without a list to update: it is named LIBREFOLIO_* or documented in .env.example (a test requires it). A test that needs a setting sets it in its own process, after any helper that configures the lane (setup_test_database() and its siblings call configure_test_runtime(), which would remove it again).
  • One setting is the lanes' own, on purpose: the failed sign-in limit is off, since the suites sign in wrongly on purpose. dev.py server --test sets LIBREFOLIO_LOGIN_LIMIT=off for the lane's server after the cleanup. backend/test_scripts/conftest.py sets it in every pytest process that does not have it already, and puts it back before each test that lost it: set once at import, it did not survive the modules that configure the lane at collection, and in a combined run the limit was on for every test. The same line sets LIBREFOLIO_PROBE_RATE_LIMIT=0: the per-user limit of the provider probe is off on the lane's server, whose E2E suites probe many times as one user; its own tests build their limiters in-process.
  • Three settings a lane may set itself, on its command line: --lane-setting NAME=VALUE (lot H-43) takes LIBREFOLIO_PROFILE, LIBREFOLIO_FRAME_PROTECTION and LIBREFOLIO_CSP_REPORT_ONLY (TEST_LANE_SETTABLE), none of them a secret, so that a suite can run on the managed profile. configure_test_runtime() sets them after the cleanup and hands them down in LIBREFOLIO_TEST_LANE_SETTINGS, under the kept LIBREFOLIO_TEST_* prefix. That variable is the runner's alone: found in .env, it stops the lane with an error, under pipenv run too. See Lane Settings.

docs.title: 🧬 Instance Key
docs.text:
One secret per installation, from which LibreFolio derives its encryption keys (backend/app/services/platform/instance_key.py). Consumers never read the key itself: each one asks for a key derived for its own purpose. The key comes from the first of these sources that is set:

  1. LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY, then LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY_FILE: configured_instance_key() in backend/app/config/platform.py, which returns env_secret("LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY");
  2. <data directory>/secrets/instance.key (instance_key_path()), generated on first use.

A key is a text of at least 32 characters (INSTANCE_KEY_MIN_LENGTH), and its UTF-8 bytes are the input of the derivation. The length is the only check: a key set by the administrator must be random, such as secrets.token_urlsafe(32), not a passphrase, because the derived keys are only as strong as it is.

Function Contract derive_key(purpose: str, length: int = 32) -> bytes HKDF-SHA256 (RFC 5869, hkdf_sha256() on the standard-library hmac and hashlib) over the key's UTF-8 bytes, with a fixed salt (_DERIVATION_SALT) and info = purpose.encode("ascii") + b"\x00" + length.to_bytes(2, "big"). The length is part of the derivation: the same purpose at two lengths gives two unrelated keys, never a key and its prefix. The same purpose and length get the same bytes while the instance key stays the same; two purposes never get the same key. length goes from 1 to 8160 bytes. purpose and length are validated first: an invalid one raises ValueError before the key is read or generated. Otherwise, without a configured key, the first call generates the key file. Raises InstanceKeyError when the key cannot be used. derive_key_from(key: str, purpose: str, length: int = 32) -> bytes The key that derive_key(purpose, length) gives on an instance whose instance key is key: the same HKDF-SHA256, salt and info. It reads neither the environment nor the data directory and never creates the key file. Checked in this order: purpose and length (ValueError, the rules of derive_key()), then the type of key (TypeError for anything but a str), then its length (InstanceKeyError under INSTANCE_KEY_MIN_LENGTH, 32 characters). No message holds the key. instance_key_status() -> InstanceKeyStatus The state, without creating the key file and without raising: source (configured; generated when something is at the key file's path, a link that leads nowhere included, or when its folder cannot be searched; not_created), problem (why the key cannot be used, None when it can), path, and loose_modes, the octal modes of the folder and the file when group or others have any access to the generated key (always empty on Windows). instance_key_path() -> Path get_data_dir() / "secrets" / "instance.key": the test data directory in test mode.

purpose names the use and its version, such as plugins.settings.v1: lowercase letters, digits and . _ : -, starting with a letter or a digit, at most 128 characters.

derive_key() and derive_key_from() validate and derive through the same private helpers (_check_purpose_and_length(), then _derive()), so the two cannot drift. derive_key_from() is for a key that is not this instance's. Its caller is the check of a restore (lot B4, _plugin_secrets() in backend/app/services/platform/instance_backup/staging.py), which re-encrypts the plugin secrets that a backup's instance encrypted with its own key. A clear archive leaves that key out; a password-protected one carries it when LibreFolio generated it (decision 39), as the entry secrets/instance.key, read into memory and never unpacked (Secure Backups). The check derives the archive's subkey with derive_key_from(archive_key, SUBKEY_PURPOSE, SUBKEY_LENGTH) (plugins.settings.v1, 32 bytes) and gives it, with this instance's subkey (settings_subkey()), to rekey_plugin_secrets(conn, old_subkey, new_subkey) in backend/app/services/plugin_settings/crypto.py, on a connection to the copy's database. It derives this instance's subkey only when the copy holds secrets, so the check of an archive without any never generates the key file. Without a key, the archive's or one given for the restore (below), or with an archive's key that derive_key_from() refuses, it only counts the secrets this instance cannot read (count_unreadable_secrets()).

A key the administrator kept, such as a copy of the old secrets/instance.key, reaches the restore from the command line only (lot B-18): dev.py backup restore --instance-key-file FILE. An upload from the app never brings one: RestoreStageRequest holds only upload_id and password, and the check it starts calls stage_archive() without instance_key (restore_jobs._run_check()); instance_key_invalid, below, is one of RestoreErrorCode only because that list holds every code stage_archive() can raise. The command reads the file before it switches to the data directory's owner, so that, started as root (docker compose exec), it reads a Docker secret only root can read; read as root, the file must be a regular file, reached through no link inside the data directory (lot B-38, the bullet «Secret files read as root» of Secure Backups). stage_archive(..., instance_key=…) checks the key before anything else, before the lock, any folder or the archive (_refuse_unusable_instance_key()). A key derive_key_from() cannot use, that is a text shorter than INSTANCE_KEY_MIN_LENGTH (32 characters, the one rule it holds a key's text to), is StagingError instance_key_invalid, «The instance key given is too short: an instance key has at least 32 characters», a message without the key or its length. A key long enough but not the old instance's is no error: the secrets it should open stay counted as unreadable, and the command warns that it reads none of them (decision D2). When the archive carries its own key, the entry secrets/instance.key, that key wins over the one given (decision D1, _stage()), and the command says that it does not use the file. Tests: section (i) of ./dev.py test services backup-secure and the B-18 cases of ./dev.py test utils backup-cli-restore; the administrator's side is «The Instance Key of Another Installation» in Command-Line Tools.

The generated file (_create_key_file()):

  • Content: secrets.token_urlsafe(32) and a newline, that is 32 random bytes in base64url: 43 characters, 44 bytes on disk.
  • Permissions: the secrets/ folder is created with mode 0700; the file is 0600, as mkstemp() creates it (or the O_EXCL fallback below).
  • One key wins: the key is written to a temporary file (mkstemp()) in the same folder, flushed and fsynced, then published with os.link(), which fails when instance.key already exists. Of several workers starting together, the first key published stays, and readers never see half a key. On a filesystem without hard links, an exclusive create (O_CREAT | O_EXCL) still lets only one key in; there the file appears before its content, so a reader that finds it unusable retries for up to half a second (_read_generated_key(): 10 reads, 50 ms apart). The temporary file is always removed, and the folder is fsynced where the platform allows it.
  • Never replaced: _key_file_present() looks at the path with lstat(), so anything there, a link that leads nowhere included, counts as the key file. A key file that is empty or blank, too short or unreadable raises InstanceKeyError, which asks to restore it from a backup: a new key could not read what the old one encrypted. A secrets/ folder that cannot be searched (another owner, mode 0000) raises InstanceKeyError too (<path>: the instance key cannot be reached (Permission denied)): the key may be there, so it is neither generated again nor reported as missing. So does a key file that cannot be created.
  • Created on use only: ensure_data_dirs() does not create secrets/, and instance_key_status() only reads, so the file appears with the first derive_key() call.
  • Test isolation: validate_test_data_dir() treats secrets/ and secrets/instance.key as managed paths: a test lane may not alias the production ones.

A lost key file still looks like a first use: a new key is generated, and nothing the old one encrypted can be read with it. The plugin settings, whose secrets are the only data stored encrypted under the instance key today, make the change visible: each row records the key_id of the key that encrypted it, and from the first start after the change the startup step plugin-secrets-check logs an error that counts the stored system secrets the current key cannot read, if there are any (Plugin Secrets Check). The administrator puts back secrets/instance.key from their copy of the data directory (a clear archive of the instance backup leaves the key out; a password-protected one carries the generated key, and its restore re-encrypts the secrets with this instance's: Secure Backups), or enters the secrets again. The order matters: saving a secret rewrites its row's secret_ciphertext and key_id under the current key (_apply() in backend/app/services/plugin_settings/service.py), so an old key brought back afterwards reads again the rows never entered again, but not the ones entered under the new key; the old key therefore goes back first (LibreFolio stopped, the copy in place of the generated file), before anyone enters a secret again, and the secrets are entered again only when no copy exists.

Tests: ./dev.py test services config-secrets (env_secret()) and ./dev.py test services config-instance-key, whose section (g) pins derive_key_from() to three known answers computed with derive_key() before the two shared their helpers. What the administrator sees and does is in Configuration, section «The Instance Key».

docs.title: 🔏 The Key Check (D6)
docs.text:
A key that is valid but not the one the data was written with starts the instance all the same: the plugin secrets stop reading, and the log says so only when some are stored. The hosting panel needs to know it before its nightly backup pushes a good copy out of the ones it keeps (contract L3, D6; lot H5-7, developer decision 26/10/2026). backend/app/services/platform/instance_key_check.py, workstream H:

  • The reference is secrets/instance.key.check in the data directory (KEY_CHECK_FILE, folder 0700, file 0600): the 64 hex characters of key_check_value(), an HMAC-SHA256 of a fixed label with derive_key("instance.key-check.v1"). Not the key, not a derived key that anything else uses. The folder is not in the backup (ARCHIVED_FOLDERS), and a restore re-encrypts the secrets with this instance's key, so a restore never moves it.
  • instance_key_state(session) -> "ok" | "mismatch" is evaluated at every call (nothing is kept in the process: a value read once at the start stays old, the lesson of the owner's guard, lot H5-5) and never raises. A key that is not created yet, or cannot be used, is ok (nothing to compare; this never generates the key). With the file: equal is ok, different is mismatch; a file that cannot be read or is not 64 hex characters is ok and one warning per process, because a broken file must not stop the backups. Without the file, the stored secrets decide (R1): mismatch only when there is at least one row with a secret, in either plugin table, and the key_id of every one is not the current key's; one readable row, or none, is ok.
  • The start, step instance-key-check right before plugin-secrets-check (which keeps its place right before stored-currencies), no skip_when, never raises (check_instance_key_at_start()): the file absent and the state ok writes it (exclusive create: of several workers the first wins); absent and mismatch writes nothing and logs an error, since writing would bless the wrong key; present and mismatch logs an error and rewrites nothing.
  • LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY_ACCEPT (instance_key_accept() in config/platform.py, the values of awaiting_restore(); one that cannot be read stops the start, in log_configuration_audit()) replaces the file with the current key's value, atomically, and logs a warning at every start while it is set. It is the only way to make a changed key ok without the old one.
  • Where it shows: PanelStatusResponse.instance_key (the panel's status, a required key, eight in all); start_panel_backup answers 409 backup_instance_key_mismatch through a dependency declared after the panel's credential, so a caller without one learns nothing (backup_awaiting_restore keeps its own answer first); _wake_run() answers the status instance_key_mismatch and runs no job; GET /security/checks adds platform.instance_key_check (error, instance.checks.instanceKey.mismatch; not the platform.instance_key check of an unusable key or loose permissions). The instance keeps serving: no 423, no page, nothing in GET /system/instance. The panel's other backup routes and its restore are not stopped.

Tests: ./dev.py test services instance-key-check and ./dev.py test api instance-key-check. The administrator's side is «The Key Check» in Configuration.

docs.title: 🔐 Secure Backups (.lfbk)
docs.text:
A secure backup (lot B4: decisions 38 and 39, P12) is the zip of a clear backup encrypted with a password its maker chooses, in an envelope of LibreFolio's own, .lfbk, made of standard pieces of cryptography: scrypt and AES-256-GCM. Decision 38 ruled out a password-protected zip, which only some tools open (7-Zip, Keka) and whose key derivation is weak. Without a password the backup is the plain zip, as before. The hosting panel's routes never take a password: they hand out a plain zip, or, with LIBREFOLIO_BACKUP_RECIPIENTS, a sealed backup, an .lfbk whose random password is encrypted for the provider's key. The format is backend/app/services/platform/instance_backup/envelope.py; what the administrator sees is Secure Backups.

The header: 52 bytes, big-endian (struct format >4sBBBBB16s16sI7s), the associated data of every chunk.

Bytes Field Written Accepted when read 0–3 Magic LFBK (MAGIC) Only LFBK, and 52 bytes at least: otherwise envelope_damaged 4 Format version 1 (FORMAT_VERSION) 1: otherwise envelope_unsupported 5 KDF id 1, scrypt (KDF_SCRYPT) 1: otherwise envelope_unsupported 6 log2(n) 15 (LOG2_N) 14 to 16 7 r 8 (R) 1 to 8 8 p 1 (P) 1 to 2 9–24 Salt 16 random bytes Any 25–40 Check value Bytes 32–47 of the derivation Compared in constant time 41–44 Chunk size (u32) 1 << 20, 1 MiB (CHUNK_SIZE) 64 KiB to 16 MiB 45–51 Nonce prefix 7 random bytes Any
  • Bounds before any derivation. EnvelopeHeader.from_bytes(), behind read_header() and unlock(), checks the header before scrypt runs: a cost or a chunk size outside the bounds is envelope_unsupported. A hostile or newer header so never makes a reader spend more than 64 MiB (128 · r · 2^log2(n), twice what is written) or work for minutes: one that asks log2(n) = 30 is refused in milliseconds. encrypt_file() checks the header it writes against the same bounds.
  • The key. Scrypt(salt, length=48, n=2**log2_n, r, p) of cryptography, on unicodedata.normalize("NFC", password).encode("utf-8"): a password typed with a composed or a decomposed accent gives one key (NFC, not NFKC). Bytes 0–31 are the AES-256 key, bytes 32–47 the check value, kept in the header and compared with hmac.compare_digest(): a wrong password is told at once, before any chunk is read (wrong_password). The written cost takes 32 MiB and about a tenth of a second, once per backup and once per check (P12: a small machine's memory). By design, a changed salt, cost or check value reads as wrong_password too.
  • The chunks (STREAM). The archive is cut into chunks of chunk_size bytes, at least one; the last one holds the rest, empty only for an empty file, and a size that is a multiple of the chunk size ends on a full chunk. Each chunk is sealed with AESGCM(key).encrypt(nonce, chunk, header), the chunk and its 16-byte tag, written in order after the header. The 12-byte nonce is the prefix (7 bytes), the chunk's counter (u32, big-endian, from 0) and a flag, 0x01 on the last chunk and 0x00 on the others. Every tampering makes a tag fail, envelope_damaged: a changed byte or tag; two chunks swapped; a chunk dropped, repeated or appended after the last; a file cut at or inside a chunk (the chunk now last was not sealed as last, or is shorter than a tag); a chunk size or a nonce prefix changed in the header. decrypt_file() also compares the first 52 bytes of the file with the header unlock() read, so a file replaced in between is refused before its first chunk.
  • The files. encrypt_file() and decrypt_file() stream with constant memory and write through <name>.part in the output's folder (_NewFile): created exclusively (O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW), mode 0600, fsynced, renamed onto the final name, the folder fsynced. An output that already exists is FileExistsError, and nothing is written; on any failure the .part is removed and the output does not exist. The salt and the prefix come from secrets.token_bytes(), so two encryptions of one archive differ; the salt, nonce_prefix and log2_n keywords of encrypt_file() are for tests. encrypt_file() returns the envelope's size and SHA-256 (EncryptedFile).
  • The codes. EnvelopeError.code is wrong_password, envelope_damaged or envelope_unsupported; the messages hold no path and no secret.

The start (job_views.start_job(), for POST /backup/instance and the hosting panel's POST /backup/panel/jobs alike). jobs.start_backup() creates the job's folder and its first state before the thread runs: a full disk or quota there (jobs.out_of_space()) answers 507 backup_no_space, Not enough free space to start the backup, logged as a warning, Instance backup could not start: not enough free space (lot B-30). Another backup running stays 409 backup_busy, and any other failure 500 backup_folder_unusable or backup_failed. The backup_busy detail names the running backup, job_id and origin, to a caller that can read it: the Backup tab always, the hosting panel only a backup of its own (lot B-8). A run records its job id in the lock it holds (backups/.jobs/.lock, its content), once its first state is written; a refused start reads it back, never through a link, and names the job only while its state says it runs. A clear start of the tab follows a backup of its own kind (ui) whose start answer was lost, and offers it only if it ends clear; it keeps that adoption across a reload (librefolio.backup.adopted). The backup the tab already follows by itself (its own, started there) is followed as its own, never adopted: its end is offered whatever its mode. A secure start never follows one: a job records no user, so nothing tells whether that backup carries this password (defect of the automatic review, 19/10). One of the command line or of the panel is never followed. The tab does not name the backup that runs; the answer does (developer, 19/10). Whatever its origin, the card says only that another backup runs, or follows its own, and never shows the job's id or origin. The tab writes them to the browser console instead, with the state, running: one console.warn per refused start (backupJob.svelte.ts), whatever the log level. None of the three is personal data.

The creation (jobs._run()). With a password, build_archive() writes the zip as for a clear backup, in the job's folder backups/.jobs/<id>/ (0700, the zip 0600), with the instance key entry when there is one to carry (below). _encrypt() then checks the free space for the envelope (the zip's size plus 64 MiB, or backup_no_space), reports the phase encrypting (done_bytes of total_bytes: the zip's bytes) and writes librefolio-backup-<UTC>.lfbk beside it. The job records encrypted: true and the envelope's name, size and SHA-256 (InstanceBackupJob); _remove_work_files() removes the clear zip with the other work files, on success as on failure. A run killed outright (a power cut, kill -9) removes nothing: the next read of its job, or the next start, ends it and removes them (What a Run Killed Outright Leaves).

The password's life.

  • In the API. InstanceBackupRequest.password (POST /backup/instance) and RestoreStageRequest.password (POST /backup/restore/stage) are SecretStr | None, max_length=1024, in models with extra="forbid"; no body, {} or {"password": null} is a clear backup, as before. Both routers use NoInputEchoRoute (backend/app/api/no_echo.py, moved out of the plugin settings router, which imports it): a 422 keeps type, loc, msg and ctx, and drops input, which for a missing field is the whole body, the password beside it included.
  • At the creation. POST /backup/instance checks archive_password_problems() first: a password that misses a rule answers 400 with {"code": "password_too_weak", "message": …, "rules": […]} in detail, rules being the codes missed in the rules' order, and no job starts. GET /backup/instance/options (administrators; allowed on a blocked instance) gives those rules (Password Rules). The password then goes to the job's thread as an argument (start_backup(password=…), run_backup(password=…) for the command line), never into state.json, the log or an exception message.
  • At the restore. restore_jobs.start_check() takes the lock of the checks, then, for an upload that is_envelope(), synchronously: read_header() first, so an envelope that cannot be opened asks for no password; then PasswordRequiredError without a password, or the EnvelopeError of unlock(). In those cases the lock is released, no check state is written and the upload is kept: a second POST with the right password needs no new upload. The route answers 400 password_required, 400 wrong_password, 400 envelope_damaged (a header cut short) or 409 envelope_unsupported. Otherwise the thread receives the EnvelopeKey, never the password: it holds the header and an AESGCM object, and its repr() shows the version and the cost, never the key. A zip ignores a password. PUT /backup/restore/upload answers kind: envelope when the stored file starts with LFBK, zip otherwise.
  • In the command line. scripts/backup_cli.py reads it from --password-file (read_secret_file(): the file's text without a leading byte order mark and its trailing line breaks, a blank file refused), from --password-stdin (one line, when the standard input is not a terminal) or with getpass at a terminal (twice for create), never from an argument. At a terminal, --password-stdin takes the getpass path too (_password(), B-25): a line read there would show the password as it is typed, and for create it would not be asked twice. The subparsers of create, inspect, restore and decrypt set allow_abbrev=False, so --password is refused instead of being taken for one of the two options.
  • Secret files read as root. Started as root (docker compose exec), the commands that work on a data directory switch to its owner (_drop_root_privileges(); decrypt too since lot B-19, _decrypt_as_owner()), but read --password-file and --instance-key-file before the switch (_password(), _instance_key_from_file()), so that a Docker secret only root can read works. Root then opens a path the server's user may have prepared, so before read_secret_file() the command opens the file with O_RDONLY|O_NONBLOCK, following links, and fstat must find a regular file: a FIFO, a folder or a device is refused at once, <label>: <path> is not a regular file, never waited on nor read. As root, a path that goes through a link at any component from the data directory down, where that user owns every folder, is refused too (os.lstat of each component; the data directory read as _decrypt_as_owner() reads it, --test-db included, and a setting it cannot use skips this check), its target never read: <label>: <path> goes through a link inside the data directory: give the file itself, from outside it. A link elsewhere is followed, as Kubernetes mounts its secrets (/etc/secret/pw → ..data/pw), and Docker and Compose secrets are plain files. Not root, there is no privilege to borrow: no link check. Both refusals keep the codes of an unreadable file, password_unreadable and instance_key_unreadable (lot B-38). Residual: the check and read_secret_file()'s own open are two opens, so a file swapped between them is still read, until read_secret_file() takes a descriptor or the flags (H's backlog, H-47).
  • In the app. The Backup tab empties its password fields as soon as a password is submitted (BackupDownloadCard.svelte, RestoreCard.svelte). The two fields of a new secure backup are autocomplete="new-password", so that a password manager does not fill in the account's password; the restore card's field stays autocomplete="off", as current-password would offer the account's. For another try after a wrong password, restoreFlow.svelte.ts keeps the file and the id of its upload (state password), never the password.

The key entry, secrets/instance.key (INSTANCE_KEY_ENTRY in paths.py):

  • Written only by a backup with a password, and only when exportable_instance_key() (secure.py) gives the key: instance_key_status() reports the source generated without a problem, and the key read_secret_file() reads from the file fits an archive (_fits_an_archive()): at least INSTANCE_KEY_MIN_LENGTH characters, and at most INSTANCE_KEY_MAX_BYTES (4096) bytes in UTF-8, as every restore reads no more (read_instance_key(); B-26). A configured key (LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY, its _FILE), no key yet, or a generated key that cannot be used gives no entry.
