    • nothing when the code that caught the failure logged it already, in this request: a warning or a higher line written with the exception (exc_info), or inside its except, marks the exception for the request the line names (LibreFolioBoundLogger, backend/app/logging_config.py), and chain_reported_for() reads that request's marks on every exception linked to the HTTPException, the suppressed contexts included. The asset and FX routes below (logger.exception(...), then from e) and the backup routes (a warning inside the except, then from None) get no second line. Only a line actually written marks: a warning that LOG_LEVEL filters out marks nothing, and the safety net then writes the failure at its own level;
    • when only another request's log has the failure, or a line written outside any request (chain_reported()), one WARNING, Request failed with an error already logged (ALREADY_LOGGED), with request_id, status, method, path, error_type when known, and logged_with_request_id, the request of the first line about the failure, when that line was written in one. No traceback and no error_chain: that first line has them.
  • An exception nobody handled. SecurityHeadersMiddleware catches it, and report_unhandled_error() writes one ERROR, Unhandled error, with request_id, method, path, error_type, error_chain and the traceback. It judges on the exception itself, not its chain: nothing when this request's log has it already (is_reported_for()), and the short Request failed with an error already logged, without status, when only another request's log has it, or a line outside any request (is_reported()). The middleware then sends the JSON 500 when the response has not started, and raises the exception again. uvicorn's own line for it, Exception in ASGI application, is dropped (Request Logs). A failure after the response started gets the same line, and no second answer.
  • What a line holds. The method and the path, never the query string (it can carry a token), never a header or the body. The failure's message reaches the log only inside the traceback.
  • AI Export. A component that fails to build is written once, where it fails: BuildContext._build() (backend/app/services/ai_export/dependencies.py) logs a WARNING, AI Export component failed to build, with component_id, error_type, reason_code when the chain has one, and the traceback. A component that cannot be built because a component it needs failed writes a short AI Export component not built: a dependency failed, with component_id and dependency_id and no traceback: the dependency's own line has it. A failure is written once per build context, never again when its cached outcome is read, and an optional component's failure is written too, so an export that comes back without a section says why. A traceback is written once too (lot H-60r). A resource that fails to load is memoized for the request as one ResourceLoadError, raised to every component that reads it, and a loader can raise an exception several requests share, the failure of a shared build. So the line carries the traceback of shown_error() only when no line has carried it yet (traceback_reported()). When a line already has it, another component's, another request's or the loader's own, the line keeps component_id, error_type and reason_code, has no traceback, and names logged_with_request_id, the request whose line has it, when that line was written in one: this very request, for a second component reading the same failed resource. Before, the 503 snapshot_source_failure left nothing in the log; now the component's line is the failure's, the 503 carries request_id and the error_type of the component's failure beside its problem detail, and the handler writes no line of its own.

Tests: ./dev.py test services server-errors (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_server_errors.py: an X-Request-Id on every answer, never the client's, and the request_id in every line of the request; a 4xx answered as FastAPI answers it; the three cases of a 5xx, a cause held in a cause attribute included; the unhandled 500 as JSON, logged once and raised again, also after its answer started; the H-33 500 as JSON; no Authorization, Cookie, body, query string or exception message in an answer or a line, the message only inside the traceback; client_log_level; since H-60r, two requests failing together on one shared build, answered with a 503 or let go: both ids in the log and the traceback once, the second request's short line pointing to the first, also when the build logged its failure itself; one exception object raised by three requests in turn, each later one pointing to the first; no secret in the short line), ./dev.py test services logging-errors (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_logging_errors.py: the helpers of errors.py, the per-request mark included, logger.exception(), the request a line marks, the mark and uvicorn's dropped line, see Request Logs) and ./dev.py test services ai-export-pure, whose backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_ai_export_build_failure_log.py pins the component's lines; since H-60r, two components reading one failed resource, two requests whose loaders raise one shared exception, and a loader that logged its failure itself: the traceback in one line only, the next lines without it.

docs.title: The Asset and FX Routes
docs.text:
A 500 of the asset and FX routes never carries the error's text, which can name the database schema (an SQL error quotes its statement): the answer's detail is a fixed message naming the action, such as «Internal error while assigning providers», and the error goes to the log with its exception (logger.exception(...)). The handler above adds request_id and error_type, and writes no line of its own.

  • Where. First the price routes (backend/app/api/v1/assets/prices.py): R13-SEC9-3 for the query and the current prices, then MF-SEC9a for the writes and the sync, and for the FX rates' delete. Since X-R74 (release 1.3), the 26 sites of the other asset and FX routes that still echoed the error (detail=str(e), or f"…: {e!s}"): providers.py, crud.py, events.py and market_data.py in backend/app/api/v1/assets/, providers.py and currencies.py (the sync's catch-all) in backend/app/api/v1/fx/. The provider probe and the five FX sites did not log the error at all before.
  • What stays. The refusals the routes author answer as before: a 400 or 404 with an authored message, the coded refusals {"error_code", "message", "params"} (the 409s, and the events' 400s), the 422s with a code, and the FX sync's 502 «Failed to sync rates: …» for an FXServiceError.
  • A failed merge. merge_assets answers an AssetSourceError with its text, 404 or 400, and its messages are authored. MERGE_FAILED is the one that wraps an unexpected error: AssetCRUDService.merge_assets() (backend/app/services/assets/crud.py) raises it for any error that stops the merge, a database error included, and logs that error with its exception. Since X-R74 it stays a 400 with its code, but its text is the fixed «Merge failed: internal error».

Tests: ./dev.py test services routes-generic-500 (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_routes_generic_500.py), parametrized over the 26 failure paths, each a 500 that holds no word of the error while the error is logged with its exception; a failed merge, a 400 that holds no word of the error while the service logs it; and guards that the authored refusals answer as before.

docs.title: 📁 Uploaded Files: Common and Personal
docs.text:
Each uploaded static file (<data directory>/custom-uploads/<uuid>.<ext>, with its JSON sidecar <uuid>.json, see Data Directory on Disk) has a scope, UploadScope (backend/app/schemas/uploads.py): common, seen by every signed-in user (icons, logos, asset photos, avatars), or personal, seen only by its uploader and the administrators (is_superuser). The rule lives in backend/app/services/files/static_uploads.py, the routes in backend/app/api/v1/uploads.py:

  • The scope. The sidecar stores it. A sidecar written before scopes existed, or by the seeding of the default avatars, has none, and effective_scope() applies the inheritance rule at every read, with no migration: the application's own files (uploader id 0, SYSTEM_USER_ID: the seeded default avatars) are common, image/* is common, anything else is personal. POST /uploads takes an optional multipart field scope, common or personal; without it, the same rule decides, and the result is stored.
  • Seeing a file (can_view_upload()). GET /uploads lists the common files and the user's own personal ones, every file for an administrator; my_files_only=true keeps only one's own files, of both scopes. GET /uploads/{id}/preview and GET /uploads/file/{id} (download, img_preview thumbnail, text window) answer a personal file of someone else with the 404 File not found of a file that does not exist, so its existence is not revealed. The check runs first, before the thumbnail cache and before any type check.
  • Changing a file (can_manage_upload()). DELETE /uploads/{id} and PATCH /uploads/{id} with {"scope": "common"} or {"scope": "personal"} (UploadUpdateRequest) belong to the uploader and the administrators. Another user gets 403 on a common file, and the same 404 on a personal one. Every UploadFileInfo carries scope and can_delete: whether the requesting user may delete the file and change its scope.
  • Private thumbnails. img_preview answers carry Cache-Control: private, max-age=3600, never public: they are signed-in content, which the browser may keep and a shared cache in front of the instance must not.
  • Several workers (dev.py server --workers N). Each worker caches a sidecar for up to an hour (upload_metadata), but checks the sidecar's stamp (inode, mtime, size) at every read, and _save_metadata() replaces a sidecar atomically (a temporary file in the same folder, then os.replace). A scope changed through one worker holds at once in the others, and no reader sees half a file.

The broker report files of BRIM answer differently, and deliberately so: their routes (/brokers/import/files/…) give 403 to a user without access to the file's broker.

Tests: ./dev.py test services static-uploads, ./dev.py test api uploads and ./dev.py test api uploads-serve-file.

docs.title: 🚧 Instance Block
docs.text:
A hosting provider blocks an instance with LIBREFOLIO_BLOCKED; backend/app/config/platform.py reads both variables from the process environment, never through Settings, and they work in every profile:

  • instance_blocked(): 1, true, yes and on block, 0, false, no and off do not, in any case; unset or blank is not blocked; any other value raises ValueError.
  • instance_deletion_date(): LIBREFOLIO_DELETION_DATE, an optional ISO date shown on the block page; any other value raises ValueError.

log_configuration_audit() reads both at startup, so a value they cannot read stops the server (see Configuration Checks).

The guard. refuse_when_blocked (backend/app/api/v1/instance_block.py) is a dependency of the /api/v1 router, APIRouter(dependencies=[Depends(refuse_when_blocked), Depends(refuse_when_awaiting_restore), Depends(refuse_when_restore_interrupted)]) in backend/app/api/v1/router.py (the second one is Awaiting Restore, the third A Restore Stopped Half Way, both read after the block), so it covers every API route (APIRoute) under it, today's and tomorrow's. FastAPI gives no router dependency to a plain Route, a WebSocketRoute or a Mount, so none of them belongs under /api/v1. FastAPI hands a dependency the endpoint function of the matched route (request.scope["endpoint"]), not its full path, so the allow-list ALLOWED_WHEN_BLOCKED is a frozenset of endpoint functions:

Endpoints Functions For POST /auth/login, POST /auth/logout, GET /auth/me auth.login, auth.logout, auth.get_me Signing in and out, and who is signed in POST /auth/tokens/inspect, POST /auth/password-reset auth.inspect_link_token, auth.reset_password_with_link A link already sent: reading it, and setting a new password with a reset link; without them, someone who lost the password could never reach the block page, the account deletion or the backup DELETE /auth/users/me, GET /auth/users/me/deletion-preview auth.delete_own_account, auth.preview_own_account_deletion Deleting one's own account, and seeing first what it would delete; the block page has no button for it yet POST /backup/instance, GET /backup/instance/options, GET /backup/instance/jobs/{job_id}, GET /backup/instance/jobs/{job_id}/file, DELETE /backup/instance/jobs/{job_id} backup_instance.start_instance_backup, backup_instance.get_instance_backup_options, backup_instance.get_instance_backup_job, backup_instance.download_instance_backup, backup_instance.delete_instance_backup_job The full backup, for an administrator: start, poll, download, delete. On a blocked instance the data can still be taken away, from the backup card of the block page (backup_available of GET /system/block, below). GET /backup/instance/options gives the rules of a secure backup's password (Secure Backups), so that the card of a blocked instance can offer a secure backup too POST /backup/panel/jobs, GET /backup/panel/jobs/{job_id}, GET /backup/panel/jobs/{job_id}/file, DELETE /backup/panel/jobs/{job_id} backup_panel.start_panel_backup, backup_panel.get_panel_backup_job, backup_panel.download_panel_backup, backup_panel.delete_panel_backup_job The same, for the hosting panel, with its token (panel_access(PanelScope.BACKUP)) instead of a session: the provider hands the data back GET /backup/restore/outcome backup_restore.get_restore_outcome The outcome of a restore, for the page that asked its restart, with the one-time ticket of that request instead of a session (The Outcome Ticket): a restart that came back blocked reads pending, waiting: "instance_blocked". It starts nothing GET /system/block, GET /system/instance block.get_instance_block, instance.get_instance_config The block page GET /system/health, GET /system/ready, GET /system/info health.health_check, ready.get_readiness, info.get_system_info Probes and version GET /system/test-lane-health health.test_lane_health The test runner's probe, 404 outside test mode POST /system/wake-sync wake.wake_sync The scheduled wake-up, with its own token instead of a session: on a blocked instance it runs no job and answers 200 with status: "blocked" (decision D-W3) GET /panel/status panel.get_panel_status The hosting panel's setup status, read by admin_setup_status(), with its own token instead of a session (lot H-61): it answers as on any other instance. Besides the setup, the mode and the restore, it holds two counts, users_used and users_limit (lot H5-1), owner_email_change (lot H5-4: pending, blocked or null, never an address), instance_key (lot H5-7) and users_over_limit (lot H5-8, a yes or no), never a name or an address GET /panel/metrics panel.get_panel_metrics The hosting panel's figures of the instance, with a signed ticket of scope metrics instead of a session (lot CL-M1): it answers as on any other instance The seven /backup/panel/restore… routes _PANEL_RESTORE_ROUTES of instance_block.py (backup_panel_restore.*) The panel's restore, with its ticket instead of a session (lot H-62): past the ticket each route answers 423 instance_blocked itself, so a caller without a valid ticket learns nothing of the block. No restore happens on a blocked instance (Awaiting Restore)

The refusal. On a blocked instance, an endpoint outside the list first runs get_current_user() with the request's own database session (FastAPI caches the dependency), then refuses:

  • without a valid session: the 401 of get_current_user();

  • with a valid session: 423 Locked, with the code INSTANCE_BLOCKED_CODE:

    {"detail": {"code": "instance_blocked", "message": "This instance is blocked by its hosting provider"}}

What a caller without a session can tell. Only signed-in users get the 423. A caller without a valid session gets these answers:

Routes Not blocked Blocked Protected routes outside the list 401 The same 401 Public routes outside the list: POST /auth/register, POST /auth/setup (the initial administrator: a blocked instance stays blocked until the subscription is paid, P16), POST /email/verification/confirm (spends a verification link), POST /email/verification/resend (sends the verification email again, with the sign-in's credentials instead of a session), GET /auth/address-probe and GET /auth/address-probe.png, GET /utilities/*, GET /ai-export/catalog Their usual answer 401 The routes of the list Their usual answer The same answer
  • The protected routes and the routes of the list do not reveal the block: /system/instance, /system/info and /system/ready answer as on any other instance. Only the scheduled wake-up and the outcome of a restore tell, and only to the holder of their token or ticket: status: "blocked", and waiting: "instance_blocked".
  • The public routes outside the list answer 401 only while the instance is blocked. From them, a caller without a session can tell that the instance is blocked, and nothing more: they return no data.

On an instance that is not blocked, the guard returns at once and leaves the session unused. On a blocked one it runs before the route's own dependencies and before the body is validated: a signed-in caller of a refused route gets the 423 even with an invalid body, never a 422.

GET /system/block (backend/app/api/v1/system/block.py) is for signed-in users only, and allowed on a blocked instance. It returns InstanceBlockResponse (backend/app/schemas/system.py): blocked; deletion_date, null without a date; billing_url, where the subscription is managed (LIBREFOLIO_BILLING_URL, from registration_service.billing_link()), for administrators only: it is null for the other users, and when the variable is unset or not an http(s) address (billing_link() logs the latter once per process); and backup_available, whether this user may still download a full backup of the instance: the user's is_superuser, so true for administrators only (decision 12). The block page (frontend/src/lib/features/instance/components/InstanceBlockedPage.svelte) checks again that billing_url is an http(s) address, then shows an administrator a Manage subscription link to it, opened in a new tab (rel="noopener noreferrer"). When backup_available is true, and only then, it shows the backup card of Settings › Administration › Backup under the block message: the card's four backup_instance routes are on the list above, and nothing else on the server changes for it (see Instance block). A workstream that owns part of the block page adds one field there and fills it in block.py with one call to its service.

Changing the list. The list is short on purpose. The two link endpoints joined it for someone who lost the password (see the table above): they read a link already sent or spend a reset link, and create no account. Registration (POST /auth/register) stays out: it is still one of the public routes that answer 401 on a blocked instance, so an invitation link can be read there but not accepted (the /invite page then says that the instance is blocked, and so does /setup for the setup link: see Links in Use). The full backup is on the list too, for the administrator (backup_instance: start, poll, download and delete; decision 12) and for the hosting panel (backup_panel: the same four, with the panel's token instead of a session), and so is the scheduled wake-up (wake.wake_sync), with its own token instead of a session: on a blocked instance it runs no job and answers blocked (decision D-W3). The routes of a restore stay out (/backup/restore/…: the upload, the check, the confirmation, the status, the cancellation and the restart): the block lets the data leave, never come in, and nobody stops the server through the API. Nor is a restore confirmed before the block applied while it lasts (developer decision P7): the startup step reads LIBREFOLIO_BLOCKED and leaves it waiting (instance_blocked) until the first start after the unblock (Restoring a Backup). The one route of a restore on the list is its outcome, read with the ticket of the restart (GET /backup/restore/outcome, lot B5c): it starts nothing, changes nothing but its own ticket, and returns three fields and no data. When the block takes effect at the restart that a page asked, that page reads instance_blocked there, where its session may be gone (without JWT_SECRET every start ends them) and the status route answers 401 or 423. The panel's restore routes (/backup/panel/restore…, lot H-62) are on the list only so that the ticket is read first: each one then refuses a blocked instance itself, 423 instance_blocked, and restores nothing. Any other addition goes through the developer first. ./dev.py test api instance-block (backend/test_scripts/test_api/test_instance_block.py) pins the list by name and by route, checks that every API route under /api/v1 resolves refuse_when_blocked first, and that the only other routes under /api/v1 are the API's documentation (H-55 R5: the two pages, their start scripts and openapi.json), so an addition, or a route the guard does not reach, shows in review.

Outside the guard. Routes outside the /api/v1 router, such as the built web app, /mkdocs and the API's documentation where it is on (/api/v1/docs, /api/v1/redoc, /api/v1/openapi.json: debug and test instances only), are not covered: the browser still loads the app, which turns the first 423 into the block page (see Instance block). The scheduler does not go through HTTP, so the guard does not reach it: run_due_jobs() checks instance_blocked() itself and runs no job on a blocked instance (Scheduler).

docs.title: ⏳ Awaiting Restore
docs.text:
Lot H-62. A hosting panel that restores an instance onto a new machine starts it with LIBREFOLIO_AWAIT_RESTORE. awaiting_restore() (backend/app/config/platform.py) reads it from the process environment at each call, with the values of instance_blocked(): any other value raises ValueError, and log_configuration_audit() stops the start on it, or logs a warning while it is on.

The guard. refuse_when_awaiting_restore (backend/app/api/v1/instance_block.py) is the second dependency of the /api/v1 router, right after refuse_when_blocked. While the mode is on, every endpoint outside ALLOWED_WHEN_AWAITING_RESTORE answers 423 with the code INSTANCE_AWAITING_RESTORE_CODE, instance_awaiting_restore, to anyone, signed in or not (decision Q5): unlike the block, it never asks for a session, since the volume is empty or holds the data being restored. The list:

Endpoints Functions GET /system/health, GET /system/test-lane-health, GET /system/ready, GET /system/info health.health_check, health.test_lane_health, ready.get_readiness, info.get_system_info GET /system/instance instance.get_instance_config POST /system/wake-sync wake.wake_sync: _wake_run() answers status: "awaiting_restore" and runs no job GET /panel/status panel.get_panel_status GET /panel/metrics panel.get_panel_metrics The four /backup/panel/jobs… routes backup_panel.start_panel_backup, get_panel_backup_job, download_panel_backup, delete_panel_backup_job: in the mode a start answers 409 backup_awaiting_restore (backup/panel.py, _awaiting_restore()), so a backup of the empty data never starts The seven /backup/panel/restore… routes _PANEL_RESTORE_ROUTES

InstanceMode (backend/app/schemas/system.py), normal or awaiting_restore, is the mode field of ReadinessResponse (/system/ready), InstanceConfigResponse (/system/instance) and PanelStatusResponse (/panel/status). The web app's root layout reads it from /system/instance: AwaitingRestoreGate.svelte shows InstanceAwaitingRestorePage.svelte instead of every route, which asks /system/instance every 30 seconds and reloads once the mode reads normal (frontend/src/lib/features/instance/components/).

The start. Step.skip_when (backend/app/services/platform/lifecycle.py) is asked when a startup step comes; a step whose predicate answers True is not run, with one Startup step skipped info line. STARTUP_STEPS (backend/app/services/platform/app_lifespan.py) marks six with skip_when=_serving_no_data (awaiting_restore() or restore_interrupted(), so A Restore Stopped Half Way skips them too): admin-bootstrap, stored-currencies, provider-prewarm, market-holidays, brim-parse-pool and scheduler. The database, the restore's own steps (pending-restore, restore-commit) and the idle monitor still run.

The restore routes. backend/app/api/v1/backup/panel_restore.py reuses the administrator's restore (api/v1/backup/restore.py: the same upload writer, limits, check on a copy, confirmation and restart); only the caller changes. Every route depends on _restore_gate, in this order: panel_access(PanelScope.BACKUP_RESTORE) (ticket only, The Hosting Panel's Access), then 423 instance_blocked on a blocked instance, then 409 restore_mode_required outside the mode, so a stolen signing key can at most fill an empty volume. Only an .lfbk envelope is kept (400 restore_envelope_required otherwise, the file removed): _receive_envelope() refuses a body that does not start with LFBK before a byte is written, and upload_panel_restore_archive() removes a finished file whose kind is not envelope. The writer finishes with finish(replace_others=False), so the uploads before it stay until this one is accepted; only then does restore_jobs.remove_replaced_uploads(keep=…) remove them (but the one a running check reads): a refused upload never costs the previous good one (SEC-3). Every 500 restore_state_unreadable of these routes carries B's reason (io, not_a_file, invalid) in its detail (_state_unreadable(exc)). The panel's views are closed models with extra="forbid" (backend/app/schemas/hosting_panel.py): PanelRestoreStageReport (the administrators as administrators_count, the control totals as a verdict and control_totals_differences_count, no tables, files or sizes), PanelRestoreStatus (confirmed_via instead of the username: a panel confirmation records confirmed_via: panel and the ticket's kid as confirmed_by) and, in /panel/status, PanelRestoreSummary (state, reason, waiting, backup_created_at, stage_id; when the state cannot be read, _restore_summary() in backend/app/api/v1/panel.py answers 200 with state unreadable and B's reason, io, not_a_file or invalid, the other three null: never null, and never a 500, decision D7). The panel sees only the checks it started (origin panel): any other check answers 404 restore_stage_not_found (_panel_check()). A repeated POST …/stage with the same upload_id while its check runs, a repeated confirmation of the same stage, or a restart while the restore is under way or committed, answers 202 with the check or the state found. The router is NoInputEchoRoute: a 422 never repeats the password.

Ending the mode. Only the panel ends it, removing the variable and restarting once the status reads committed. For a blocked instance (contract R4), the panel starts the machine with the block off and, at committed, changes the variables in one machine update (mode off, LIBREFOLIO_BLOCKED on, LIBREFOLIO_DELETION_DATE unchanged): both guards read the environment at each request, so the first request after that single restart already gets 423 instance_blocked.

Tests: ./dev.py test api await-restore-mode (backend/test_scripts/test_api/test_await_restore_mode_api.py: the list pinned by name and route, both switches, R4), ./dev.py test api panel-restore (backend/test_scripts/test_api/test_panel_restore_api.py: the scope, the order of the refusals, the routes, the report) and ./dev.py test services await-restore-mode (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_await_restore_mode.py).

docs.title: 🧩 A Restore Stopped Half Way
docs.text:
Lot B-33, the start's part (workstream H; the command-line side is workstream B's, «An Unreadable Restore State» in Command-Line Tools). When the state of the restore, .restore/restore.json, cannot be read (its owner or permissions changed, a disk error, a link or a folder in its place, content no LibreFolio wrote), a restore may have stopped half way and LibreFolio cannot tell which data it holds.

The probe. backend/app/services/platform/restore_guard.py owns it. The startup step restore-state, right after pending-restore, calls probe_restore_state() in a thread, which asks workstream B's apply.restore_state_problem() (backend/app/services/platform/instance_backup/apply.py: the RestoreStateUnreadableError, or None when the state can be read or there is none; it never raises). The answer is kept in the module for the whole process, and restore_interrupted() returns it: False in a process that never probed. When it cannot read the state, the step logs one error with B's reason (io, not_a_file, invalid), never the state's content, The state of the restore cannot be read: LibreFolio serves no data until the administrator runs ./dev.py backup pending --recover previous; it never stops the start. A state made readable while the process runs counts only at the next start: the way out is ./dev.py backup pending --recover previous with LibreFolio stopped, then a restart.

The start. While restore_interrupted(), STARTUP_STEPS skips what repairs, writes or warms up the data: post-migration-fixes and lone-transfer-legs (skip_when=restore_interrupted), and the six steps of Awaiting Restore (skip_when=_serving_no_data): admin-bootstrap, stored-currencies, provider-prewarm, market-holidays, brim-parse-pool and scheduler. The other steps carry no skip, the database, global-settings, restore-commit, backup-leftovers, serving-lock and idle-monitor among them.

The guard. refuse_when_restore_interrupted (backend/app/api/v1/instance_block.py) is the third dependency of the /api/v1 router, after refuse_when_blocked and refuse_when_awaiting_restore. While restore_interrupted(), every endpoint outside ALLOWED_WHEN_RESTORE_INTERRUPTED answers 423 with the code INSTANCE_RESTORE_INTERRUPTED_CODE, instance_restore_interrupted, to anyone, signed in or not. ALLOWED_WHEN_RESTORE_INTERRUPTED is ALLOWED_WHEN_AWAITING_RESTORE itself (a test pins them equal): the probes, /system/info, /system/instance, /system/wake-sync and the hosting panel's routes. One of them answers otherwise (D7): backup_panel.start_panel_backup answers 409 backup_restore_interrupted (BACKUP_RESTORE_INTERRUPTED_CODE), since a backup of data in doubt would pass the coordinator's checks and push a good copy out of those it keeps. The guard first runs the panel's credential check by hand, panel_caller(request, PanelScope.BACKUP) (backend/app/services/platform/hosting_panel/access.py), so a caller without a valid credential gets the same 401, 404, 429 or 503 as outside the state; following, downloading and deleting a panel job still answer. In this state:

  • InstanceConfigResponse (backend/app/schemas/system.py, GET /system/instance) says restore_interrupted: true; the field is false otherwise;
  • _wake_run() (backend/app/api/v1/system/wake.py) answers status: "restore_interrupted" and runs no job (after awaiting_restore, which wins);
  • GET /panel/status answers 200 with restore.state unreadable and its reason, as whenever the state cannot be read (D7).

The web app. AwaitingRestoreGate.svelte reads instanceConfig.config.restore_interrupted; while it is true it shows InstanceRestoreInterruptedPage.svelte instead of every route, and wins over the awaiting-restore page (frontend/src/lib/features/instance/components/). The page, on the login's AnimatedBackground, asks /system/instance every 30 seconds and reloads once restore_interrupted reads false. The recovery is a command on the server (./dev.py backup pending [--recover previous|owner]), so the help depends on the prop selfHosted (default selfHostedConfirmed(), frontend/src/lib/features/instance/profile.ts; FB-27):

  • Self-hosted: the administrator is whoever runs the server, so the page links the recovery guide, data-testid="instance-restore-interrupted-docs" («How to recover»: admin/cli_backup/#backup-pending-unreadable), and still links the support address when the instance has one. It never shows the «contact whoever provides the service» line.
  • Managed: the customer cannot run the command, so there is no guide link. When instanceConfig.config.support_url (LIBREFOLIO_SUPPORT_URL, or the prop supportUrl) gives a usable address, the page shows a «Contact support» link (data-testid="instance-restore-interrupted-support"): supportChannel(supportUrl, {githubFallback: false}) (frontend/src/lib/features/support/supportChannel.ts) checks it again and keeps a mailto: address or an http(s) page, opened in a new tab, and reportHref() adds the report of buildCheckReport() with the code platform.restore_interrupted (the same report as a security check's support button). Anything else shows no link but a line, instance-restore-interrupted-support-missing (instance.restoreInterrupted.supportMissing), telling the user to contact whoever provides the service; never the project's GitHub (D7).

The API client's response interceptor (frontend/src/lib/api/zodios-client.ts) reads the configuration again on a 423 instance_restore_interrupted (isInstanceRestoreInterruptedError(), frontend/src/lib/features/instance/instanceBlockState.ts), so the gate shows the page even when the configuration was read before.

The owner's account (lot H5-3). A second reason closes the instance the same way. After a restore from the app on a managed instance (confirmed_via == "admin" with an owner_user_id, see Backup and Restore), the startup step restore-owner, right after restore-commit, awaits workstream B's assign_restored_owner() (backend/app/services/platform/instance_backup/owner.py), which calls workstream A's assign_owner_and_send_reset once and records the outcome in the restore's state; the step then calls probe_owner_assignment(), which asks B's apply.owner_assignment_problem() (None, pending, or the code of the refusal, from error:<CODE>), keeps it in _owner_problem and logs one error with the value when it is not None. restore_interrupted() is true for either reason, so the steps after restore-owner that carry the skip, the 423, the 409 of the panel's backup start, /system/instance and the wake-up follow with no other code; restore_interrupted_reason() says which (restore_state wins over owner_assignment), and InstanceConfigResponse.restore_interrupted_reason carries it. With several workers only the one holding the owner lock (.restore/owner.lock) calls A, so another worker's probe can find pending and would stay closed for good: the router dependency awaits refresh_restore_state() first, which, for pending only and at most every OWNER_RECHECK_SECONDS (2 s), asks again in a thread. A code is never asked again for the process: the way out is ./dev.py backup pending --recover owner (B) and a restart. The page (InstanceRestoreInterruptedPage.svelte, prop reason) says «the owner's account is not ready», cites that command.

Tests: ./dev.py test services restore-owner-guard and ./dev.py test api restore-owner-guard (test_restore_owner_guard.py, test_restore_owner_guard_api.py: the probe, the lazy recheck with a patched clock, two workers with a real state, the step's place, the 423 walk of every route), and ./dev.py test services restore-guard (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_restore_guard.py: the probe, its log line, the step's place and the skipped steps) and ./dev.py test api restore-interrupted (backend/test_scripts/test_api/test_restore_interrupted_api.py: the list pinned by name and route, the third dependency, /system/instance, wake-sync, /panel/status).

docs.title: 🎟️ Single-use Account Tokens
docs.text: Invitations, password-reset links, email verification and the setup link of the initial administrator all hand someone a secret inside a URL. backend/app/services/accounts/token_service.py is the building block of these single-use links in the accounts domain: it issues, checks, spends and revokes their tokens, with the same guarantees for all four, and all four use it (Links in use): invitations, password-reset links, email verification (Email Verification) and the setup link of the initial administrator.

docs.title: 🎲 Generation and Storage
docs.text:
• issue_token() draws a new token with secrets.token_urlsafe(32): 32 random bytes (256 bits), written as 43 URL-safe characters. One caller gives its own instead (token=): the initial administrator's setup link, with the value of LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN, whose format the configuration has checked (32 to 200 unreserved URL characters). A given token is stored like a drawn one, by its hash; an empty one is a ValueError.
  • The plaintext is returned once, in IssuedToken.token, beside the new row (IssuedToken.record). The database keeps only hash_token(token) — the SHA-256 of the UTF-8 token, 64 lowercase hex characters — in account_tokens.token_hash, which is unique. A link cannot be rebuilt from the database: a lost one is replaced by a new token, never recovered.
  • A fast hash is enough: unlike a password, 256 random bits are out of reach of guessing, so no slow salted hash is needed. Being deterministic, the hash is also the lookup key: inspect_token() and consume_token() hash the token they receive and search token_hash. A token given through LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN is as random as the hosting panel makes it: the configuration checks only its length and its characters, and the administrator manual makes it with openssl rand -hex 32, 256 bits.

docs.title: 🎯 Purposes, Lifetimes and Links
docs.text:
Each token serves one AccountTokenPurpose, stored in purpose. Every lookup matches the hash and the purpose: a token presented for another purpose is unknown, exactly like a token never issued — a reset link is never an invitation.

Purpose Default lifetime (DEFAULT_TTL) user_id grants_admin Link (token_path()) invite 7 days Refused: the account does not exist yet Allowed /invite#token=… password_reset 30 minutes Required Refused /reset-password#token=… email_verification 24 hours Required Refused /verify-email#token=… admin_setup 72 hours Required Refused /setup#token=… email_change 7 days Required (the owner) Refused /confirm-email-change#token=…

expires_at is created_at plus the lifetime; a ttl argument replaces the default. issue_token() raises ValueError on a refused or missing user_id, on a refused grants_admin and on a lifetime that is not positive, before writing anything. token_path(purpose, token) returns the link as a path with the token in the fragment, never in the query string: see Links in Use for why.

docs.title: 🚦 Checking and Spending a Token
docs.text:
inspect_token(session, token, purpose) returns a TokenInspection — a TokenStatus and the row — and writes nothing. The status is unknown (with no row), revoked, consumed, expired or valid, checked in that order: a revoked token that has also expired reports revoked. A token expires at expires_at exactly; it is valid until the microsecond before.

consume_token(session, token, purpose, consumed_by_user_id=…) spends a token with one conditional UPDATE, which amounts to:

UPDATE account_tokens
SET consumed_at = :now, consumed_by_user_id = :consumer
WHERE token_hash = :hash AND purpose = :purpose
  AND consumed_at IS NULL AND revoked_at IS NULL
  AND expires_at > :now

When the statement changes exactly one row, consume_token() returns that row, read again from the database; otherwise it returns None and nothing changed — inspect_token() tells why. The check and the write are one statement, with no gap between them: of two requests racing for the same link, only the one whose UPDATE changes the row gets it.

docs.title: 🚫 Revocation
docs.text:
revoke_tokens(session, token_id=…) revokes one token, revoke_tokens(session, user_id=…) the tokens of one account, optionally of one purpose. It sets revoked_at on the matching tokens that are neither consumed nor revoked — expired ones included — and returns how many; consumed and revoked tokens keep their timestamps. Without a token_id or a user_id it raises ValueError rather than revoke every token. An invitation has no user_id: it is revoked by its id.

retire_tokens(session, user_id=…, purpose=…) (lot A7b-2) ends the tokens of one account and one purpose for good, when what they were for was done another way. Every one not consumed — live, expired or already revoked — gets consumed_at, and revoked_at unless it already had one, both at the same moment: an earlier revocation keeps its moment, and consumed_by_user_id stays NULL, since nobody spent the link. It returns how many it retired; a second call finds none. A retired token reads revoked, since inspect_token() checks the revocation first, and consume_token() refuses it.

Only admin_setup tokens are retired today, and there the difference matters. The initial administrator waits for its setup while it is inactive and none of its setup links is consumed (registration_service.pending_admin_filter()): a revoked link leaves it waiting, for a new link; a retired one ends the wait, so an account set up another way never waits for its setup again, not even once deactivated. Every account that holds a setup link follows the same rules, waiting or not, in the transaction of the change; what each rule guards against is in The Setup Link's Lifecycle:

Change Entry point Its setup links An activation ./dev.py user activate → user_service.set_user_active(…, True), the waiting administrator included; PATCH /api/v1/users/{user_id} with is_active: true → user_service.update_user_status(), which the waiting administrator never reaches (409 PENDING_SETUP first) Retired A new password ./dev.py user reset → user_service.reset_password(); a reset link spent → user_service.complete_password_reset(); POST /api/v1/auth/change-password Retired A setup link presented for an account already active, or for an account another of whose setup links was already consumed (lot A-42) POST /api/v1/auth/setup → bootstrap_admin_service.complete_admin_setup(), which refuses it (400 TOKEN_INVALID) Every one not consumed retired, not only the one presented A deactivation of the initial administrator waiting for its setup: the cancellation of its link (lot A-43) ./dev.py user deactivate → user_service.set_user_active(…, False); PATCH /api/v1/users/{user_id} with is_active: false → user_service.update_user_status(), refused for a protected account; the Users tab adds cancel_setup: true, refused with 409 SETUP_COMPLETED when the account waits no more (lot A-51) Revoked, not retired: the account still waits, for a new link A deactivation of any other account (lot A-43) The same entry points Retired A new address, not the same one in another A–Z case (decision P18) LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_EMAIL at a start (bootstrap_admin_service._follow_variables()); user_service.update_profile(), behind ./dev.py user set-email and PUT /api/v1/auth/profile Revoked, not retired: they went to the earlier address, and the account still waits, for a link that reaches the new one The setup A live setup link spent by POST /api/v1/auth/setup That one consumed, the others revoked A new setup link ./dev.py user setup-link (issue_setup_link()); a LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN never stored, at a start The earlier ones revoked first; an account set up in the meantime gets no new link (lot A-42)

The retirements are logged as Account tokens retired (count, user_id, purpose); a refused setup adds a WARNING with the user_id, Setup link refused and retired: the account is already active or Setup link refused and retired: the account was set up before, and a cancellation the WARNING of The Setup Link's Lifecycle.

A restore revokes the live tokens of the whole restored database at once, at its first start (Restoring a Backup): in the transaction that sets the session versions (Session Revocation), every row of account_tokens that is neither consumed nor revoked, whatever its purpose and expired or not, gets revoked_at = the restore time, written as SQLAlchemy writes it (UTC, without offset). A link spent or revoked on the instance after the backup was taken is live again in the backup's database: without this it would work a second time. The links issued after the backup are not in the restored database at all. The count is logged, as links_revoked of Restore committed: every session ended, the backup's one-time links revoked. When the restore keeps the owner's password (a panel restore, B5-1l), the line reads Restore committed: every session ended but the owner's, the backup's one-time links revoked.

An account the backup held waiting for its email verification (inactive, with an unspent verification token: verification.awaiting_verification()) loses its token with the others, the hold included, and so stops waiting. The sign-in page's resend then answers 403 ACCOUNT_DISABLED, and nothing sends it a new link: an administrator activates it (PATCH /users/{user_id}, email_verified_at stays NULL), or deletes it so that its owner signs up again. Such an account never signed in, so it holds no data. Towards the administrator, the report of the check gives one notice only (developer decision P11, scripts/backup_cli.py): the invitations and links sent before the restore will have expired, and can be sent again.

docs.title: ♻️ The Setup Link's Lifecycle
docs.text:
Lots A-42 and A-43 (release 1.3) make sure that no setup link left behind sets its account up again, and that deactivating the initial administrator while it waits cancels the link handed over. Two words, as the code uses them:

  • Revoke (revoke_tokens()): the link stops working (revoked_at). The waiting administrator keeps waiting, for a new link.
  • Retire (retire_tokens()): revoked and counted as used (consumed_at too). The account no longer counts as waiting (pending_admin_filter()), so no new link is issued for it.

Issuing under the write lock (A-42). issue_setup_link(), behind ./dev.py user setup-link, and the re-arm of a start by a LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN never stored (_keep_pending_admin()) find the waiting administrator by a read, and a setup could commit between that read and their write: the new link would then be live on an account already set up, able to set its password again. Both now revoke the earlier setup links first, with one UPDATE that takes SQLite's write lock («Several workers» in The Initial Administrator), then read «waiting» again under that lock (registration_service.is_pending_admin()), where no setup can commit any more. An account set up in the meantime gets nothing, and the transaction is rolled back:

  • issue_setup_link() returns None, with the INFO line No setup link issued: the initial administrator was set up meanwhile; the command prints ❌ No administrator account is waiting for its setup link and exits with 1;
  • the start answers ignored, with the INFO line LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN not re-armed: the initial administrator was set up meanwhile: no link is stored, none is logged or emailed.

«Waiting» is read on what the database holds under the lock, not on what the UPDATE changed: a rival that only revoked the links, as a new address does, leaves the account waiting, and the link is issued. So revoke_tokens() always runs its UPDATE, even when no live token can match: selecting the live ids first, and skipping the write when there are none, would give the lock up.

Spending refused once the account was set up (A-42). complete_admin_setup() spends the link first (consume_token(), which takes the write lock too), then refuses it in two cases, with the same 400 TOKEN_INVALID as a link that is not valid: the account is already active (lot A7b-2), or another setup link of the account was already consumed (_setup_spent_before()): the setup done through it, or the links retired. A link left live by the race above, or in the database of an earlier 1.3 build, so sets no password. Either way the spending is rolled back, the account's setup links not consumed are retired, the one presented included, and a WARNING is logged with the user_id: Setup link refused and retired: the account is already active, or Setup link refused and retired: the account was set up before. Both refusals come before bcrypt, which a refused link never costs. Only a consumed sibling counts: a link re-armed after a revoked or an expired one still sets the account up.

Deactivating is the cancellation (A-43). A deactivation ends the account's setup links in its own transaction, through user_service._end_setup_links(), behind set_user_active(…, False) (./dev.py user deactivate) and update_user_status() (PATCH /api/v1/users/{user_id} with is_active: false, plus cancel_setup: true from the Users tab: below). Whether the account waits is read before anything changes, under the write lock since lot A-51:

  • The initial administrator waiting for its setup, inactive already: its setup links are revoked. That is the cancellation of the link handed over, the Cancel setup link of the Users tab (UserRow): whoever holds the link can no longer set the account up, and the account keeps waiting, still pending_setup and still holding its place, for a new link from ./dev.py user setup-link or from a new LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN. The same token at a restart re-arms nothing, its value being stored already (_token_known()): the start finds no live link and answers expired, with the WARNING The initial administrator's setup link was withdrawn (cancelled, or its address changed) and its remedy, run ./dev.py user setup-link, followed by , or set a new LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN when the variable is set. Since lot A-50 the start tells a withdrawn link from an expired one by the account's latest setup link (by created_at, then id): revoked and never consumed, it was withdrawn; otherwise the WARNING still says has expired. A cancellation that revokes a link logs the WARNING Setup link of the initial administrator revoked: its setup was cancelled; ./dev.py user setup-link gives a new one (user_id).
  • Any other account: its setup links not consumed are retired, so that none sets it up again. An account that holds a stray live setup link and no consumed one would otherwise start waiting for its setup once deactivated: inactive, with a setup link, none of them consumed. update_user_status() retires directly the links of an account it deactivates while active, which cannot be waiting.

Protection and the other actions. A protected account refuses the cancellation on the administrator API as it refuses a deactivation: update_account() reads «waiting» once, and asks the hook about a cancellation (is_active: false on the waiting administrator, inactive already) as about a deactivation or a demotion, before any other refusal. The answer is 409 ACCOUNT_PROTECTED, and nothing changes: the link handed over keeps working. The Users tab turns Cancel setup link off for such an account, with the reason protected. The command line stays above protection, as for every protected action.

The waiting administrator keeps its role until its setup: its demotion is refused (409 PENDING_SETUP; ./dev.py user demote stops with an error), while its deletion needs no demotion first: DELETE /api/v1/users/{user_id} is the hard cancellation, its setup links going with it by the cascade of account_tokens.user_id. The routes and their answers are in The Initial Administrator.

A setup completed meanwhile (A-51). Each of these decisions reads «waiting», and the setup can complete between that read and the write: from a Users tab loaded before it, or in the same millisecond. Read stale, the cancellation, sent as {is_active: false}, the body of a deactivation, would have deactivated the new owner; a deletion would have removed an active administrator never demoted; and on a new instance, where the waiting administrator is the only account, ./dev.py user demote removed the only administrator, while ./dev.py user deactivate answered success and ended the new owner's sessions without deactivating it. The cure is the one of A-42, the write lock first:

  • update_user_status(), set_user_active() and set_user_admin() take SQLite's write lock and read the account again (user_service.refreshed_under_lock(): backend.app.db.session.begin_writes(), then session.refresh(); an account deleted meanwhile is not found, lot A-54), and only then decide: a deactivation or a demotion, the last active administrator, «waiting». On a new instance, the command line's two then refuse the administrator just set up as the last active one, nothing changed.
  • The Users tab cancels with {is_active: false, cancel_setup: true}: the cancellation and nothing else. An account that no longer waits answers 409 SETUP_COMPLETED, rolled back, with an INFO line. A plain {is_active: false} keeps its meaning, a deactivation decided on the account as the lock finds it, and its answer matches the database.
  • DELETE /api/v1/users/{user_id} reads under the lock, on the account read again, whether it is an administrator and whether it still waits (every deletion since lot A-55, which also catches a promotion): a setup completed in the meantime makes it 409 DEMOTE_FIRST, nothing deleted.

The details, with the answers of each route: A setup completed meanwhile; every path decided this way: Decided under the write lock.

Tests: A42-001 to A42-006, A43-001 to A43-005, A50-001 to A50-004 (the WARNING of a start after a cancellation or an address change, and of an expiry) and A51-007 and A51-008 (user deactivate and user demote while the setup completes) of ./dev.py test services admin-bootstrap, SETUP-016 to SETUP-018 of ./dev.py test api admin-setup, and UADM-072 to UADM-079 and A51-001 to A51-006 of ./dev.py test api users-admin (UADM-079: the cancellation of a protected waiting administrator refused, its link still working; A51: the setup completed while the Users tab acts); the Users tab's side, UTAB-55 to UTAB-62, UPS-12 to UPS-23 and AERR-13 and AERR-14, is in Users Tab and Account Deletion Tests.

docs.title: 🧾 Transactions and Logs
docs.text:
• The service never commits. issue_token() flushes, so the new row has its id; consume_token(), revoke_tokens() and retire_tokens() run their UPDATEs in the session's transaction. The caller commits: spending an invitation and creating the account it opens share one transaction, and fail together. A rollback undoes an issue, a consumption, a revocation or a retirement.
  • The service never logs the plaintext token, nor its hash. The events Account token issued, Account token consumed and Account tokens revoked carry the token id, the purpose and the user ids; Account tokens retired carries the count, the purpose and the user id. One caller logs a link, by design: the setup link of the initial administrator, when the server generated its token, is written once in the log (Links in Use).

./dev.py test services account-tokens (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_account_tokens.py) pins this contract, including two sessions consuming one token at once, a search of the logs and of every database column for the plaintext, and retire_tokens() (its contract 9); a given token (issue_token(token=)) is pinned by ./dev.py test services admin-bootstrap (TOKEN-001 to TOKEN-005). The table — columns, constraints, foreign-key actions — is described in ACCOUNT_TOKEN.

docs.title: 🔗 Links in Use: Invitations, Password Resets, Email Verification and the Setup Link
docs.text:
All four purposes have callers: invitations, password-reset links, email verification and the setup link of the initial administrator. The rules of invitations and reset links — who may register, the user limit, what each endpoint answers — are in Registration, Invitations and the Admin API; those of email verification in Email Verification; those of the setup link in The Initial Administrator. What protects their tokens:

  • Only an administrator, or whoever runs the server, issues a link it can see. POST /api/v1/users/invites and POST /api/v1/users/{user_id}/password-reset-link require an administrator; ./dev.py user invite and ./dev.py user reset-link run on the server. The token is in that response, or printed by that command, once. A lost link is replaced with a new one. The setup link has no route that issues it: the startup issues it, from the variables the operator set on the server, and ./dev.py user setup-link replaces it. «Forgot password» issues a reset link for an anonymous request, but only by email, to the account's own address, and within its limits: nobody sees that token but the mailbox (A Forgotten Password).
  • Only the newest reset or setup link of an account works. Issuing a reset link revokes the account's live reset links, and spending one revokes any other. Likewise, a setup link re-armed by a new LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN, or issued by setup-link, revokes the earlier ones, and the setup revokes any other; a setup link left live beside a consumed one sets nothing (The Setup Link's Lifecycle). A password change, an email change and ./dev.py user reset also revoke the account's live reset links (lot A-27, Session Revocation).
  • A setup link works only while its account waits for it. An activation or a new password, by any way but the link, retires the account's setup links in the same commit, and a new address revokes them. A deactivation revokes those of the waiting administrator, the cancellation after which it waits for a new link, and retires those of any other account: the table of Revocation lists every case.
  • A verification link is never shown, only emailed, and only to the account's own address. Registration issues a token without an address (the «hold»), whose text never leaves the server; the link itself goes by email, built from LIBREFOLIO_PUBLIC_URL, and «send the link again» asks for the account's password first. Each new link revokes the account's others, and spending one activates the account in the same commit. confirm_email() refuses a token without an address, and revokes one emailed to an address the account no longer has.
  • Spending is atomic with its effect. An invitation is consumed in the transaction that creates its account; a reset link in the commit that sets the new password, raises the session version and revokes the other links; a setup link in the commit that sets the password, activates the account, raises the session version and revokes the other setup links. If the account cannot be created, the invitation stays unspent. A setup link presented for an account already active, or for an account another of whose setup links was consumed, is refused, and every setup link of that account retired.
  • Inspecting tells a guesser nothing. POST /api/v1/auth/tokens/inspect is public and writes nothing. Only a valid token gets details: the expiry, plus the role and email of an invitation or the username of a reset or setup link. Any other token gets its status alone, and a token presented for another purpose is unknown.
  • Anonymous answers say nothing about the users but whether there is one. The 409 USER_LIMIT_REACHED of POST /auth/register carries no count and no billing link; only the administrator's routes add limit, used and billing_url, and the hosting panel's GET /panel/status, behind its token, users_used and users_limit: two counts, no billing link, and users_over_limit, a yes or no. About accounts, GET /system/instance publishes only the registration mode, whether a variable locks it, whether the instance has no account yet (The First-Account Flag), and the password rules, the same on every instance.
  • The token rides in the fragment, never in the query string. token_path() builds /invite#token=…, /reset-password#token=…, /verify-email#token=… and /setup#token=…. A browser never sends the fragment to the server, so the token is not in the request for the page: it stays out of the server's access log and out of the logs of every proxy on the way. A browser never puts the fragment in a Referer either. A token in the query string would be in all those logs. The page reads it with JavaScript (location.hash); a token in the query string is not read at all. A token given through LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN is made of the unreserved characters of a URL only, so the hosting panel builds the very same link itself, with nothing to encode.
  • The setup link is the one link written in the log, once, by design. When the server generated its token, deliver_setup_link() writes the link at WARNING right after the creation, then emails it when email works: a scripted install without email still gets its link. Restarts never write it again, the link works once and for 72 hours, and ./dev.py user setup-link replaces it. Whoever reads that log before the link is spent can take the administrator account: keep the log private, or give the token through the variable. A token from LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN is stored only as its hash and never logged nor emailed, and no error holds it: AdminBootstrapConfigError names the variable only.
  • The link pages hide and keep the token. /invite, /reset-password, /verify-email and /setup read the token when they mount, then put the bare path in the address bar (replaceState), so the token stays out of the history and of a bookmark; they keep it in memory only. They also listen to hashchange: a link pasted into a tab already on the page changes only the fragment and loads nothing, so the page reads the new token there. All four declare <meta name="referrer" content="no-referrer">: a link followed from them sends no Referer at all. Their components are in Authentication Components, except those of /verify-email, which does not inspect its token first and spends it only on its owner's click (lot E-25), so that a mail filter opening the link in a browser of its own verifies nothing: In the Frontend.
  • A 401 never takes a link page to the sign-in. The API client's response interceptor sends a 401 to the sign-in page from any page but / and these four, matched on the exact path (a trailing slash allowed). Their calls are public: a 401 there is the instance block refusing an anonymous caller, and the sign-in would lose the token, already out of the address bar. The page answers it itself: /setup and /invite say that the instance is blocked. Details: A 401 on a Link Page.

docs.title: 💾 Restoring a Backup
docs.text:
A restore of the whole instance comes in two moves, and neither touches the live data. The check (lot B2) unpacks an archive into .restore/stage/<stage id>/, brings the copy to this LibreFolio's revision and checks it. The confirmation (lot B3) records the restore; the next start of the server applies it, before any startup step reads the data. The code is in backend/app/services/platform/instance_backup/: apply.py (the state, the swap, the rollback, the commit), restart.py, outcome.py (the ticket of the outcome), restore_jobs.py (the checks of the API) and paths.py; the routes are in backend/app/api/v1/backup/restore.py, the command line in scripts/backup_cli.py. The administrator's side is «Restore an Archive» in Command-Line Tools.

The check also compares the ledger's control totals (Ledger Control Totals) that the backup recorded in its manifest with the copy's, once it is up to date (lot B-13, instance_backup/totals.py): a difference is a warning (control_totals_changed), never a refusal, since a migration may correct data. The copy's totals, like the snapshot's at the backup, come from J's compute_control_totals() on an engine of their own over an immutable, read-only connection (mode=ro&immutable=1), because every engine of the process sets the journal mode when it connects (set_sqlite_pragma, db/session.py), which a plain read-only connection to a rollback-journal file refuses. The totals the manifest recorded go as they are to J's ControlTotals.from_json(), which reads an amount only as plain decimal text, at most 60 digits on each side of the point, and refuses any other before reading it (J-27): an exponent an archive recorded is never expanded, and the comparison is then absent. The rule has one home, J's: compare_totals() does not repeat it (B-22). The copy's own totals go through the same reader: an amount J computes but cannot read back (more than 60 digits, as an exact huge quantity of an old or hand-edited database gives) makes the comparison unreadable, with the warning «The control totals of the copy cannot be read: they are not compared», never a failed check (B-29).

docs.title: 🧱 Triggers, Views and Virtual Tables
docs.text:
The database of an uploaded archive brings its own schema, and a schema can hold SQL that runs by itself (lot B-28, after E's security review of B3). A trigger fires when the check writes the copy: the post-migration fixes, the rekey of the plugin secrets. A view that takes the name of an app table runs whenever that name is read. A recursive one never ends: it would hold the lock of the checks until a restart, and keep a managed instance awake. After a restore, they would run in the server. LibreFolio's migrations create none of them, only tables and their indexes: such an object means that LibreFolio did not make the database, or that it was changed, so the check refuses it before anything of it can run.

  • First, before anything else opens the copy. _refuse_foreign_objects() (staging.py) runs in _stage() right after the unpacking, and after a secure backup's decrypted archive is removed: before describe_database() (the integrity check, the rows), the upgrade, the post-migration fixes, the rekey, the administrators and the totals. It opens the copy read only (mode=ro), turns trusted_schema off, and reads SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master, every row: it runs nothing of the archive, and writes nothing.
  • By the SQL text. _schema_object_kind() reads each object from its SQL, since SQLite builds its schema from that text whatever the row's type says. It takes the first words, past spaces and SQL comments (-- …, /* … */), case-insensitive: CREATE TABLE is a table, CREATE INDEX or CREATE UNIQUE INDEX an index, and SQL NULL one of SQLite's own automatic indexes. Anything else is foreign: CREATE TRIGGER (trigger), CREATE VIEW (view), CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE (virtual), and any other text, CREATE TEMP … included (other). A comment between the keywords, as in CREATE/**/TRIGGER, hides nothing.
  • The refusal. One foreign object or more: StagingError database_foreign_objects, The backup's database holds triggers, views or other objects LibreFolio never creates: it cannot be restored, and one warning in the log, A backup's database holds schema objects LibreFolio never creates, with objects (their count) and kinds: never a name nor any SQL, which are the archive's text. As for every refusal, the whole copy is removed. The code is in RestoreErrorCode; the restore card shows backup.restore.errors.database_foreign_objects, and the command line prints ❌ … (database_foreign_objects).
  • A schema SQLite refuses to read is database_damaged: any sqlite3.DatabaseError of that read, such as a row whose SQL does not parse, or a row that disguises its object, a trigger whose row says type = 'table' (SQLite then refuses the whole schema, «malformed database schema», checked on 3.54.0).
  • What the check cannot read. _refuse_foreign_objects() takes each object's kind, never the expressions inside a table or an index. An index's expression calling a function plain sqlite3 lacks, such as regexp, fails the integrity check of describe_database() («unknown function»), read only or not, and so does a generated column calling one when that check computes it (a virtual column with a declared type, a NOT NULL one, one an index or a STRICT table relies on; an untyped virtual column or a stored one passes, checked on 3.54.0). A CHECK calling one passes that check: on a read-only connection SQLite leaves the CHECK constraints out, and its integrity_check answers ok even for a violated built-in CHECK (checked on 3.54.0). Such a CHECK fails at the first read-write integrity_check, the post-migration fixes', as it would at a write to its table. That error, and any other sqlite3 error while the check reads or checks the copy's database (not a ProgrammingError, a bug of LibreFolio's), ends the check with database_damaged, The backup's database cannot be read or checked: it cannot be restored (lot B-43). It is logged as a warning with the error's class and SQLite's error name only: the error's message names the archive's function, and no text of the archive reaches the log, as with the kinds above. Before B-43 such an error escaped as it was: the app's check answered stage_failed, and dev.py backup restore stopped with a traceback. The schema itself is first read as the server's connections read it: _refuse_foreign_objects() registers the functions SQLAlchemy registers there, regexp and floor, as stand-ins that never run (_register_server_functions()). A schema that calls one in an index or a generated column, which every connection of the server refuses since H-51 («unsafe use of …»), so that the first start after the restore would fail, cannot be read there either: database_damaged, before anything else opens the copy. A CHECK or a DEFAULT calling them passes that read, since SQLite resolves them only when used: after a restore, the writes that need them fail, and nothing of the archive runs (backlog B-45). When the copy needs an upgrade, the upgrade runs first: a CHECK calling regexp, which its connections refuse since H-51 (below), or one on a table it writes, ends the check there, as upgrade_failed.
  • Text that is not UTF-8 is database_damaged too (lot B-49). The server's driver decodes every text it reads, and a value that is not UTF-8 makes it raise («Could not decode to UTF-8 column …»): the whole read fails, not the row, so after a restore every list holding such a value would fail, and no page could correct what it cannot read (checked in process through the app's own engine, on SQLite 3.54.0). LibreFolio writes UTF-8 only: such text means that another program wrote to the database, or that the archive was changed. _refuse_undecodable_text() reads every text value of the copy right after the manifest's counts are compared, before the upgrade, so no migration meets it first: every table but SQLite's own, unknown ones included, every column, generated ones included (table_xinfo: table_info hides them), values by storage class (typeof(…) = 'text': dates and timestamps are text in their DATE and DATETIME columns). It reads each table by keyset windows of its rowid, 200 000 rows a query, each column's text values joined by SQLite with a comma and decoded once by a strict text_factory that raises UnicodeDecodeError. The comma, a byte of its own, never completes a character split over two values. A table without a rowid, or whose columns take all of rowid, _rowid_ and oid, is read row by row, in constant memory, and so is the rest of a table whose window SQLite cannot join (texts past its length limit, DataError). On a 488 MB database (2 million prices, 1 million exchange rates, 200 000 transactions) it took 3.3 s, against 5.5 s for one integrity_check (checked at a normal load). The refusal says The backup's database holds text that is not UTF-8: it cannot be restored, and logs one warning, A backup's database holds text that is not UTF-8, with the number of tables (tables): never a text, its bytes, a table or a column name, which are the archive's.
  • trusted_schema off on every connection to the copy. Every connection to the copy runs PRAGMA trusted_schema=OFF before any other statement: this read, describe_database() (snapshot.py, which also describes the backup's own snapshot), _refuse_undecodable_text(), _plugin_secrets(), _administrators() and E-19b1's _holds_non_iso_currencies() (staging.py), the totals' aiosqlite connection (totals.py), the post-migration fixes and the upgrade. The SQL the schema keeps in its tables and indexes (a CHECK, a DEFAULT, a generated column, an index's expression) may then call only the functions SQLite marks innocuous. run_post_migration_fixes() (db/post_migration/__init__.py), shared code that runs after the refusal, turns it off first on its own connection, on the live database too, where nothing changes, since LibreFolio's schema holds only tables and indexes (lot B-37); its count(*) of each table quotes the name, doubling ", since an archive's tables may be named anything (lot B-36). The upgrade runs alembic upgrade head in a process of its own, stopped after an hour (UPGRADE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS). On its connections set_sqlite_pragma() turns it off first, since lot H-51 (trusted_schema Off in the Server's Engines), and backend/alembic/env.py turns it off again with a connect listener of its own, _schema_untrusted, once the dialect has registered regexp and floor, whatever the URL: the copy's, given with -x sqlalchemy.url, and the live database's alike (lot B-37).
  • Why the upgrade needs it. SQLAlchemy's SQLite dialects (pysqlite, which aiosqlite inherits; SQLAlchemy 2.0.52, SQLiteDialect_pysqlite.on_connect()) register two Python functions on every connection: regexp (re.search), behind the REGEXP operator, and floor (math.floor), in place of SQLite's own floor() where the build has one. The upgrade runs on such connections. With _schema_untrusted, an insert of the upgrade that needs an archive's DEFAULT calling them is refused («unsafe use of …»), and the upgrade fails (upgrade_failed) instead of running Python code on the archive's pattern. A CHECK or an index's expression calling regexp is refused there only since lot H-51, at the first statement: before it, set_sqlite_pragma() read the schema on those connections before the dialect registered the functions, and such a call then ran at the insert (trusted_schema Off in the Server's Engines).

Tests: ./dev.py test services backup-staging (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_backup_staging.py, section (l): a trigger, a recursive view, an fts5 virtual table and a comment between the keywords, each refused before describe_database() runs, the log with the count and the kinds and no name; a disguised row and a row that does not parse, database_damaged; the head database, tables and indexes only, a guard for the day a migration adds a trigger or a view; trusted_schema off first on every connection of a whole check, the post-migration fixes' included, lot B-37), ./dev.py test db post-migration (backend/test_scripts/test_db/test_post_migration.py: tables named x"y or a" WHERE 1 --, counted while a fix runs, lot B-36) and ./dev.py test utils dev-cli-db-path (backend/test_scripts/test_utilities/test_dev_cli_db_path.py: the connect listener of env.py, lot B-37). Lot B-43: ./dev.py test services backup-staging (a function plain sqlite3 lacks, in an index's expression, a generated column and a CHECK, each database_damaged; regexp in a generated column and floor in an index, refused at the read of the schema, before anything else opens the copy; one warning, the function named in no log; a CHECK on a built-in function, restored as usual; LibreFolio's own index on lower(), read with the stand-ins) and ./dev.py test utils backup-cli-restore (the refusal on the command line, no traceback).

docs.title: trusted_schema Off in the Server's Engines
docs.text:
set_sqlite_pragma() in backend/app/db/session.py is the connect listener every SQLAlchemy engine of the process gets: it is registered on the Engine class, so it holds for each engine, the synchronous one under the async engine included. Since lot H-51 it turns trusted_schema off first, before foreign_keys, WAL and busy_timeout, and ends with PRAGMA writable_schema=RESET.

  • Why. The check refuses triggers, views and virtual tables by their kind (lot B-28), but does not read the expressions inside tables and indexes, and its plain sqlite3 connections never evaluate a DEFAULT: PRAGMA integrity_check answers ok. Before H-51, an archive whose column had DEFAULT (regexp(…)) passed the check, and in the server every insert that omitted that column ran SQLAlchemy's Python regexp with the archive's pattern and value, through the async engine too. An index's expression calling a function plain sqlite3 lacks, such as regexp, stops the check at the PRAGMA integrity_check of describe_database() («unknown function»), before the upgrade runs, and so does a generated column calling one when that check computes it (a virtual column with a declared type, a NOT NULL one, one an index or a STRICT table relies on). A CHECK calling one passes that read-only check, which SQLite runs without the CHECK constraints, and stops the check at the first read-write one, the post-migration fixes' integrity_check. Either way the check ends with database_damaged (lot B-43), unless an upgrade runs before and fails on the CHECK first (upgrade_failed, below).
  • Why the reset, last. SQLAlchemy calls the listeners registered on a class before those of one engine, so this one runs before the dialect's on_connect() registers regexp and floor, and its PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL makes SQLite read the schema right then. SQLite marks a call as the schema's own only when it finds the function, and checks nothing again later: read then, a CHECK or an index's expression calling regexp would run SQLAlchemy's Python function at each insert into its table, trusted_schema off or not. writable_schema=RESET drops that reading: SQLite reads the schema again at the next statement that needs it, with the functions registered and trusted_schema off. It costs one more read of the schema per new connection, and both engines of session.py open a new connection for each use (NullPool).
  • When SQLite refuses. A CHECK or an index's expression calling regexp: at the first statement of the connection that needs the schema, a SELECT of another table included (malformed database schema (<object>) - unsafe use of REGEXP()). A DEFAULT calling regexp or floor: at the insert that needs it («unsafe use of regexp()»). The refusal comes at a statement, never inside the listener: SQLAlchemy's pool does not close a connection whose connect listener raised (_ConnectionRecord.__connect()).
  • Nothing of the app changes. LibreFolio's own schema calls only the built-in lower() (the index ux_users_email_lower, step 6 of migration 005_release_1_3_0_schema), and the pragma restricts only the SQL the schema holds, never top-level SQL.
  • In the upgrade's process too. backend/alembic/env.py imports backend.app.db.base, so the package's backend/app/db/__init__.py, which imports session.py: the upgrade's connections get set_sqlite_pragma() as well, before _schema_untrusted, which env.py registers on its own engine. Before H-51, set_sqlite_pragma() read the schema there before _schema_untrusted turned the pragma off and before the functions existed: _schema_untrusted stopped a DEFAULT, refused at the insert, but not a CHECK or an index's expression. Since H-51, with the pragma off first and the schema reset last, the rule holds for all of them there too.

Tests: ./dev.py test db session-pragmas (backend/test_scripts/test_db/test_session_pragmas.py, through a sync and an async engine: trusted_schema at 0 on two new connections in a row; a DEFAULT calling regexp or floor refused at the insert that needs it, nothing written; a CHECK calling regexp through REGEXP refused at the first statement of every new connection, a SELECT of another table included, both tables left as the archive wrote them; guards: foreign_keys, WAL and busy_timeout as before, lower(), length() and abs() in the schema, REGEXP, regexp_match and floor in a statement's own SQL, and the schema at head, migrated under the listener, taking a user through the async engine).

docs.title: 📏 The Restore Limit
docs.text:
