  • Write. The application writes utcnow() (backend/app/utils/datetime_utils.py), an aware UTC datetime. The plain DateTime column drops the offset when it binds the value: an aware datetime in another zone would be stored as its local wall-clock time, so convert it to UTC first.
  • Read. A value read back is naive. Treat it as UTC: ensure_utc() adds the offset, and the API schemas' UTCDateTime type serializes it with Z.

  • Declare the column. Every datetime field of a model sets sa_type=DateTime. Since SQLModel 0.0.48 a field without it maps to SQLModel's UTCDateTime, which refuses a naive value on write and in a filter, and reads every value back aware: the same column would then answer differently from the rest of the schema. A new timestamp field follows the same pattern:

    created_at: datetime = Field(default_factory=utcnow, sa_type=DateTime)

  • Moving to aware datetimes (backlog D-UTC, release 1.4) needs no migration: both mappings store the same text and declare the same DATETIME column. What changes is every naive value written or compared by the tests, and the API fields that format a stored value with isoformat().

docs.title: 🧬 Migrations
docs.text:
Schema changes ship as Alembic revisions in backend/alembic/versions/ (workflow: Database Migrations). At startup, the database step of the lifespan runs ensure_database_exists() (backend/app/services/platform/database_bootstrap.py), which builds a missing, empty or table-less database from scratch, and runs alembic upgrade head when the revision stored in alembic_version is not the head of the scripts. The head comes from alembic_head_revision() (backend/app/services/platform/readiness.py), the reader GET /system/ready uses too.

The chain is linear:

File Revision id Revises Change 001_initial.py 001_initial — Squashed baseline: the 12 original tables with their indexes and constraints. 005_release_1_3_0_schema drops 13 of these indexes; the file stays as released 002_identifier_other_json_list.py 002_identifier_other_json_list 001_initial Data only: assets.identifier_other becomes a JSON list 003_scheduler_timezone.py 5b1333fa6b07 002_identifier_other_json_list Data only: the stored scheduler sync times move from UTC to scheduler_timezone wall-clock time 004_release_1_2_0_schema.py 004_release_1_2_0_schema 5b1333fa6b07 assets.is_benchmark and the two onboarding progress tables 005_release_1_3_0_schema.py 005_release_1_3_0_schema 004_release_1_2_0_schema The whole of release 1.3, in seven steps that each check before they act, so a run that stopped half way can run again: (1) four users columns, session_version, email_verified_at, last_seen_version and is_instance_owner (BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT 0: the owner of a managed instance), with plain ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN, never a batch, and the partial unique index ux_users_instance_owner ON users (is_instance_owner) WHERE is_instance_owner = 1 (at most one owner; the owner query plans SEARCH users USING COVERING INDEX ux_users_instance_owner); (2) the account_tokens table of single-use account links, with its two indexes and a ck_account_tokens_purpose that accepts invite, password_reset, email_verification, admin_setup and email_change; (3) data only: the global setting enable_registration becomes registration_mode, open when the old value read as true (true, 1, yes, on, any case), disabled otherwise; (4) the plugin_system_settings and plugin_user_settings tables, created empty; (5) data only: where registration_mode is missing and users holds an account, open is written, the earlier default (decision 36); (6) the unique index ux_users_email_lower on lower(email), so that an email address belongs to one account whatever its A–Z case, after a check that stops the upgrade when two accounts already share one; (7) 13 indexes of 001_initial that no query needs, dropped with DROP INDEX IF EXISTS (Indexes: Only the Ones a Query Uses). The downgrade goes back step by step: the 13 indexes again with their 001 definitions, and enable_registration again (true for open, false for invite and disabled); the tokens, the plugin settings and the values of the new columns are lost

The revision id is the contract, not the filename

v1.1.0 shipped the scheduler migration as 5b1333fa6b07_scheduler_times_use_configured_timezone.py. The file was later renamed 003_scheduler_timezone.py so that the files sort in order, but its revision is still 5b1333fa6b07: released databases store that id in alembic_version, and changing it would orphan them. Chain a new migration from the head's revision id (down_revision), never from a filename, and keep the graph linear — two revisions with the same down_revision create two heads, and alembic upgrade head refuses to choose between them.

Retired revision ids

Release 1.3 ships one migration, as release 1.2 ships 004 (One Migration per Release). The revisions written during the 1.3 cycle were in no released tag, and are gone: 005_accounts_invites, 006_registration_mode, 007_plugin_settings, 008_registration_invite_default, 009_email_unique_ignoring_case, 010_provider_reported_currency, 011_provider_exchange_timezone and 006_owner_email_change. The first five and the last are steps 1 to 6 of 005_release_1_3_0_schema; 010 is not kept (asset_provider_assignments has no reported_currency column), and 011 had been removed before. A database stamped with one of these ids comes from an unreleased build, and no code handles it: the server does not start on it (alembic upgrade head cannot locate the revision, the database step logs Failed to apply database migrations and exits), and a backup archive at one is refused as from a newer LibreFolio (Restoring a Backup). A developer brings such a database forward by hand, with the sqlite3 procedure of the developer journal (the plan of workstream H, section «Procedura manuale»).

docs.title: 🩹 Post-migration fixes
docs.text:
Some repairs cannot be Alembic revisions. Rebuilding a table that others reference with ON DELETE CASCADE is one: the Alembic process imports backend.app.db.session, whose engine listener turns foreign keys on, and dropping the old table would then empty the tables that point at it. These repairs live in backend/app/db/post_migration/ as ordered PostMigrationFix subclasses (FIXES: a new fix is appended, never inserted before an older one). Right after the database step, the post-migration-fixes step of the lifespan runs run_post_migration_fixes_at_startup() (backend/app/services/platform/database_bootstrap.py) in a worker thread; it never lets an error stop the startup. run_post_migration_fixes() works on a direct sqlite3 connection, with trusted_schema off before anything else (lot B-37):

  1. It holds an exclusive fcntl.flock on <db file>.post-migration.lock, beside the database, from the integrity check to the cleanup, dry runs included: the workers of a multi-worker server and the offline script take turns, and the later runs find nothing to do. The lock file is never deleted. It is opened with O_NOFOLLOW and, when missing, created 0600: a symbolic link in its place raises OSError before the database is opened, and nothing behind the link is created or locked. At startup that is logged as the WARNING Post-migration fixes could not run; starting normally (error) and the server starts without the fixes; the offline script does not catch it and ends with the traceback, exit code 1. On a non-POSIX system the runs are not serialised.
  2. It touches nothing unless PRAGMA integrity_check answers ok.
  3. Every fix detect()s its anomaly without writing: nothing found, nothing written or logged.
  4. It checkpoints the WAL (wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)) and copies the database with SQLite's backup API to <db file>.pre-<fix ids>-<UTC %Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ>.bak. No copy, no fix.
  5. Each pending fix runs prepare() outside the transaction (filesystem work to undo on failure), then, with foreign_keys = OFF (SQLite switches it only outside a transaction), BEGIN IMMEDIATE, apply(), verify() and the common checks — no PRAGMA foreign_key_check row that was not there just before the fix, the row count of every table unchanged but for the changes the fix declares (row_count_changes(), {table: delta}, checked exactly) — before COMMIT. Any problem rolls back. finish() runs after either outcome, and a failed fix stops the ones after it. A broken reference the database already held is not the fix's to judge: it stays, and the run logs those it found once, as the WARNING Foreign key violations already in the database, left as they are (count, and up to 20 of the rows foreign_key_check gives).
  6. All applied: the backup is deleted and Post-migration fixes applied and verified is logged. Otherwise the backup is kept and Post-migration fix failed: the database was left as it was gives its path and the errors. Both lines carry seconds.

python -m backend.app.db.post_migration [--db PATH] [--data-dir PATH] [--dry-run] (__main__.py) runs the same function with the server stopped, which it does not check, then, as at startup, the step for the lone giving legs. Each fix reports clean, would_apply (dry run), applied or failed (PostMigrationReport); the exit code is 1 when a fix, the integrity check or that step failed. Run that way, it also logs what the server logs at startup — the warnings, each fix's own lines and the step's, the closing line with seconds — on the console only (configure_logging(LOG_LEVEL, enable_file_logging=False), as JSON on stdout between its summary lines), so it writes no log file in the data directory; main() called from code configures nothing.

The first fix, autoincrement (autoincrement.py), gives AUTOINCREMENT to the id of the tables whose ids leave the backend (AUTOINCREMENT_TABLES: users, brokers, assets, transactions, fx_conversion_routes, asset_events). Without it SQLite gives a new row max(id) + 1, so a row created after the newest one was deleted inherits its id, and whatever outside the database still points at it: a saved URL, a benchmark in localStorage, a broker_<id> report folder. New databases get it from 001_initial.py; the fix converts existing ones, once.

  • Each table is rebuilt from its current CREATE TABLE text with that single change, so the columns added by later migrations stay: renamed aside under legacy_alter_table = ON (the foreign keys of the other tables keep naming it), recreated, rows copied as they are, old table dropped, indexes recreated. Any other shape of the id column stops the fix before anything is touched.
  • Its own checks: the stored DDL and indexes match the plan, and sqlite_sequence is not behind max(id).
  • When brokers is converted and the database lies inside the data directory, the broker_reports/<status>/broker_<n> folders whose broker no longer exists are first renamed to .quarantine-autoincrement-<UTC>-broker_<n> (out of the listing's broker_* glob), deleted once the fix is verified, renamed back if it fails: the first broker created afterwards may reuse <n> once, and must not inherit them.

The second fix, orphan_pair_halves (orphan_pair_halves.py), converts the half of a pair whose partner is gone. Until 1.3, deleting a broker left the other half of each pair it had with another broker as a TRANSFER, CASH_TRANSFER or FX_CONVERSION without its partner: its link cleared (related_transaction_id NULL) or, when foreign keys were off, naming a row that no longer exists. The FIFO lots refuse such a TRANSFER (TRANSFER_PAIR_MISSING), and the Dashboard counts it as capital at its market value on its date. Since 1.3, delete_by_broker() converts that half as it deletes the broker (Broker Deletion); this fix converts, once, the halves already in a database.

  • detect() writes nothing. It selects the rows of the three paired types whose link is NULL or names a missing row, and the rows of any other type whose link names a missing row. A row whose partner exists is never selected.
  • It converts a half as a split of the pair leaves it (STANDALONE_TYPES, the values of TransactionService.SPLIT_TYPE_MAP). A received TRANSFER (positive quantity) becomes an ADJUSTMENT with its quantity, asset, cost basis and its currency. When no cost basis was recorded it stays without one, since the sender is gone: MISSING_COST_BASIS until the user enters it (the 1.3 deletion writes the sender's Auto cost instead). A CASH_TRANSFER or FX_CONVERSION becomes a WITHDRAWAL when its amount is negative, a DEPOSIT otherwise, without asset. The link goes, updated_at moves to now, every other column stays.
  • It leaves the giving leg of a TRANSFER (negative quantity) to the step after the fixes: counted, not changed (see Lone giving legs). It also leaves a row whose quantity or amount sign cannot be read, and the rows of other types (an ADJUSTMENT can carry a link). Each of these keeps its type, and loses its link only when that link names a missing row, so that the run's foreign_key_check can pass.
  • Its own checks, on top of the common ones: no convertible half left, and each row it changed has its expected type and no link.
  • Its detection logs whenever it finds such a row, dry runs included, even with nothing to change: a WARNING with count (every row found), conversions (the ids per TYPE->TYPE), without_cost_basis, unlinked_only, left_giving_transfer_legs and left_unreadable_sign. It comes back at every start while a giving leg, or a row of unreadable sign, remains — a giving leg remains only when the step after the fixes did not run or failed; with nothing left to change, the outcome is clean. After the commit, finish() logs one INFO line per row changed — Transaction without its pair converted or … unlinked — with transaction_id, broker_id, date, from_type, to_type, quantity, amount, currency, asset_id, cost_basis, cost_basis_currency, missing_cost_basis and former_partner_id (the missing row the link named, null when the link was already cleared). The offline script prints them too, on the console.

./dev.py test db post-migration-orphan-pairs (backend/test_scripts/test_db/test_post_migration_orphan_pairs.py) pins this contract.

The fix event_types (event_types.py) repairs the asset events stored with a type the app does not know. Until 1.3 an event type was saved as it came — a CSV written by hand could store dividend or dividendo — while the column is the AssetEventType enum: every later read of that asset's events failed (LookupError, a 500) and none of them was shown. Since 1.3 FAAssetEventPoint trims and upper-cases the type on the way in and refuses one that is still unknown (422); this fix repairs the rows already stored, once (decision 23 of release 1.3).

  • detect() writes nothing. It selects the events whose type is not exactly one of the enum's values.
  • A type that becomes valid once trimmed and upper-cased (Python's str.strip().upper(), the schema's own rule) is corrected in place: the event keeps its id, and its transactions stay linked.
  • Any other event is deleted, a provider's included (they are not shown already). Its transactions are unlinked first — asset_event_id NULL, updated_at now — and stay, without their event.
  • It declares its deletions (row_count_changes() → {"asset_events": -n}), so the framework checks that exactly those rows went; its own verify() wants no unknown type left, each correction in place, each deleted event gone and named by no transaction.
  • Logs: the detection WARNING (dry runs included) with count, corrections (ids per stored->CORRECTED), deletions (ids per stored type) and unlinked_transactions; after the commit, one INFO line per corrected event (Asset event type corrected), per unlinked transaction (Transaction unlinked from an asset event of unknown type) and per deleted event (Asset event of unknown type deleted, with its date, value, currency, is_auto and the transactions unlinked).

./dev.py test db post-migration-event-types (backend/test_scripts/test_db/test_post_migration_event_types.py) pins this contract and the declared row counts.

The admin side (log lines, the offline run) is in Command-Line Tools.

docs.title: 📤 Lone giving legs, after the fixes
docs.text:
Until 1.3, deleting a broker also left the giving leg of each TRANSFER it had received units through as a TRANSFER without its partner. Since 1.3 the deletion turns such a leg into an ADJUSTMENT taking its units out, and such an ADJUSTMENT has no value: its units only leave the quantity, and the FIFO lots and the Dashboard realize their cost as a loss (decision 47 of release 1.3, as the developer changed it on 21/10/2026, N78-1; until then the leg left at the Auto cost of its own broker; see Broker Deletion). The legs already in a database get the same from backend/app/services/transactions/lone_transfer_legs.py, a step that runs right after the fixes, in two places:

  • At startup, as the lone-transfer-legs step of the lifespan, right after post-migration-fixes. convert_lone_giving_legs_at_startup() does not read the fixes' report: it opens its own session on the configured engine and first looks for one lone giving leg. With none, it returns at once and checks nothing, so the common case costs one query. Otherwise the database must pass PRAGMA quick_check first: any answer but ok leaves every row as it is, with the WARNING Lone transfer legs left as they are: the database failed its quick check. Then it converts and commits. It never stops the startup: a failure is logged as the WARNING Lone transfer legs could not be converted; starting normally, every row stays as it was, and the next start tries again.
  • In python -m backend.app.db.post_migration, after the fixes, only when their integrity check passed and no fix failed: run_lone_giving_legs(db_path, dry_run=...), on the same file through an engine of its own.

So neither path touches a damaged database, as the fixes never do. One difference remains: after a fix that failed on a database that passes the check, the startup step still runs, and the offline script does not.

Both call convert_lone_giving_legs(session, *, dry_run=False):

  • Selection. A TRANSFER with a negative quantity is lone when its link is NULL or names a row that no longer exists: the fix clears such a link first, and a dry run, which applies no fix, still sees the leg. SQLite reads the sign (quantity < 0 in the query), so a row whose quantity it cannot read as a number is never selected. A lone receiving leg (the fix's) and a linked TRANSFER are never touched.
  • Conversion. Every lone giving leg found becomes an ADJUSTMENT (make_standalone(): the same quantity, asset, date, description and tags, no link, a new updated_at), and its cost_basis_override and cost_basis_currency are cleared. No cost is computed, so no leg needs a rate or a readable pool, and every one is converted.
  • Transaction. The function commits nothing: its caller commits, or rolls back after a dry run, which changes nothing. Outside a dry run it first calls begin_writes(session, Transaction), which takes the write lock: of several workers starting together, the first converts and the next find nothing to convert.
  • Answer and logs. It returns one LoneLeg per lone giving leg found (id, broker_id, date, quantity, asset_id). Each leg gets an INFO line with transaction_id, broker_id, date, quantity and asset_id: Lone transfer leg converted to an ADJUSTMENT-out without a value (on a dry run, Lone transfer leg would become an ADJUSTMENT-out without a value).

After the fixes' lines, the offline script prints one line per lone giving leg (LoneLeg.describe()), became instead of would become on a real run:

Lone transfer leg <id> (broker <id>, <date>, quantity <quantity>, asset <id>): would become an ADJUSTMENT-out without a value

When the step itself raises, the script prints Error: lone transfer legs: <error> and exits with 1.

./dev.py test services lone-transfer-legs (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_lone_transfer_legs.py) pins this contract.

docs.title: 📏 asset_type and transactions.type lengths
docs.text:
assets.asset_type and transactions.type are plain VARCHAR columns with no CHECK constraint: the allowed values live in the Python enums (AssetType and TransactionType in backend/app/db/models.py), so adding a value is a code change, not a migration. Since 22/09/2026, 001_initial declares both columns VARCHAR(32). They were VARCHAR(14), shorter than ETF_REAL_ESTATE (15 characters).

Databases created before that change keep the VARCHAR(14) declaration, on purpose: no migration rebuilds assets and transactions for it. SQLite does not enforce a declared length, so both declarations accept the same values. A schema built from the migrations on an engine that enforces lengths gets VARCHAR(32).

docs.title: 📂 Data Directory on Disk
docs.text:
get_data_dir() (backend/app/config/__init__.py) picks the root: in test mode LIBREFOLIO_TEST_DATA_DIR (default backend/data/test), otherwise LIBREFOLIO_DATA_DIR (default backend/data/prod); a relative path resolves from the project root. At every startup ensure_data_dirs() creates sqlite/, custom-uploads/, broker_reports/{uploaded,parsed,failed}/ and logs/ and, outside test mode, writes the .librefolio-production-data marker: validate_test_data_dir() refuses a test root that overlaps a production root, lies inside a marked one or aliases one of its paths. The admin view of the same layout is Filesystem Structure.

Path Written by (under backend/app/) Content sqlite/app.db (+ -wal, -shm) the engines of db/session.py The database; every connection sets journal_mode=WAL and foreign_keys=ON sqlite/app.db.post-migration.lock db/post_migration/ Empty lock of the post-migration fixes, created 0600 and opened with O_NOFOLLOW, never deleted sqlite/app.db.pre-<fix ids>-<UTC>.bak db/post_migration/ Backup kept after a failed fix custom-uploads/<uuid>.<ext> + <uuid>.json services/files/static_uploads.py Uploaded file and its sidecar: id, original_name, extension, mime_type, size_bytes, uploaded_at, uploaded_by_user_id, description and scope, absent from older sidecars and from the seeded avatars' (Uploaded Files: Common and Personal); the sidecar is written to a temporary file, then renamed (File Upload) custom-uploads/.avatars_seeded seed_default_avatars() in services/files/static_uploads.py Marker: the PNGs of backend/staticResources/Avatars/ were copied, uploader 0 (system); without it the next start copies them again broker_reports/ services/brim/brim_provider.py Reports and sidecars by status and broker, plus .locks/ (File Lifecycle) logs/librefolio.log logging_config.py structlog JSONRenderer lines; TimedRotatingFileHandler (when="W0", utc=True, backupCount=52) whose rotator gzips each archive to librefolio.log.<date>.gz scheduler_state.json services/platform/scheduler/state.py Last run of the current_price and history_sync jobs, with the count of items a provider's pause deferred (last_items_deferred) and their retry_at, and the failures in a row (consecutive_failures) and next_attempt_at, the end of the wait after them (Provider Pauses and Failures); written then renamed; a missing or corrupt file means a fresh state .scheduler.lock services/platform/scheduler/run_lock.py Empty lock that serialises the scheduler's runs across the worker processes (Several Workers): an exclusive flock, the file created 0600 by the first run that takes it and opened with O_NOFOLLOW, never deleted. Safe to leave in place; never delete it while LibreFolio runs. Not used where Python has no fcntl secrets/instance.key services/platform/instance_key.py The instance key, only when neither LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY nor LIBREFOLIO_INSTANCE_KEY_FILE is set. Created by the first derive_key() call, not by ensure_data_dirs(): secrets.token_urlsafe(32) and a newline (43 characters, 44 bytes), folder 0700, file 0600. Published with a hard link so that the first key wins, then never rewritten; a file that goes missing is generated again, see the known limitation. validate_test_data_dir() keeps a test root from aliasing it cache/pdf-fonts/<package>/<file> services/files/pdf_fonts.py (cache_dir()) The PDF viewer's CJK fonts, fetched once by the server and kept only when their sha256 matches pdf_font_hashes.json (The PDF Viewer's CJK Fonts): written to a temporary name in the same folder, then renamed; a file of the wrong size is fetched again. Safe to delete, never archived by a backup (ARCHIVED_FOLDERS of services/platform/instance_backup/paths.py does not hold it); validate_test_data_dir() keeps a test root from aliasing it scenario_catalog/{historical,hypothetical}/ the administrator Optional host scenarios (Scenario Catalogue)

docs.title: 📊 Assets & Pricing
docs.text: Global financial instruments and their pricing sources. Assets are shared across all users — only the transactions referencing them are user-specific.

docs.title: 📦 ASSET
docs.text:
Global definition of a financial instrument. display_name is unique; the identifier columns (identifier_isin, identifier_ticker, …) are indexed but not unique. Each asset belongs to an Asset Type.

  • 📋 classification_params (JSON): Stores flexible metadata like Sector, Geography, and Industry without requiring schema changes.
    • Distributions (FAClassificationParams.geographic_area and .sector_area, backend/app/schemas/assets/metadata.py:235-258) store their weights as fractions that sum to exactly 1, with 4 decimals. The UI works in percent: the distribution editor and the distribution CSV import accept a total within 0.005 points of 100, and divide each weight by 100 before saving (DistributionEditor.svelte:132,192, DistributionDataImportModal.svelte:35,42).
    • Backend check. BaseDistribution._validate_and_normalize_weights (metadata.py:54-133) rejects a sum farther than 0.01 from 1. Otherwise it renormalizes the weights, quantizes them to 4 decimals with ROUND_HALF_EVEN, and puts the rounding residue on the smallest weight.
  • 💰 currency: The asset's native currency (e.g., USD for Apple, EUR for ASML).
  • 🏷️ asset_type: One AssetType value — see Asset types and subtypes below.
  • ⭐ is_benchmark (BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT 0): The asset is offered as a comparison benchmark. The risk benchmark selector (BenchmarkSelect.svelte) and the chart's comparison-asset picker (SignalAssetParamControl.svelte) list flagged assets in a section of their own, apart from the other assets; GET /api/v1/assets/query?is_benchmark=true|false filters on the flag (omitted = both).
    • Shared, not per-user: assets has no owner column, so the flag is the same for every user.
    • Independent of asset_type: any asset can be a benchmark, and an INDEX asset does not have to be one.
    • Seeded once: migration 004_release_1_2_0_schema set the flag on the existing INDEX assets, only when it created the column — a flag the user cleared later is never restored.

docs.title: 🏷️ Asset types and subtypes
docs.text:
assets.asset_type stores exactly one AssetType value (backend/app/db/models.py):

Level Values Base types STOCK, ETF, BOND, CRYPTO, FUND, CROWDFUND, HOLD, COMMODITY, REAL_ESTATE, INDEX, OTHER ETF subtypes (family ETF) ETF_STOCK, ETF_BOND, ETF_COMMODITY, ETF_REAL_ESTATE, ETF_CRYPTO, ETF_MONETARY Crowdfunding subtype (family CROWDFUND) CROWDFUND_REAL_ESTATE

A subtype says which base type the instrument contains: ETF_BOND is an ETF that holds bonds, CROWDFUND_REAL_ESTATE a crowdfunding loan backed by property. ETF_MONETARY (money-market funds) is the one subtype with no base-type counterpart. The plain ETF and CROWDFUND values stay valid, as the residual for mixed or unstated content.

  • 🗄️ Stored as is. The column keeps the exact value and nothing rolls up in the database; the backend aggregates by the stored value too (the allocation by type, DailyStateBuilder._distribute_allocation() in financial_math/portfolio/daily_state.py). Grouping a subtype with its family is a frontend concern: ASSET_TYPE_FAMILY / assetTypeFamily() in frontend/src/lib/utils/assetTypes.ts files every ETF_* value under ETF and CROWDFUND_REAL_ESTATE under CROWDFUND, for the asset-type select and for both allocation charts (see the Allocation Panel).
  • 🚫 INDEX is the one value with backend behaviour: transactions on an INDEX asset are refused (batch_creates.py). It does not imply is_benchmark.
  • ➕ Adding a value needs no migration: the column is a plain VARCHAR(32) with no CHECK constraint (databases created before 22/09/2026 still declare VARCHAR(14), harmless on SQLite — see Migrations). The frontend tables keyed on the enum must follow: frontend/src/lib/utils/__tests__/assetTypeTables.test.ts reads the enum from backend/app/db/models.py and fails when one of them misses the new value.

docs.title: 📈 PRICE_HISTORY
docs.text:
Daily OHLCV (Open, High, Low, Close, Volume) price data for each asset, one row per (asset_id, date). Populated by asset pricing providers. open, high, low and close are all nullable: the price resolver values a day from close, and uses the day's range only when open, high and low are all present.

The prices (open, high, low, close, adjusted_close) are RealDecimal(24, 12): up to 12 digits before the decimal point and 12 decimal places, read back as written; volume is RealDecimal(24, 0) (W-B63): up to 24 digits before the point. A provider's prices are truncated to 12 decimal places and 15 significant digits, and a date with a value no column can keep (a price not finite or past 12 digits before the point, a volume past 24) is skipped; a manual price over any of these limits, or a manual volume past 24 digits, is refused (see Decimal Columns).

docs.title: 🔌 ASSET_PROVIDER_ASSIGNMENT
docs.text:
Decouples the asset from its data source. This table configures which provider to use for fetching prices and metadata.

  • 📋 Example: "Use Yahoo Finance (yfinance) for Apple (AAPL)"
  • ⚙️ provider_params (JSON): Provider-specific configuration (e.g., exchange suffix, custom identifier).

The provider system uses the Registry Pattern for extensibility.

docs.title: 📅 ASSET_EVENT
docs.text:
Asset-level events that affect pricing or generate distributions. Events are distinct from transactions:

  • Events describe what happens to the asset globally (e.g., a dividend, a stock split).
  • Transactions describe what happens in a user's portfolio (e.g., buy, sell).
Event Type Effect on Price Description DIVIDEND Price drops by event value (ex-date) Cash distribution from equity/ETF INTEREST Price drops by event value Interest payment from debt/loan PRICE_ADJUSTMENT Algebraic change (+/-) Non-cash value change (write-down, haircut, re-rating) SPLIT Changes quantity, not total value Stock/unit split MATURITY_SETTLEMENT Final capital return Asset reaches maturity — no further calculations

Deduplication strategy: events are upserted in place, per source, on (asset_id, date, type): a sync matches only the events of its own assignment, and a matched row keeps its id, so the transactions linked to it stay linked. Manual events (provider_assignment_id = NULL) are edited by id or matched on date and type, except in a create item (the transaction form's + New event), which is refused on a date and type the asset already has instead of overwriting it; a sync never deletes them. See Asset Events.

Indexes: (asset_id, date), (asset_id, type, date), (provider_assignment_id).

docs.title: 🏦 brokers
docs.text:
Represents a brokerage account (e.g., Interactive Brokers, Degiro, a bank account).

Column Description name Unique identifier in the UI description Free-text notes portal_url Link to the broker's web portal icon_url Custom icon for the UI default_import_plugin Default BRIM plugin code for imports allow_cash_overdraft When true, permits negative cash balances (margin trading) allow_asset_shorting When true, permits negative asset quantities (short selling) is_active false = account closed (historical data preserved) opened_at Real-world account opening date

No base_currency

Unlike some portfolio trackers, brokers do not have a single base currency. A broker can hold positions in any number of currencies simultaneously. Cash balances are tracked per-currency via summation of transaction amounts.

docs.title: 🤝 broker_user_access
docs.text:
RBAC model — per-broker, per-user role grants.

Role Can view Can edit Can manage access VIEWER ✅ ❌ ❌ EDITOR ✅ ✅ ❌ OWNER ✅ ✅ ✅

The first user to create a broker is automatically OWNER. Owners can grant EDITOR/VIEWER to other users, enabling shared household portfolios.

docs.title: 💰 transactions
docs.text:
The single source of truth for all financial operations. Each transaction belongs to exactly one broker.

Column Description broker_id FK to broker — required asset_id FK to asset — nullable for cash-only ops (DEPOSIT, WITHDRAWAL) type TransactionType value: BUY, SELL, DIVIDEND, INTEREST, DEPOSIT, WITHDRAWAL, FEE, TAX, ADJUSTMENT, TRANSFER, FX_CONVERSION, CASH_TRANSFER. A plain VARCHAR(32) with no CHECK constraint; databases created before 22/09/2026 still declare VARCHAR(14), which SQLite does not enforce — see Migrations date Trade date: the day the operation was made, not the day its cash settles (B-52) quantity Signed asset delta (+in, −out). Default 0, NOT NULL. RealDecimal(22, 10): up to 15 digits before the decimal point (decision N63) and 10 decimal places, read back as written (see Decimal Columns) amount Signed cash delta (+in, −out). Default 0, NOT NULL. RealDecimal(18, 6): up to 15 digits before the decimal point (decision N63) and 6 decimal places, read back as written (see Decimal Columns) currency ISO 4217 code — required when amount ≠ 0 related_transaction_id Bidirectional self-FK for paired ops (TRANSFER, FX_CONVERSION, CASH_TRANSFER) tags Comma-separated user tags description Free-text cost_basis_override Frozen per-unit cost for incoming seeded lots: receiving TRANSFERs, positive ADJUSTMENTs, imported snapshots, inheritances (see below). A per-unit price, so RealDecimal(24, 12) like the prices: up to 12 digits before the decimal point and 12 decimal places, read back as written (see Decimal Columns) cost_basis_currency ISO currency code for cost_basis_override; nullable with the amount asset_event_id FK to AssetEvent — links transaction to a global asset event

Design rules:

  • quantity and amount are signed and NOT NULL — a balance is the plain sum of the rows, done in Python by financial_math, never with an SQL SUM() (see Decimal Columns)
  • Paired transactions are bidirectional (A→B and B→A) using DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED FK
  • link_uuid is accepted by create payloads only as transient batch correlation; it is not a transactions column
  • Tags are stored as CSV for simple LIKE queries without a join table

docs.title: 🧊 cost_basis_override — Snapshot Architecture
docs.text: The cost_basis_override field implements a frozen acquisition cost pattern for incoming lots that did not originate from a normal BUY in the same broker: asset transfers, positive ADJUSTMENT seeds, inheritances, and broker-import snapshots.

docs.title: ❓ Problem
docs.text: When assets move from Broker A to Broker B, or when a broker-import plugin seeds a historical position from a snapshot/succession report, the receiving broker needs the historical cost basis (PMC — Prezzo Medio di Carico) for FIFO/tax calculations. Without a snapshot, the system would need to query unavailable history every time it calculates P&L.

docs.title: ⚙️ Solution
docs.text:
Create and update payloads can request backend WAC with cost_basis_mode="auto" or "auto-detail". After create-link resolution, the batch service computes a per-unit WAC and writes its amount and currency to the staged receiver row. A manual payload instead supplies the cost_basis_override currency object directly.

Batch promote is a separate boundary: TXPromoteBatchItem has no cost_basis_mode, and the promote stage does not calculate WAC. Its resolved per-unit value comes from resolved_fields.cost_basis_override, which only an API client sends: the merge dialogs send description and tags alone.

See 📊 Weighted Average Cost (WAC) for the full formula, transaction effects, and examples.

docs.title: 📏 Rules
docs.text: Side cost_basis_override Sender (qty < 0) Never required. A TRANSFER sender takes none: a promote clears it from that side, with or without resolved_fields. An ADJUSTMENT taking units out has no value (developer decision N78-1, 21/10/2026): the API refuses one (costBasisNotAllowed, rule 12b), and every engine ignores one an older row still stores (FifoInputTransaction.from_transaction()). A split of a TRANSFER pair or a broker deletion clears it on the former sender (decision 47, see Broker Deletion) Receiver (qty > 0) Required for TRANSFER and ADJUSTMENT; supplied manually, resolved by promote, or computed for a create/update auto mode

docs.title: 🧮 How batch auto-WAC is staged
docs.text:
• compute_wac_and_fx_issues() runs after create, promote, and create-link resolution.
  • _compute_wac_for_auto_items() selects only parsed create/update rows whose cost_basis_mode is auto or auto-detail.
  • _auto_cost_source() picks the pool: the receiving side of a TRANSFER (a TRANSFER row with related_transaction_id, set by create-link resolution or a promote, or loaded with a saved pair) averages its partner's broker as of the partner's date, without the partner's outgoing leg or itself; any other row averages its own broker as of its own date, without itself.
  • compute_wac_iterative() reads the session-visible transaction history and returns the WAC; _compute_wac_for_auto_items() writes its per-unit amount and currency to cost_basis_override and cost_basis_currency.
  • The giving leg of each TRANSFER pair the batch splits needs no cost: the split itself (apply_splits()) leaves it an ADJUSTMENT without a value (see Split & Promote).
  • Missing FX data becomes a wacFxUnavailable batch issue instead of silently persisting an unresolved cost.
  • A split-linked ADJUSTMENT skips stored auto-WAC because the portfolio engine rescales total cost from the live split relationship.

The service only mutates and flushes the existing session. The /transactions/validate caller always rolls it back; the /transactions/commit caller commits only when response.committed is true.

docs.title: ✍️ Manual override cases
docs.text: Exit Tax, inheritances, gifts, corporate actions — these require a user-specified value because the fiscal basis differs from the mathematical average. The frontend shows a warning when no override is set on an ADJUSTMENT with positive qty.

docs.title: 📥 BRIM import seeds
docs.text:
BRIM plugins may set cost_basis_override directly when the source report already contains the fiscal book value:

  • Intesa Sanpaolo patrimonio snapshots create a cash DEPOSIT when non-zero liquidity is present plus one cashless ADJUSTMENT per holding. The plugin divides total Controvalore di carico fiscale € by quantity and stores the result as a per-unit override.
  • Crédit Agricole succession rows (GIRO ALTRO DOSSIER, VERS.TITOLI) are cashless transfer-ins from an untracked dossier, so they are positive ADJUSTMENTs with per-unit override and no DEPOSIT.

docs.title: 🚪 opened_at and BRIM preview gate
docs.text: brokers.opened_at is also used by the frontend BRIM wizard as an import-preview guard. The shipped check is frontend-only and strict: txDate < info.openedAt. Rows strictly before the opening date receive local status before_opening, are deselected, and cannot be imported; rows dated exactly on opened_at remain valid. Users can click Edit broker date and then refresh/re-check the preview.

docs.title: 💱 Currency & FX Integration
docs.text:
The currency field in transactions is an ISO 4217 string (e.g., EUR, USD, JPY). There is no foreign key to an FX table — currencies are standard codes, validated with pycountry at the application layer:

  • What a request writes — a transaction's cash or cost basis, an asset's currency, a manual event, a manual FX rate or conversion route, a BRIM import, a user's base currency (E-19a) — must be an ISO 4217 alphabetic code (iso_currency_code() in schemas/common.py, E-18). Case and surrounding spaces do not matter (eur is stored as EUR); a currency name (Euro), a numeric code (978) or a crypto ticker (BTC) is refused with a 422, which names the code the text stands for when there is one ('840': USD; E-19a, suggested_iso_currency()).
  • What is read back is not checked again (Currency.validate_code, the lenient rule): a value stored by an earlier version still loads, lists and can be deleted.
  • What is stored and not canonical is reported, never changed (E-19a): a warning at every start and ./dev.py db currencies (admin guide, «Currency Codes That Are Not ISO Codes»; services/platform/stored_currencies.py, 14 places), and the BRIM gap-fix refuses to compare a broker whose cash holds such a code (guide). The currency picker shows such a value with the ISO code it stands for, and the check of a backup for a restore warns non_iso_currencies when the archive holds one (E-19b1; GET /utilities/currencies/suggest, on iso_currency_candidates(), the rule behind suggested_iso_currency()).

The dotted line in the ER diagram represents a logical relationship, not a relational one:

  • When the system needs to convert between currencies (e.g., aggregating a multi-currency portfolio), it queries the FX Rates subsystem.
  • The backend resolves conversion chains automatically — e.g., RON → JPY may route through EUR.

Why no currency table?

Currencies are an international standard (ISO 4217) with a fixed, well-known list. Storing them as strings avoids unnecessary joins while keeping validation strict at the application layer.

docs.title: 💱 Implied FX Rate Derivation
docs.text:
For FX_CONVERSION paired transactions, the effective exchange rate applied by the broker can be derived from the two linked rows:

implied_rate = |amount_to| / |amount_from|

The frontend compares this with the market rate obtained via POST /fx/currencies/convert (amount=1, single date). The rate is cached in the fxStoreRegistry TimeSeriesStore — subsequent lookups for the same pair+date are instant.

This comparison is displayed in:

  • The promote-suggest banner (BulkModal) — when two standalone TX are detected as a potential FX conversion
  • The FX conversion form — as an info tooltip between the "From" and "To" panels

docs.title: 💱 FX Rates & Routes
docs.text: Currency exchange rates and routing configuration. The FX subsystem stores daily rates and manages multi-provider data supply chains.

docs.title: 📐 ER Diagram
docs.text:
erDiagram
    FX_RATE
    FX_CURRENCY_PAIR_SOURCE

    FX_RATE {
        date date
        string base
        string quote
        decimal rate
    }

    FX_CURRENCY_PAIR_SOURCE {
        string base
        string quote
        string provider_code
        int priority
        json provider_params
    }

docs.title: 💱 FX_RATE
docs.text:
Stores daily exchange rates. Each row represents the rate for a currency pair on a specific date.

  • 🔤 Alphabetical ordering: Enforces base < quote (alphabetical) to prevent duplicate storage. For example, EUR/USD is always stored as base=EUR, quote=USD regardless of the query direction. The system automatically inverts the rate when needed.
  • 🔒 Uniqueness: The composite key (date, base, quote) ensures no duplicate rates.

docs.title: 🔌 FX_CURRENCY_PAIR_SOURCE
docs.text:
Configures which data provider to use for each currency pair. Supports multi-provider fallback via priority ordering.

  • 🏛️ provider_code: References a registered FX provider (ECB, FED, BOE, SNB, etc.)
  • 🔢 priority: Lower number = higher priority. If priority-1 provider fails, the system tries priority-2.
  • ⚙️ provider_params (JSON): Provider-specific configuration if needed.

The provider system uses the Registry Pattern for extensibility.

docs.title: 🔀 Data Supply Chains
docs.text:
For exotic currency pairs (e.g., RON/JPY), the system can construct multi-step conversion chains through intermediate currencies. For example:

RON → EUR (via ECB) → JPY (via ECB)

This is configured via FX Configuration & Routing and executed by the FX Chain Algorithm.

docs.title: 👤 USER
docs.text:
The core identity table. Each user has a unique username, compared exactly, and a unique email, compared regardless of A–Z case (step 6 of migration 005_release_1_3_0_schema, below). Since lot A-21a a new username holds no @, since lot A-46 it has 3 to 50 characters whatever the way it is written, ./dev.py user create included, and a new email address cannot be another account's username, A–Z case aside (user_service.address_is_a_username(), a comparison of lower(username) that no index serves: an instance has few accounts). All three are checks of the service, not constraints of the table (SQLite does not enforce the VARCHAR(50) of the column): the usernames written before keep their @ or their length, with no migration (see Which Account an Identifier Names). The hashed_password is stored using bcrypt. The first account registered through POST /api/v1/auth/register becomes a superuser (is_superuser = true), whatever the registration mode: registration accepts it while users is empty, an inactive account counting as a row (first_account_open()); a later one gets the role of its invitation (grants_admin), or a regular account without one. From the command line, ./dev.py user create makes a superuser unless given --role user (see Superusers and the User CLI and Registration, Invitations and the Admin API). With LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_EMAIL, the startup creates the first row itself: a superuser with is_active false, whose hashed_password is the hash of a random secret nobody knows, until its setup link is spent (The Initial Administrator).

Step 1 of migration 005_release_1_3_0_schema adds three columns:

  • 🔄 session_version (INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0): the session generation of the account. Each session cookie carries the version it was issued at (the JWT's sv claim), and get_current_user() refuses, on every request, a cookie whose version is not the account's. user_service.end_sessions() raises it by one on a password change or reset (a reset link included), an email change, a deactivation or a demotion (from the CLI or the administrator API), when an administrator signs the account out everywhere, and when the initial administrator spends its setup link, ending every older session of the account. See Session Revocation. The first start after a restore gives every account the restore time in milliseconds instead (or one more than the largest version either database held, when the clock is behind it): a time, not a counter, which a later end_sessions() still raises by one.
  • ✅ email_verified_at (DATETIME, nullable): when the email address was verified, set by confirm_email() when the owner of an account confirms it on the page of its verification link (Email Verification). It is a record, not a gate: nothing reads it to let an account in. The accounts that existed before the migration stay NULL — not verified, which is true — with no backfill, and so do the first account, the accounts created from the command line or while the option was off, and an account an administrator activated by hand: the wait is decided in the logic (an inactive account holding an unspent verification token), not in this column (coordinator decision, 15/10/2026). An email change sets it back to NULL, in the commit of the new address (user_service.update_profile()): the verification was of the old address (Changing the Email).

  • 📰 last_seen_version (VARCHAR(40), nullable): the release whose changelog the user last saw, as a base release X.Y.Z (whats_new_service.release_of(); lot C-54, «What's new since your last version»). Written by user_service.create_user() with the running release, so a new account has nothing to catch up on, and by POST /api/v1/auth/whats-new/seen when the user closes the «What's new» window: the server writes its own running release, never a value from the client, and never a lower one than the column holds. NULL is an account from before the feature, or one created while the running version named no release (unknown, or a checkout with no tag): it sees the running release's chapter once (What's new).

  • 👑 is_instance_owner (BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, migration 005_release_1_3_0_schema): the account that owns a managed instance, the paying administrator. At most one row holds 1: the partial unique index ux_users_instance_owner ON users (is_instance_owner) WHERE is_instance_owner = 1, read by SELECT id FROM users WHERE is_instance_owner = 1 (SEARCH users USING COVERING INDEX ux_users_instance_owner). It exists because the address of LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_EMAIL cannot identify the owner once the host has changed it. Set by the managed bootstrap that creates the initial administrator and by the startup step owner-sync (services/accounts/instance_owner.py), never in another profile; read by user_service.account_protection() and by instance_owner. It is in no API schema, and no setting: a global setting is readable by every signed-in user and editable by any administrator. See The Owner's Address.

Only confirm_email() gives email_verified_at a date. The accounts that existed before lot C-54 hold last_seen_version NULL, and keep it until their user closes the window once. The migration adds the three columns with plain ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN, never with a batch: a batch rebuilds users — copy, drop the original, rename — and with foreign_keys=ON dropping the original fires the ON DELETE actions of every table that references it (the same trap as in Post-migration fixes). Its downgrade removes them with DROP COLUMN, which rewrites the table in place and fires no foreign-key action.

Step 6 of migration 005_release_1_3_0_schema makes the email unique regardless of case (developer decision P18): alice@example.com and Alice@Example.com are one address, which only one account can hold. Beside the UNIQUE constraint on email, which compares the address as written, it creates ux_users_email_lower, a unique index on lower(email); the model declares it after the User class (backend/app/db/models.py), so create_all builds it too. SQLite's built-in lower() folds A–Z and nothing else, so letters outside ASCII compare as written: Émile@example.com and émile@example.com are two different addresses, a documented limit. user_service.email_fold() is the same fold in Python, and same_email() compares two addresses with it. get_user_by_email() and the email half of get_user_by_username_or_email() — tried first, and only for an identifier holding @ (lot A-21a) — compare lower(email), so sign-in, «forgot password» and the duplicate checks of create_user() and update_profile() find an address whatever its case; the username half stays exact. The stored email keeps the form last written: its owner changing its case alone is no email change (Changing the Email).

Before the index, the upgrade groups the accounts by that fold: after steps 1 to 5, as the retired 009 ran after 005 to 008. If two accounts share an address apart from case, it stops with a RuntimeError that names them as #id 'username', never by address (workstream E's rule: no address in a log), and gives the remedy: ./dev.py user set-email <username> <address> on all but one account of each group (what the administrator does: Command-Line Tools, «Two Accounts with the Same Email Address»). No account is changed, and accounts are never merged. The database stays at 004_release_1_2_0_schema, yet it holds what the 1.3 model, and so set-email, needs: pysqlite opens a transaction only before the first data change, so the DDL of steps 1 and 2, which change no data, is committed as it runs, and the three users columns and account_tokens are there. The first data change — step 3, or step 5 when there is no enable_registration row to convert — opens the transaction that the stop rolls back, with everything after it. The next start runs 005 again from the top, and every step checks before it acts. Otherwise the upgrade creates the index; the downgrade drops it. ./dev.py test db migration-005 (backend/test_scripts/test_db/test_migration_005_release_1_3.py) covers the stop on temporary databases, the set-email remedy included, and ./dev.py test services email-case (backend/test_scripts/test_services/test_email_case.py) the fold, the index and the lookups.

docs.title: ⚙️ USER_SETTINGS
docs.text: One-to-one with USER. Stores user-specific preferences: display language, base currency (base_currency), theme (light, dark or auto), and avatar URL. When a setting is not defined here, the system falls back to the corresponding GLOBAL_SETTING.

docs.title: 🌍 GLOBAL_SETTING
docs.text:
System-wide configuration managed by the admin. Includes settings like session_ttl_hours, max_file_upload_mb, registration_mode (who may create an account), and default values for user preferences. The startup seeding creates only the rows that are missing, each with its default from GLOBAL_SETTINGS_DEFAULTS: for registration_mode, invite since decision 36. The startup step that creates the initial administrator writes registration_mode = invite too, in the same transaction, with updated_by_user_id NULL.

Step 3 of migration 005_release_1_3_0_schema changes data only: the row enable_registration (bool) becomes registration_mode (value_type str). The new value is open when the old one, lower-cased, was true, 1, yes or on — what the settings service read as true — and disabled otherwise, so an odd value stays closed; the updated_at and updated_by_user_id of the row are kept, and the old row is deleted (a registration_mode already there is kept as it is). A database without the old row has nothing to convert: if it already holds accounts, step 5 writes open; otherwise the startup seeding creates registration_mode with its default, invite. The downgrade writes true for open, and false for invite and disabled, since the old setting had no middle ground. Each direction checks before it acts, so an interrupted run can be repeated.

Step 5 changes data only too: an install upgraded with accounts keeps the registration it had. Releases before the invite default read a missing row as open, so where registration_mode is missing and users holds at least one row, active or not, it inserts registration_mode = open, the earlier default made explicit: value_type str, the registry's description (a copy frozen in the migration), updated_at the time of the upgrade, updated_by_user_id NULL. The migration runs at the database step of the startup, before the seeding of the global-settings step could write the new default. A row that is there is never touched, whatever its value, and a database without accounts gets nothing: it is a new install, and the seeding gives it invite. The step checks before it acts, so it can run again. The downgrade has no step of its own for it: an open row, what the earlier default meant, becomes enable_registration = true like any other. ./dev.py test db migration-005 (backend/test_scripts/test_db/test_migration_005_release_1_3.py) covers steps 3 and 5 on temporary databases: both directions, the metadata, the idempotence, and a populated 1.2 install taken to the revision.

docs.title: 🏢 PLUGIN_SYSTEM_SETTING
docs.text:
Table plugin_system_settings, created by step 4 of migration 005_release_1_3_0_schema: one row per plugin setting of the whole instance (a system field), written by an administrator. What the plugins declare, and how the values are resolved, encrypted and delivered to a call, is in Plugin Settings.

  • 🏷️ family (VARCHAR(16)), plugin_code and field_key (VARCHAR(64)): the field, UNIQUE (family, plugin_code, field_key) (uq_plugin_system_settings_field). family is asset or fx.
  • 📝 value_json (TEXT, nullable): a plain value, as JSON.
  • 🔐 secret_ciphertext (BLOB, nullable): a secret, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key derived from the instance key and bound to its row.
  • 🗝️ key_id (VARCHAR(32), nullable): the id of the key that encrypted the secret, 32 hex characters. A changed instance key shows as another id, without decrypting anything.
  • ⏱️ updated_at (DATETIME NOT NULL): when the value last changed.
  • 🧾 updated_by_user_id (nullable): the administrator who wrote it.

Two CHECK constraints keep each row consistent:

Constraint Expression Meaning ck_plugin_system_settings_one_value (value_json IS NULL) <> (secret_ciphertext IS NULL) Exactly one of the plain value and the ciphertext ck_plugin_system_settings_key_id (secret_ciphertext IS NULL) = (key_id IS NULL) A key_id if and only if there is a ciphertext

updated_by_user_id references users.id with ON DELETE SET NULL: deleting that administrator keeps the value and forgets who wrote it. A value given by an environment variable is never stored here: a variable that is set wins over the row. Clearing a field deletes its row. Rows of fields that no plugin declares any more stay, ignored.

docs.title: 🙋 PLUGIN_USER_SETTING
docs.text:
Table plugin_user_settings, created by the same migration: one row per user and plugin setting of that user (a user field), written by that user only. No endpoint shows these rows to anyone else, an administrator included. The same columns as plugin_system_settings, without updated_by_user_id, plus:

  • 👤 user_id (NOT NULL): the owner. It references users.id with ON DELETE CASCADE: the rows go with the account. It is part of the row the encryption binds a secret to, so a ciphertext copied to another user's row does not decrypt.

UNIQUE (user_id, family, plugin_code, field_key) (uq_plugin_user_settings_field), and the same two checks: ck_plugin_user_settings_one_value and ck_plugin_user_settings_key_id.

Two tables rather than one with a nullable user_id: in SQLite NULLs never collide in a UNIQUE constraint, so one table would need two partial unique indexes, which nothing else in the schema uses. The unique constraints are the only indexes: their leading columns serve the reads of one plugin's rows and, in plugin_user_settings, of one user's rows and the cascade. The ids are plain INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, without AUTOINCREMENT: no row id leaves the backend.

Step 4 of migration 005_release_1_3_0_schema creates both tables empty: no setting existed before. The downgrade drops them, and the values and secrets in them are lost. Each direction checks before it acts, so a run that stopped half way can be run again.

docs.title: 🔑 BROKER_USER_ACCESS
docs.text:
The pivot table for the Many-to-Many relationship between Users and Brokers. It stores:

  • 🛡️ role: One of OWNER, EDITOR, or VIEWER — see Access Control (RBAC) for the full permission matrix.
  • 📊 share_percentage: The ownership fraction, NUMERIC(7, 6) from 0 to 1 (CHECK constraint), used for aggregated portfolio calculations (e.g., 0.5 for a joint account). The API exchanges the fraction as-is; the frontend shows it as a percentage.

docs.title: 🧭 USER_ONBOARDING_PROGRESS
docs.text:
Table user_onboarding_progress: one row per user and guided onboarding flow, UNIQUE (user_id, flow) (uq_user_onboarding_progress_user_flow). user_id references users.id with ON DELETE CASCADE.

  • 🧭 flow (VARCHAR(50)): an OnboardingFlow value — welcome, intro_tour, transactions_page_guide, transaction_create_guide, transaction_bulk_guide, import_guide, broker_page_guide, broker_guide, broker_detail_guide, fx_page_guide, fx_guide, fx_detail_guide, asset_page_guide, asset_guide, asset_detail_guide, tools_page_guide.
  • 🚦 status (VARCHAR(20)): an OnboardingStatus value — pending, completed or skipped — enforced by CHECK (ck_user_onboarding_progress_status). completed_at and skipped_at record the last terminal transition: the service sets one and clears the other.
  • 🔢 version: the content version the status refers to, CHECK (version >= 1) (ck_user_onboarding_progress_version). The current version of every flow is ONBOARDING_FLOW_VERSIONS in backend/app/services/accounts/onboarding_service.py. A row behind it is reported with update_available (optional replay); a complete or skip request must send the current version as expected_version, or it gets 409 onboarding_version_mismatch.

Rows are created lazily: reading a user's progress (GET /api/v1/settings/onboarding), or any transition, first inserts the missing flow and step rows as pending (INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) and never rewrites an existing row.

docs.title: 🪜 USER_ONBOARDING_STEP_PROGRESS
docs.text:
Table user_onboarding_step_progress: per-step progress of the step-managed flows, those listed in ONBOARDING_FLOW_STEPS — transaction_bulk_guide (transaction.bulk.* steps) and import_guide (import.*, one step per import wizard step plus import.bulk). Same columns as the flow table plus step_id (VARCHAR(100)), with UNIQUE (user_id, flow, step_id) (uq_user_onboarding_step_progress_user_flow_step), the same status and version checks and the same cascading foreign key to users.

There is no foreign key between the two onboarding tables: a step row belongs to its flow row through (user_id, flow). For a step-managed flow, the flow row is an aggregate that the service recomputes on every step transition: pending until every registered step is completed or skipped at the current version, then skipped if all of them were skipped, completed otherwise.

Existing accounts are grandfathered

Migration 004_release_1_2_0_schema seeds every user that already exists when it runs: welcome as completed (their settings are already configured), the fourteen other flows as skipped, and skipped rows for the steps the migration lists for transaction_bulk_guide and import_guide. skipped suppresses the automatic trigger like completed, but keeps "never shown this" distinct from "went through it", so a flow can still be offered later.

Users created after the migration get no seeded rows: their pending rows appear on the first read of their progress. The same lazy insert adds any row the migration did not seed — such as the import.gapFix step, which is not in the migration's list — for every user.

docs.title: 🎟️ ACCOUNT_TOKEN
docs.text:
Table account_tokens, created by step 2 of migration 005_release_1_3_0_schema: one row per single-use account link — an invitation, a password-reset link, an email verification or the setup link of the initial administrator. The row holds the SHA-256 of the token, never the token itself. How tokens are issued, checked, spent and revoked is in Single-use Account Tokens.

  • 🎯 purpose (VARCHAR(32)): an AccountTokenPurpose value — invite, password_reset, email_verification, admin_setup or email_change — enforced by CHECK (ck_account_tokens_purpose). A token is looked up by hash and purpose, so a token of one purpose is never accepted for another.
  • 🔐 token_hash (VARCHAR(64)): the SHA-256 of the token, 64 lowercase hex characters, UNIQUE (uq_account_tokens_token_hash). Its unique index serves the lookups.
  • 👤 user_id (nullable): the account the token acts on — password reset, email verification, admin setup. NULL for an invitation: its account does not exist yet.
  • ✉️ email (nullable): an address stored with the token; an invitation, which has no account yet, may carry one.
  • 🛡️ grants_admin (BOOLEAN NOT NULL, default false): whether the invitation grants the administrator role. Only an invitation may set it: issue_token() refuses it for the other purposes.
  • ⏳ created_at and expires_at (NOT NULL), consumed_at and revoked_at (nullable): a token is valid while it is neither consumed nor revoked and expires_at has not been reached. Ending a token sets consumed_at or revoked_at, or both when a setup link is retired (Revocation); the row stays.
  • 🧾 created_by_user_id and consumed_by_user_id (nullable): who issued the token and who spent it.

The three foreign keys reference users.id:

Column ON DELETE Why user_id CASCADE The token acts on that account: when the account is deleted, its tokens go with it created_by_user_id SET NULL It only records who issued the token: deleting that account keeps the token as it is and forgets the name consumed_by_user_id SET NULL It only records who spent the token, likewise

Three purposes are in use, with the rules of Registration, Invitations and the Admin API and of The Initial Administrator. This is how they use the table:

invite password_reset admin_setup user_id NULL The account whose password the link resets The administrator waiting for its setup email What the administrator wrote, if anything: a note, never compared with the address of the new account NULL NULL grants_admin Whether the account it opens is an administrator false false created_by_user_id The administrator who created it; NULL from the command line The same NULL: the startup or the command line issues it Issuing While live, it takes a place of the user limit (user_usage() counts the live invitations) First revokes the account's live reset links By the startup that creates the administrator, with the token of LIBREFOLIO_ADMIN_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN or a generated one; a new value of that variable and ./dev.py user setup-link first revoke the earlier setup links, then read «waiting» again under the write lock that revocation took: an account set up in the meantime gets no new link (lot A-42) consumed_at, consumed_by_user_id Set by the registration that creates the account, to that account, in the same transaction Set by POST /api/v1/auth/password-reset; consumed_by_user_id stays NULL, as the account is user_id Set by POST /api/v1/auth/setup, consumed_by_user_id to the account, in the commit that activates it. consumed_at alone, consumed_by_user_id staying NULL, on every setup link not yet consumed when the account's setup links are retired: the account set up another way; a link presented for it while it is already active, or once another of its setup links was consumed (lot A-42), the one presented included; the deactivation of an account that does not wait for its setup (lot A-43). Never by the cancellation of the waiting administrator's link: its links stay unconsumed, so it still waits revoked_at Set by DELETE /api/v1/users/account-links/{link_id} Set on the account's other live reset links when a new link is issued, or when one is spent; by DELETE /api/v1/users/account-links/{link_id} Set on the earlier setup links, expired ones included, when a new one is issued; on the other ones when one is spent; on those neither consumed nor revoked, expired ones included, when the account's address really changes, and when the administrator waiting for its setup is deactivated, the cancellation of its link (lot A-43; PATCH /api/v1/users/{user_id} with is_active: false, refused for a protected account, or ./dev.py user deactivate); on every one not consumed, unless already set, when the setup links are retired

Two indexes: ix_account_tokens_purpose_expires_at on (purpose, expires_at), and ix_account_tokens_user_id on user_id, used by the revocation of an account's tokens and by the cascade when the account is deleted. The model declares the indexes and constraints in __table_args__, under the same names as the migration.

The id is a plain INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, without AUTOINCREMENT. Decision D1 gives AUTOINCREMENT to six tables, those whose ids leave the backend (AUTOINCREMENT_TABLES, see Post-migration fixes), and test_autoincrement_schema.py keeps that census. The service never deletes a token — consuming or revoking one sets a timestamp — so token ids are not handed out twice. The one exception is the cascade from a deleted account: if its tokens include the newest ones, the next tokens issued get their ids again.

./dev.py test db migration-005 (backend/test_scripts/test_db/test_migration_005_release_1_3.py) checks the table and the three users columns on a new database and on an upgraded 1.2 install, the downgrade (which cascades into no other table), an upgrade interrupted half way, and that SQLModel.metadata.create_all builds users, account_tokens and the two plugin tables as the migration does. The test's in-process Alembic harness is backend/test_scripts/test_db/alembic_harness.py.
