docs.title: 🕐 Market Data Scheduler
docs.text: LibreFolio embeds an automatic background daemon to fetch current prices, historical pricing, and exchange rates without requiring external scheduler systems (like crontab or Celery).

docs.title: 🏗️ Overview
docs.text:
The scheduler runs as an independent asyncio.Task inside the FastAPI lifespan. Every run goes through one function, run_due_jobs(reason), which checks whether the configured sync jobs are due and runs those that are: at startup, at each 60-second tick, when a user comes back after a silence, and on a scheduled wake-up, when a hosting panel or a cron job calls POST /api/v1/system/wake-sync. A run at startup, on a return or for a wake-up is a catch-up, which the web app shows as Updating prices… while one of its jobs runs (see Catch-up Progress).

graph TD
    Start["🚀 Server Lifespan Startup"] --> FirstWait["⏳ Wait 5s or a nudge"]
    FirstWait -->|startup| Run["⚙️ run_due_jobs(reason)"]
    User["👤 User request after 60s of silence"] -.->|nudge| Wait
    Wake["⏰ POST /system/wake-sync"] -.->|wake| Run
    Run -->|"return, wake: wait 2s first"| Lock["🔒 Run lock of the process"]
    Lock --> Checks{"🚦 May it run?"}
    Lock -->|"wait limit (LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS) reached: not_leader"| Report
    Checks -->|"No: disabled, blocked, or not_leader without fcntl"| Report["📋 RunReport"]
    Checks -->|Yes| FileLock["🗝️ With fcntl: .scheduler.lock, one run at a time across the workers"]
    FileLock -->|"state and time read after the wait"| Jobs["⚡ Each due job in turn: current price, then history sync"]
    FileLock -->|"wait limit (LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS) reached: not_leader"| Report
    Jobs --> Report
    Report -->|"startup, tick, return"| Wait["💤 Wait 60s, a nudge or the shutdown"]
    Wait -->|"60s: tick"| Run
    Wait -->|"nudge: return"| Run
    Wait -->|shutdown| Stop["🛑 Loop stopped"]

docs.title: 🔄 Async Loop Daemon (scheduler.py)
docs.text:
The main entry point is scheduler_loop() located in backend/app/services/platform/scheduler/scheduler.py. Every run of the jobs goes through run_due_jobs(reason), in the same module: the loop calls it, and so does the scheduled wake-up route (backend/app/api/v1/system/wake.py).

  • Lifespan Task: The scheduler startup step, followed only by idle-monitor in STARTUP_STEPS (backend/app/services/platform/app_lifespan.py), spawns it with asyncio.create_task(). On shutdown, the scheduler step, right after idle-monitor at the head of SHUTDOWN_STEPS, sets the shutdown event and awaits the task before the providers are shut down, a run in progress included; when the shutdown deadline cuts the step, the task is cancelled (see the lifecycle contract).
  • Shutdown Event: The loop waits on shutdown_event: asyncio.Event, its timer and the return nudge at once, so a shutdown ends a wait immediately. The event does not interrupt a run: the loop stops once the run in progress is over, then removes its return listener and its response header, and resets the catch-up tracker (see Catch-up Progress).
  • Environment Bypass: Any non-empty value of LIBREFOLIO_NO_SCHEDULER keeps the loop from starting and from registering its return listener and its response header; a run asked for anyway answers disabled. ./dev.py server --no-scheduler and the gallery screenshot generation set it to 1.

docs.title: ⏰ When a Run Happens
docs.text:
Each run has a reason (RunReason), which its log line carries; any other value is refused with ValueError before anything happens.

Reason When startup The first run, FIRST_RUN_DELAY_SECONDS (5 s) after the loop starts, while the application finishes starting. A nudge brings it forward; a shutdown in the meantime ends the loop without it. tick TICK_SECONDS (60 s) after the end of the previous run. return At once, when a user's request comes after at least CATCH_UP_AFTER_SECONDS (60 s) of silence: see the nudge below. wake A call to the scheduled wake-up route, POST /api/v1/system/wake-sync, which streams the run's report back to its caller.

The nudge on return. The loop registers a return listener, scheduler-catch-up (CATCH_UP_LISTENER), on the process's activity record (current_activity(), in backend/app/services/platform/sleep_wake/activity.py). The record calls it at the start of a user's request that comes after at least 60 seconds without one; the health and readiness probes do not count. The listener announces the catch-up (PRICE_REFRESH.announce("return"), see Catch-up Progress) and sets the loop's nudge event, with loop.call_soon_threadsafe() so that it works from any thread; the waiting loop runs return at once. The record measures the silence on the wall clock, so the time a machine spends suspended counts; the loop's own timer runs on the monotonic clock, which does not count it, so after a resume the next tick could still be up to a minute away. The nudge is cleared when a run starts: nudges that arrive during a run make one return run right after it.

docs.title: 🔒 One Run at a Time
docs.text:
• Run lock: run_due_jobs() takes an asyncio.Lock, one per event loop, for its checks and its jobs, so two runs of the process never overlap. The second one waits, then loads the state the first one saved, and does not run again what the first one just ran; past the wait limit, ten minutes, it gives up instead.
  • Across processes: where Python has fcntl, the runs of different worker processes take turns the same way, on an exclusive flock of .scheduler.lock in the data directory, which a run takes after its checks: one run at a time for the data directory, in whichever worker it starts. See Several Workers.
  • Busy work: from its start to its end — the clock settle and the waits for both locks included, whether it returns, raises or is cancelled — the run is busy work on the activity record (current_activity().busy("scheduler")): for the idle suspension, a scheduler run is work in progress, so the idle monitor never suspends the machine in the middle of a run.
  • Clock settle: a return or wake run first waits CLOCK_SETTLE_SECONDS (2 s), before the locks and before it reads the time; startup and tick never wait. After a Fly.io resume the wall clock is corrected within a few hundred milliseconds, and a request may be served before that: the wait lets the due checks read the corrected time.

docs.title: 🚦 Inside a Run
docs.text:
Under the run lock of its process, a run goes through these checks, in this order. The first one that stops it gives the run's status: no job runs, and the state is not loaded. A run that waits too long for a lock stops the same way, with not_leader: the wait limit, LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS (ten minutes, counted after the clock settle), bounds its wait for the run lock of its process and, after these checks, for the lock across processes.

  1. The scheduler is off, LIBREFOLIO_NO_SCHEDULER (scheduler_disabled()): disabled.
  2. The instance is blocked, LIBREFOLIO_BLOCKED (instance_blocked()): blocked. A blocked instance runs no job at all, so its prices and exchange rates are not updated; once the block is lifted (a restart), the first run catches up the history-sync slot missed in the meantime (decision D-Z3-4, and missed slots).
  3. Only where Python has no fcntl (Windows): this process is not the leader worker (am_i_leader(), see Leader Election): not_leader. With fcntl (Linux, macOS) this check does not exist and am_i_leader() is never called: any worker may run the jobs.
  4. The scheduler_enabled setting is off: disabled. The settings are read from the database (load_scheduler_settings()) at each run that gets this far.

Otherwise, where Python has fcntl, the run takes the lock across processes (scheduler_run_lock()), waiting while another worker's run holds it; without fcntl there is no such lock. Then, holding it where there is one, the run loads the state (load_state()), reads the wall clock once (utc_now()) for both due checks, and takes the jobs of JOBS in order, current_price then history_sync. A job that is not due is reported not_due. A due job runs on the loaded state, and the state is saved right after it (save_state()). So a run that waited for another worker's run reads the state that run saved, and the time after the wait: what that run just did is not_due. am_i_leader(), each attempt at the lock across processes, load_state() and save_state() block on the process table or on the disk, so they run off the event loop (asyncio.to_thread()).

Each job runs in its own try:

  • A job that raises, or the save after it, is reported error with the exception's class name only. The message and the traceback stay in the server log (Scheduler job failed, with job and reason), never in the outcome, which a caller may pass on. The next job still runs. The failure is recorded in the job's state, saved at once: the job keeps the last_run_at of its last run that ended, so its regular rule still finds it due, but it is not tried again before a wait that doubles at each failure in a row (see Provider Pauses and Failures).
  • A cancellation is not caught: it goes through, and the run releases its locks, the one across processes included, and its busy span. It records no failure, so no wait. A job it cuts before its state is saved stays due, so after a shutdown the next start runs it again.
  • An exception outside the jobs — the settings or the state cannot be read, or the lock across processes cannot be taken (a symlink in its place, a permission problem) — leaves run_due_jobs(): the loop logs it (Scheduler run failed) and goes on, and the scheduled wake-up answers status: "error" with its class name.

docs.title: ⏸️ Provider Pauses and Failures
docs.text:
Two things move a job's next run, in opposite directions. A price provider that pauses after «too many requests» defers some of the job's items, and the job is retried as soon as the first pause is over, unless its regular round comes first. A job that raises is held back, for a wait that doubles at each failure in a row.

Deferred items. The provider-call boundaries, call_provider() for the assets and call_fx_provider() for the exchange rates, pause a provider after it answers «too many requests» (HTTP 429), and until the pause ends refuse every call to it at once, without reaching the provider. A pause lasts 60 s by default and doubles at each refusal in a row, up to 1 h; a Retry-After sent by the provider is honoured, up to one day. LIBREFOLIO_PROVIDER_COOLDOWN_BASE_SECONDS and LIBREFOLIO_PROVIDER_COOLDOWN_MAX_SECONDS tune them (.env.example, section «Sleep and Wake», and for administrators Provider Pauses); Provider Pauses and Paused Providers tell the rest. An item refused that way comes back with error_code="RATE_LIMITED" and retry_after, the seconds until the provider may be called again, and the jobs (jobs.py) count it as deferred, whatever its status or value: neither ok nor failed. A current price that fell back on the last stored price is deferred, and so is a history item that saved some prices anyway, even one marked ok; an FX pair carries RATE_LIMITED only when it ended failed or partial, not when another route served it.

  • Status. _classify_job_status(ok, total, deferred) gives ok when every item succeeded (or there was none), error when none did and none was deferred, and partial otherwise: a job with deferred items is partial, even when all of them were deferred.
  • retry_at. At its end, the job records when to retry them: now, in UTC, plus the shortest retry_after among its deferred items, by when the first pause is over. An item that does not know its wait (with the pauses turned off, a refusal that sent no Retry-After) does not count; when none knows it, retry_at stays null and the deferred items wait for the regular round.

The due rules. _retry_rule() comes first in both due_current_price() and due_history_sync(), each on its own job's state:

  1. A next_attempt_at still ahead holds the job back: it is not due, whatever the reason of the run, a wake-up included.
  2. A retry_at that has come makes it due: before the regular round, never after. When the regular round comes first, the job runs then, and the items whose provider is still paused are deferred again, without a call.
  3. Otherwise the regular rule applies: the frequency for the current price, the slots for the history sync.

A timestamp that cannot be read counts as none. No timer waits for these moments: the loop sees them at its next run, within a tick (60 s). A machine that sleeps runs nothing, so the answer of the scheduled wake-up reports retry_at, for a hosting panel to plan its next wake-up.

Failures. A job that raises, or whose state cannot be saved after it, goes through _record_failure():

  • consecutive_failures grows by one;
  • next_attempt_at is now, in UTC, plus 60 s × 2^(failures − 1) (FAILURE_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS), capped at 3600 s for the history sync (FAILURE_BACKOFF_MAX_SECONDS) and at its own frequency for the current price (scheduler_current_price_frequency_minutes × 60), so a failing refresh is never tried less often than its schedule asks. With the default settings, the current price waits 60, 120, 240 and 480 s, then 10 minutes at each further failure; the history sync waits 60 s doubling up to 1920 s, then an hour;
  • last_status becomes "error" and last_error the exception's class name; the rest of the state is kept, a pending retry_at included;
  • last_run_at and last_duration_s stay those of the last run that ended, so a missed slot stays due: the job is normally due again as soon as its wait is over;
  • the state is saved at once; a save that fails again is only logged (Scheduler state not saved after a failed job).

A job that ends — that returns instead of raising — writes a new JobState, whatever its status, error included, with consecutive_failures back to 0 and no next_attempt_at. Only a job that raises waits: items that fail do not hold a job back.

Where it shows.

Where Fields scheduler_state.json (JobState, state.py) last_items_deferred and retry_at, written by the job at its end; consecutive_failures and next_attempt_at, written by _record_failure() and reset by a job that ends. retry_at and next_attempt_at are ISO 8601 in UTC. load_state() ignores the keys it does not know, so a state file written by a newer version does not reset the state, and a file without the new keys loads with their defaults Job log (joblog.py) deferred: true and retry_after on a deferred item, deferred (or assets_deferred and fx_deferred) in summary, with err counting the failed items only, and retry_at on the entry: see Execution Logs Run report (JobOutcome) items_deferred, and retry_at as a datetime in UTC: see The Run Report. The scheduled wake-up passes both on to its caller (WakeSyncJob)

docs.title: 📋 The Run Report
docs.text:
Each run returns a RunReport(reason, status, started_at, finished_at, jobs). It is generic: a future job — notifications, say — is one more entry of JOBS, and one more outcome.

  • status: ok when no job ran or every job that ran is ok, error when every job that ran is error, partial otherwise; or, with jobs empty, the check that stopped the run, disabled, blocked or, without fcntl only, not_leader; not_leader too, with or without fcntl, for a run that gave up at the wait limit.
  • started_at and finished_at: in UTC, from the moment the run holds the run lock of its process, before its checks: a wait for another worker's run falls between them. A run that gave up waiting for the run lock of its process has both at the moment it gave up; one that gave up at the lock across processes has them as any run, its wait between them.
  • jobs: one JobOutcome(name, status, started_at, duration_s, items_ok, items_err, error, items_deferred, retry_at) per job, in order, with status ok, partial, error or not_due. A job that ran reports what its JobState holds after it: status (ok when it wrote none), duration, item counts (the deferred ones in items_deferred), error and retry_at. A job that raised reports error, its duration, the exception's class name in error, and the end of its wait (next_attempt_at) in retry_at. A job not due reports its name, not_due and, in retry_at, the end of a wait after a failure if it is still ahead, else a deferred retry still ahead, else None. retry_at is a datetime in UTC (see Provider Pauses and Failures).

The loop logs each report, Scheduler run finished with the reason, the status and the jobs that ran: at INFO when a job ran, at DEBUG otherwise, so the runs with nothing due stay out of an INFO log.

docs.title: ⏳ Catch-up Progress
docs.text:
A run at startup, on a return or for a wake-up is a catch-up (CATCH_UP_REASONS): the run a user may be waiting for, after the server started, woke up or went a minute without requests. While one of its jobs runs, the web app shows the notice Updating prices…: Updating prices… tells the web app's side. A tick is never a catch-up: the notice would come back every few minutes. The server tells the web app in two ways, both read from one tracker, PRICE_REFRESH:

  • the header X-LibreFolio-Price-Refresh (PRICE_REFRESH_HEADER), starting or running, on every /api/ answer while a catch-up is pending;
  • GET /api/v1/system/price-refresh, which the web app asks every 3 s once it has seen the header, until the answer is idle.
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Web app
    participant MW as ActivityMiddleware and routes
    participant Sched as scheduler_loop
    participant Tracker as PRICE_REFRESH

    App->>MW: first request after 60 s of silence
    MW->>Tracker: announce(return), from the return listener
    MW->>Sched: nudge
    MW-->>App: /api/ answers carry X-LibreFolio-Price-Refresh starting
    Sched->>Tracker: run_started(return), in run_due_jobs
    Note over Sched: clock settle (2 s), run lock, checks
    App->>MW: GET /system/price-refresh, every 3 s
    MW-->>App: state starting
    Sched->>Tracker: job_started(current_price)
    App->>MW: GET /system/price-refresh
    MW-->>App: state running, the notice shows
    Sched->>Tracker: job_finished(items_ok), then run_finished()
    App->>MW: GET /system/price-refresh
    MW-->>App: state idle, the notice goes

docs.title: 🧮 The Tracker
docs.text:
PRICE_REFRESH is a PriceRefreshTracker (scheduler.py): one per process, in memory, behind a threading.Lock, since the loop, the activity record and the route (a plain def, which FastAPI runs in its thread pool) reach it from different threads. price_refresh_progress() returns its state now, a PriceRefreshProgress(state, reason, job, since, last_finished_at, last_refreshed).

  • Pending. A catch-up is pending from announce(reason) or run_started(reason), whichever comes first, until the last run counted by run_started() has ended (run_finished()). The loop announces startup as it starts, FIRST_RUN_DELAY_SECONDS (5 s) before its first run; the return listener announces return on the request's thread, before the request runs. run_due_jobs() calls run_started(reason) for a catch-up reason before the clock settle, and run_finished() in a finally, so also when the run raises or is cancelled: that is how a wake-up begins one. Runs overlap: a wake-up during a return run is a second counted run, and the catch-up ends with the last of them. A catch-up announced while another is pending changes nothing: the first reason and its start (since) stay.
  • States. starting while a catch-up is pending and no job runs: from the announcement through the settle, the checks and the waits for the locks, another worker's run included, and between two jobs. running while it is pending and a job runs, with the job's name. idle otherwise.
  • Jobs. _run_job() calls job_started(name) before each job of every run, and job_finished(items_ok) after it, None when the job is cancelled. A job that finishes while a catch-up is pending counts for it, a tick's included: the user waits for the prices, whatever run brings them. So when a user comes back while a tick's job runs, the state is running at once, with that job.
  • The end. When the last counted run ends, the catch-up is over and the state is idle. If at least one job finished while it was pending, the tracker keeps when the catch-up ended (last_finished_at) and whether one of those jobs brought an item up to date (last_refreshed: an items_ok above 0; a job that raised reports 0, and a deferred item is not brought up to date). A catch-up that ran no job — nothing due, or a run stopped by its checks with disabled, blocked or not_leader — leaves both as they were.
  • Guards. announce() and run_started() refuse a reason outside CATCH_UP_REASONS, tick included, with ValueError; run_finished() without a counted run does nothing. reset() forgets everything: the loop calls it as it stops.

docs.title: 📨 The Header
docs.text:
As it starts, the loop registers PRICE_REFRESH.header_value for X-LibreFolio-Price-Refresh on the activity record, with current_activity().register_response_header(), and removes it as it stops (remove_response_header()). ActivityMiddleware (backend/app/services/platform/sleep_wake/activity.py) adds every registered header to each answer whose path starts with /api/ (API_PATH_PREFIX), the probes excepted, the answer of wake-sync included:

  • Read when the answer starts, on its http.response.start message, not when the request arrives. The return listener runs before the request, so the answer to the request that ended the silence, when it is an /api/ one, already says starting, although the run starts at least 2 s later (clock settle).
  • Only while a catch-up is pending. header_value() gives starting or running, and None while idle: a provider that returns None or an empty string adds nothing. Without a catch-up no answer carries the header, so the web app asks nothing.
  • The route's own header wins. A header of the same name that the answer already has is kept. Names are compared in any case, and the header goes out with its name in lower case.
  • A provider that fails — it raises, or returns a value a header cannot carry (a line break, a character beyond Latin-1) — is skipped while the others still answer, and its first failure in a row is logged as a warning, Response header provider failed.

The mechanism is generic: activity.py imports nothing from the scheduler, and MIDDLEWARE_STACK does not change. The web app is served from the same origin, so it reads the header without any CORS setting.

docs.title: 🛰️ The Route
docs.text:
GET /api/v1/system/price-refresh (backend/app/api/v1/system/price_refresh.py, one module of the system package, like wake.py) answers the tracker's state, PriceRefreshResponse (backend/app/schemas/sleep_wake.py). It reads the same tracker as the header, so the two agree.

  • Signed-in users only, any role: get_current_user answers 401 without a valid session, and the answer tells nothing about anyone's data. On a blocked instance the route is not on the allow-list: a signed-in user gets the 423 of the Instance Block. The web app stops asking at the first 4xx (After a 4xx).
  • A request of the user. For the activity record it counts like any route but the probes, the wake-up and the hosting panel's routes: while the web app asks, the idle suspension sees a user.
Field What it holds state idle, starting or running reason Why the pending catch-up runs: startup, return or wake; null when idle job The job running now, current_price or history_sync; only while running since When the pending catch-up began, in UTC; null when idle last_finished_at When the last catch-up that ran a job ended, in UTC; null before the first last_refreshed Whether that catch-up brought at least one item up to date

The last two describe the last catch-up that ran a job, also while another one is pending: the web app reads them once the answer is idle. An answer during the history sync of a return, indented here for reading:

{
  "state": "running",
  "reason": "return",
  "job": "history_sync",
  "since": "2026-10-16T07:12:03.120044Z",
  "last_finished_at": "2026-10-16T05:00:14.611230Z",
  "last_refreshed": true
}

docs.title: 👥 One Process, Several Workers
docs.text:
The tracker belongs to its process, like the loop and the activity record. With several workers, each one runs its loop and announces its own catch-ups, and the jobs run in the worker whose run holds the lock across processes: the notice shows on that worker's answers only, as it did on the leader's. Another worker's catch-up stays starting while its run waits for that lock, ten minutes at most (the wait limit), then finds its jobs not_due, or gives up, and goes back to idle without ever answering running; a worker with no catch-up pending answers idle. A question that one of these workers answers may end the web app's tracking early: the notice may be missing, never stuck. Without fcntl, only the leader runs the jobs, and the other workers' runs end not_leader within seconds. The Docker image runs one worker.

With the scheduler off there is no notice either. With LIBREFOLIO_NO_SCHEDULER the loop does not start, so the header is never registered and the web app never asks: the test runner's server and the gallery, both started without the scheduler, never show the notice. With the Scheduler Enabled setting off, the loop still announces its catch-ups, whose runs end disabled without a job: the answers say starting for a few seconds, and the notice never shows.

Tests: ./dev.py test services scheduler-price-refresh (the tracker, the wiring of run_due_jobs() and of the loop, the header through ActivityMiddleware), ./dev.py test services sleep-wake-activity (the response headers of the activity record) and ./dev.py test api system-price-refresh (the route).

docs.title: 🔐 Several Workers (run_lock.py, leader.py)
docs.text:
With several uvicorn workers (./dev.py server --workers N), each worker is a process of its own, with its own loop, its own run lock and its own activity record. Two mechanisms keep their runs from doing the same jobs at once, and cross_process_lock_available() (run_lock.py) says which one applies: it is true where Python has fcntl.

  • With fcntl (Linux and macOS, so the Docker image too): a lock across processes. Any worker runs the jobs, one run at a time for the data directory.
  • Without fcntl (Windows): the leader election. One worker, the leader, runs the jobs; the others answer not_leader.

docs.title: 🗝️ The Lock Across Processes (run_lock.py)
docs.text:
scheduler_run_lock() (backend/app/services/platform/scheduler/run_lock.py), an async context manager, holds an exclusive flock on .scheduler.lock, at the root of the data directory next to scheduler_state.json (run_lock_path()). _run_locked() takes it after its checks, and holds it while it loads the state, reads the time and runs the due jobs, each one saving the state after it.

  • The wait. Each attempt opens the file and tries the lock without blocking, in a thread (asyncio.to_thread()); while another process holds it, the run tries again every POLL_SECONDS (0.2 s), up to the wait limit below. No thread stays blocked on the lock, and the wait can be cancelled — at shutdown, when the shutdown deadline cuts the scheduler step — without leaving the lock held: an attempt still running when the wait is cancelled releases the lock if it got it. The release, in a finally, runs in a thread too.
  • The wait limit. A run waits for other runs ten minutes at most: LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS (600 s), a constant of run_lock.py with no environment variable (Z-26, night decision N79). Without it, a stuck job would hold back for good every run waiting behind it, in its own worker or in another, a wake-sync included. After the clock settle, _run_within_deadline() fixes the run's own wait deadline once, time.monotonic() + LOCK_WAIT_SECONDS, and that one instant ends both waits: first the one for the run lock of the process (acquire() under asyncio.timeout()), then the one for this lock (scheduler_run_lock(deadline=…)), so the time spent in the first is taken from the second. Without fcntl only the first exists. scheduler_run_lock() always makes at least one attempt, so a free lock is taken even past its deadline; while another process holds the lock, the next attempt comes min(POLL_SECONDS, time left) later, and an attempt refused at or past the deadline raises SchedulerRunLockTimeout (a TimeoutError), with no attempt in flight and its descriptor closed. With deadline=None, the default, it waits as long as needed. The jobs have no limit: a run that holds its locks runs its jobs to the end.
  • Giving up. A run that reaches the wait limit runs no job and neither loads nor saves the state: _run_within_deadline() catches the TimeoutError of the first wait, _run_locked() the SchedulerRunLockTimeout of the second. _log_gave_up() logs a WARNING, Scheduler run gave up waiting for another run, with reason, lock (process or data_dir, the lock it was waiting for), waited_s (the seconds since its wait began) and limit_s, and the run reports not_leader, with no jobs. It closes like any run: its busy span ends, it releases the run lock of its process if it got it, and a catch-up calls PRICE_REFRESH.run_finished(). The run that holds the locks goes on untouched, and the next tick (60 s) tries again. The Docker image, and so a Fly.io machine, runs one worker (Per Process, Either Way): there only the first wait can reach the limit, a run — a wake-up, say — behind a stuck run of the same process. Several workers come from ./dev.py server --workers N, or from a command of one's own.
  • Whoever comes second. A run that waited for another worker's run reads the state that run saved, and the time after the wait: what that run just did is not_due, and only what is still due runs.
  • Where the jobs run. In any worker: the one whose loop ticks, the one that received wake-sync, or the one that served a user's return, which runs the catch-up at once (after the clock settle) instead of waiting for another worker's tick. A wake-sync that reaches a worker while another one runs the jobs waits for that run, at most ten minutes (the wait limit, above), then answers, its jobs not_due; past that limit it gives up and answers not_leader, with no jobs. Its 409 (wake_in_progress) stays per process: a second call that reaches another worker is not refused, it waits for the run in progress. A call that gave up has ended its wake-up, so the next call to its worker is accepted, not answered 409.
  • The file. Hidden and empty, created with mode 0600 and opened with O_NOFOLLOW: a symlink in its place is refused with an OSError, and nothing behind the link is created or locked. It is never deleted: a worker that opened the file before its removal and another that created it again after would hold two different locks, and two runs would overlap. Leave it in place, and never delete it while LibreFolio runs (Data Directory on Disk).
  • A crash. The kernel releases a flock when its process dies: a worker killed in the middle of a run leaves no stale lock. The next run, in any worker, goes ahead, and runs again a job whose state the dead worker did not save.
  • An error. A lock that cannot be taken (a symlink, a permission problem) raises like any other error outside the jobs: the loop logs it and goes on, and wake-sync answers status: "error" with the class name (Inside a Run).

docs.title: 👑 Without fcntl: Leader Election (leader.py)
docs.text:
Where Python has no fcntl, _run_locked() asks am_i_leader() instead, right after the blocked check, and only the leader runs the jobs; with fcntl, am_i_leader() is never called. It decides at every run with psutil, without any lock file; it reads the process table, so it runs off the event loop (asyncio.to_thread()):

  • Among the running, non-zombie children of the uvicorn master, the process with the lowest PID is the leader. If it dies, the next run promotes the new lowest PID.
  • Fast paths return True: no parent process (e.g. PID 1 in a container), a parent started with --reload (one logical worker), a single sibling, or any introspection error — safe because the jobs are idempotent.
  • Another worker answers not_leader and runs no job. A return nudges only the worker that served the request: when that one is not the leader, the catch-up waits for the leader's next tick, within 60 seconds.

docs.title: 🧩 Per Process, Either Way
docs.text: The catch-up tracker (PRICE_REFRESH, and its header X-LibreFolio-Price-Refresh), the activity record and the idle monitor stay per process. With several workers, the notice Updating prices… shows on the answers of the worker that runs the jobs, as it did on the leader's, and may be missing (One Process, Several Workers); each worker counts only its own requests for the idle suspension. The Docker image runs a single worker (its CMD starts uvicorn without --workers), and so does a Fly.io machine that runs it; ./dev.py server --workers N starts several.

docs.title: 💼 Job Definitions (jobs.py)
docs.text: The scheduler runs two types of background synchronization jobs defined in backend/app/services/platform/scheduler/jobs.py:

docs.title: ⏱️ 1. Current Price Refresh
docs.text:
• Purpose: Keeps the current prices of all active assets that have a price provider up-to-date. This updates the local pricing cache, feeding the frontend's live prices on the Assets list and the asset detail page.
  • Frequency: Defined by scheduler_current_price_frequency_minutes (default: every 10 minutes).
  • Execution: Calls AssetSourceManager.get_current_prices_bulk() (concurrency 3) on every active asset that has a provider assignment.

docs.title: 📅 2. History Sync
docs.text:
• Purpose: Synchronizes historical price series (closing prices) for assets and FX rates.
  • Frequency: Configured for specific days of the week (e.g., mon,tue,wed,thu,fri,sat) and times of the day (e.g., 06:00 and 23:00), as local wall-clock values in scheduler_timezone (see Configuration Integration).
  • Missed slots: After a previous run, the most recent slot of a configured day — today or up to MISSED_SLOT_LOOKBACK_DAYS (7) days back, in scheduler_timezone — is due when it fell after that run (decision D-Z3-1). A week holds every configured day, so the most recent slot is always found: a slot missed while the server was off, asleep or blocked runs at the next run — startup, tick, return or wake-up — instead of at the next slot (after a failure, at the first run once its wait is over), and several missed slots make one run. Without a previous run (no last_run_at, or one that cannot be read), only today's slots count. An always-on instance, which runs every minute, sees no difference.
  • Example: slots 06:00 and 23:00, days Monday to Saturday. The history sync last ran on Saturday at 06:00, and the server was off from Saturday 20:00 to Sunday 10:00. When it starts on Sunday, the startup run syncs the history, because Saturday's 23:00 slot fell after the last run; with today's slots only, it would have waited for Monday 06:00, Sunday not being a configured day.
  • Execution: Calls AssetSourceManager.bulk_refresh_prices() for the same assets, one FARefreshItem per asset with its own window, then sync_pairs_bulk() once, for the pairs of every FX conversion route without a MANUAL step, all over one window. Every window ends today.
  • Window: _history_sync_start(today, horizon_days, last_saved) is the one place a window's start is decided. The window always covers the horizon: it starts at today − horizon (scheduler_history_sync_horizon_days, 1–365, default 14: the Lookback horizon of the schedule), or earlier when the item's last saved value is older than that — the day after it, but not before today − HISTORY_CATCH_UP_MAX_DAYS, 365 days, the horizon's own maximum. Without a saved value, or with one dated in the future, the start stays at the horizon: the scheduler never fetches a whole history, which stays with the syncs a user starts (with start="resume", backend/app/services/assets/refresh.py falls back to the provider's full history when nothing is saved). So an instance that is up to date syncs exactly the horizon, and one that was off, asleep, suspended or blocked for longer than the horizon fills its gap at its first history sync, whichever run brings it: JOBS always calls run_history_sync() with the horizon of the settings. The reach back has no setting or environment variable: HISTORY_CATCH_UP_MAX_DAYS is a constant of jobs.py.
  • Last saved values: _last_price_dates() reads max(PriceHistory.date) per asset, and _last_fx_dates() max(FxRate.date) per pair, one grouped SELECT each. FxRate stores a pair in alphabetical order (base < quote), so the lookup sorts the pair first: USD-EUR reads the rows of EUR-USD. Each asset gets its own window; the FX pairs share their single sync_pairs_bulk() call, which starts at the earliest of their starts. The providers fetch by currency, so a pair behind widens the days of the call, not the number of requests, and every pair of the call gets the wider window.
  • In the server log: when at least one asset or pair starts before the horizon, the job logs Scheduler: history sync reaches back at INFO, just before its closing Scheduler: history sync line, with assets_behind and fx_pairs_behind (how many assets and pairs start before the horizon) and earliest_start (the earliest start of all, an ISO date). Nothing else records the window: neither the job log entry nor scheduler_state.json, so the admin panel does not show it. An item that stays behind — an asset its provider no longer quotes, a pair it no longer serves — is asked again for its gap, up to a year, at every history sync, and the line comes back each time; a pair behind also widens the window of every other pair.

Both jobs classify their run as ok (every item succeeded, or there was nothing to process), error (no item succeeded, and none was deferred), or partial otherwise, a run whose items were all deferred included.

docs.title: 📜 Execution Logs (joblog.py)
docs.text:
Every job run that completes is appended to logs/scheduler_jobs.jsonl in the data directory, one JSON object per run:

  • Header fields: ts (ISO timestamp with offset), job (current_price or history_sync), duration_s, status (ok, partial or error), and retry_at (when the deferred items are retried, ISO 8601 in UTC; null when there is none).
  • summary: ok, err and deferred counts for the current-price refresh; assets_ok, assets_err, assets_deferred, fx_ok, fx_err and fx_deferred for the history sync. A deferred item counts in neither ok nor err.
  • Per-item detail: items for the current-price refresh (asset, ok, error); assets and fx for the history sync (status, provider, errors, and prices_changed/events_changed or points_changed). A deferred item adds deferred: true, and retry_after (seconds) when it knows its wait: a history item keeps its status, a current-price item has ok set to false.
  • Rotation: after each append, the file is trimmed to its last 500 entries (MAX_ENTRIES).

A job that raises appends no entry: its failure is in the server log, Scheduler job failed (see Inside a Run), and in its state (see Provider Pauses and Failures). An entry does not say which days a history sync covered: a run that reached back past the horizon says so only in the server log, Scheduler: history sync reaches back (see History Sync).

The state of each job — its last run that ended, the deferred retry and the wait after a failure — is also kept in scheduler_state.json at the root of the data directory (state.py, atomic write-then-rename). The admin UI reads both through admin-only endpoints: GET /api/v1/settings/scheduler/state (last runs, scheduler_timezone, the server's UTC clock) and GET /api/v1/settings/scheduler/log?since=ISO (newest first). Both pass on the fields of the pauses and failures: the state route gives each job its last_items_deferred, retry_at, consecutive_failures and next_attempt_at (SchedulerJobStateInfo), and the log route returns the entries with every field listed above, the deferred ones included (SchedulerLog*); both response models are in backend/app/schemas/settings.py. For a state file or a log entry written before these fields, the routes return their defaults: 0, false or null.

The admin panel shows them (see Market Data Scheduler). The Scheduler Status row adds a line with the current-price job's next_attempt_at if it is still ahead as the tab loads the state, else its retry_at if that one is (pendingSchedulerRetry()). The log marks each deferred item with a pause icon, counts them with ⏸ in the entry's summary and shows the entry's retry_at (Retry at) in its header. The code is in frontend/src/lib/features/settings/: tabs/GlobalSettingsTab.svelte and schedulerRetry.ts for the row, SchedulerLogModal.svelte for the log.

docs.title: ⚙️ Configuration Integration
docs.text:
Scheduler options are fully integrated into LibreFolio's database-backed Global Settings system. When an administrator modifies settings in the UI:

  1. Settings are saved to the GlobalSetting table.
  2. The frontend triggers a settings reload.
  3. The backend scheduler loop loads the settings dynamically on the next loop iteration (every 60 seconds), adapting the polling frequency and execution times instantly without requiring a server restart.

History-sync times and days are stored as local wall-clock values in scheduler_timezone. due_history_sync() builds each slot in that timezone, on its own local date, and converts it to a UTC instant only when deciding whether it is due, so the slots follow daylight saving time. A slot is due once its instant has passed and the last history run is older than it; History Sync says which slots count. A timezone that zoneinfo cannot load falls back to UTC (_scheduler_zoneinfo()). zoneinfo reads the system's time zone database, since the PyPI tzdata package is not a dependency: the Docker image installs Debian's tzdata and tzdata-legacy, which holds old names such as Asia/Calcutta and US/Eastern (see Docker Image). An empty or invalid day list falls back to Monday–Saturday. The backend also refuses such values when they are saved: PATCH /api/v1/settings/global/bulk checks each one with validate_global_setting_value() against GLOBAL_SETTINGS_CONSTRAINTS (backend/app/schemas/settings.py): 1–1440 minutes, 1–365 days, at least one HH:MM time and one day, a timezone the server knows. One refusal answers 422, listing every refused value, and writes nothing. The fallbacks remain for values stored before that check existed, or written to the database by hand.

docs.title: 💰 Asset Pricing & Metadata Architecture
docs.text: The Asset system in LibreFolio manages financial instruments (Stocks, ETFs, Bonds, Crypto, etc.), fetches their prices from external providers, and maintains their metadata.

docs.title: 📦 Package Layout and Imports
docs.text:
Asset pricing services live in backend/app/services/assets/. Each module owns one responsibility:

Module Responsibility base.py Provider contract: AssetSourceProvider, AssetSourceError, history start-date types, and the OHLC guard; AssetRateLimitedError and the helpers that recognise a refusal for too many requests (rate_limited_from_response(), rate_limited_from_exception(), raise_if_rate_limited()). core.py Shared infrastructure: the five cache singletons; configured_provider(), a new provider instance with its plugin settings bound; call_provider(), the single boundary of every provider call, which refuses a provider that is not configured with NOT_CONFIGURED, refuses a paused one with RATE_LIMITED and pauses one that refuses (Provider Pauses), masks its secrets in the call's log lines and errors (hiding an error's texts whole when the call carries a personal secret), and runs the call in a thread of its own (_run_provider_in_thread); public_asset_url(), which withholds an asset URL that shows one of the provider's secrets; cooldown_scope_for(), the part of a provider a pause covers, from the plugin's cooldown_scope() hook; settings_cache_part() and settings_cache_part_for(), the part of a cache key that depends on the provider's settings; asset_cache_key(), the one key of the history and current caches (provider, identifier, input type, parameter hash, settings), and drop_asset_cache_entries(), which drops both entries of an assignment; provider-parameter hashing; error sanitization. registry.py AssetProviderRegistry, which discovers the pricing plugins in backend/app/services/asset_source_providers/. provider_policy.py What the instance decides about each provider: the search tier and search_priority a plugin declares, overridden by LIBREFOLIO_ASSET_PROVIDERS_PREMIUM and LIBREFOLIO_ASSET_PROVIDERS_ORDER (read at every call); provider_tier(), provider_priority(), search_rank() and search_order(), which GET /assets/provider and the search use. provider_management.py Provider assignment, removal and lookup; parametric-provider data invalidation and the removal, which unlink the transactions linked to the events they delete and are refused, nothing written, while a SPLIT they would delete has linked incoming adjustments without a cost (Parametric Provider Change, Provider Removal); the dry run of both, provider_change_impact() (Provider Change Impact); and the non-persisting provider probe. metadata.py Explicit provider metadata refresh, metadata caching, and application of returned patches through AssetCRUDService. price_store.py Price upserts/deletes, OHLC integrity checks (both bounds real and inconsistent: refused for every source; a manual price whose only real bound lies on the wrong side of the close: refused, a provider's widened around the close), count_stored_prices() (the stored and manual rows of a range, behind POST /assets/prices/stored-count), the digit limits of prices (a manual price or volume refused; a provider's truncated, and a provider's date with a value no column can keep skipped and reported), the last storable date of a stored price (a manual date after it refused, a provider's skipped and reported), the currency of a manual call's prices (refused before any write), and bounded write chunks. currency_change.py What a currency change deletes (N68): the asset's prices and every event except the SPLITs, with asset_event_id set to NULL on the transactions linked to the deleted events; the helpers PATCH /assets calls and the counters behind the market-data summary and wipe endpoints; never refused (Market-Data Wipe). split_guard.py The SPLITs among the events a provider change would delete that have linked incoming adjustments without a cost, named as the caller may see them (splits_with_costless_adjustments(), adjustments_count()): the refusal of the parametric provider change and of the provider removal, and the provider dry run's blocking_splits. Not used by the currency change since N68, which keeps the splits. event_links.py The transactions linked to asset events, as a refusal names them for its caller: visible_transaction_ids(), the ids on a broker the caller holds an access to, none without a caller (the rule split_guard.py imports), and events_with_linked_transactions(), the events among those given that transactions are linked to, each with the caller's view: the count of transactions the provider-change dry run reports. event_store.py Event upserts (rows updated in place: a provider refresh commits them in the same bounded chunks as prices, the manual upsert once for the whole request, all or nothing, after deleting the events its items list in delete_ids) and deletes scoped to one asset, plus the event queries and reads by id behind /assets/events. price_query.py DB-backed history/event queries, backward fill, FX and signal preparation, plus current-price lookup and today's OHLC write-back. period_changes.py The fixed-period changes of the Assets table, and on request the whole-range change of the Assets cards: each asset's price on the days the change needs, read in grouped queries and converted at each day's rate (Fixed-Period Changes). refresh.py Provider-driven price refresh and its explicit PREPARE/FETCH/PERSIST phases. crud.py Asset create, list, patch, delete, and merge operations. search.py Cross-provider batch search, SSE search, query caching, link-finder fallback, and URL resolution; for each provider that did not answer, the reason the client needs (Interactive Search Stack). web_link_finder.py The last-resort web lookup of search.py: an external metasearch engine that turns a query into candidate provider-domain URLs (see Asset Search & Link-Finder). manager.py The single AssetSourceManager class, composed from the provider, metadata, price-store, currency-change, event-store, query, and refresh operation mixins. market_calendar.py Market holidays and the rule that tells a stored carry from a quote, shared by risk and by the signal price query (see Market Calendar).

These are behavioral boundaries, not only file boundaries: refresh.py orchestrates remote acquisition, price_store.py and event_store.py own the reusable price and event persistence primitives, and price_query.py owns database-backed reads plus the separate live-quote path.

backend/app/services/assets/__init__.py holds only a docstring: the package re-exports nothing, and no compatibility facade exists.

Import from the defining module

Import every name from the module that defines it: the provider base class and error from backend.app.services.assets.base; AssetSourceManager from backend.app.services.assets.manager; AssetCRUDService from backend.app.services.assets.crud; and AssetSearchService from backend.app.services.assets.search. The thread runner and all cache patch points live in backend.app.services.assets.core.

docs.title: 1️⃣ AssetSourceProvider (Plugin Base Class)
docs.text:
Abstract base class for all asset pricing plugins, defined in backend/app/services/assets/base.py. Each provider auto-registers via @register_provider(AssetProviderRegistry).

Property / Method Required Default Description provider_code ✅ — Unique identifier (e.g., "yfinance") provider_name ✅ — Human-readable name test_cases ✅ — Test data for automated testing test_search_query ✅ — Search query for tests (None if search unsupported) get_current_value() ✅ — Fetch latest price → FACurrentValue get_history_value() ✅ — Fetch historical OHLCV → FAHistoricalData validate_params() ✅ no-op Validate provider-specific configuration params_schema — [] Schema for dynamic form generation in the frontend get_asset_url() — None URL to the provider's page for this asset resolvable_url_domains — [] Domains accepted by resolve_url; non-empty means supports_url_resolution = True resolve_url(url) — None Interactive-search hook: provider page URL → one search-item dict, list of dicts, or None accepted_identifier_types — [TICKER, ISIN] Input types accepted by this provider supports_history — True False for current-price-only providers search() — raises NOT_SUPPORTED Search for assets by name/ticker/ISIN fetch_asset_metadata() — None Fetch asset metadata (type, sector, identifiers) cooldown_scope() — None The part of the provider a pause after «too many requests» covers (the CSS Scraper: the page's host); None pauses the whole provider. See Provider Pauses provider_help_url — None URL to the provider's documentation page

supports_search heuristic

The list_providers endpoint determines search support via instance.test_search_query is not None — a local property check, not an HTTP call. This avoids cold-start latency on GET /assets/provider.

docs.title: 2️⃣ AssetSourceManager
docs.text:
The stable manager class in assets/manager.py composes the responsibility-specific operation mixins:

  • Provider Assignment: Link an asset to a provider (e.g., "AAPL" → "yfinance").
  • Price Sync: 3-phase pipeline: PREPARE → FETCH → PERSIST (see Data Flow below).
  • Price Query: DB-only bulk query with backward-fill via POST /assets/prices/query.
  • Current Price: Bulk live-price endpoint via POST /assets/prices/current. Calls each asset's provider get_current_value() with DB fallback, and serves, caches and writes a quote only as the price columns keep it (Current Quotes and Today's OHLC). Polled by the Assets list and the asset detail page for their live prices.
  • Event Sync: Persist asset events from providers into the asset_events table, filtered by provider_assignment_id (manual events survive sync).
  • Probe: Dry-run provider config testing via probe_provider_config().

docs.title: 3️⃣ AssetProviderRegistry
docs.text: Uses the Registry Pattern for auto-discovery of provider plugins.

docs.title: 4️⃣ AssetEvent Table
docs.text:
Stores asset-level events produced by providers or created manually by users. Events are distinct from portfolio transactions:

  • Events describe what happens to the asset globally (DIVIDEND, INTEREST, SPLIT, etc.)
  • Transactions describe what happens in a user's portfolio (BUY, SELL)

Dedup strategy: Events with a provider_assignment_id (auto-generated) are replaced per (asset_id, date, type, provider_assignment_id) key during sync. Events with provider_assignment_id = NULL are user-created manual events and are never replaced by a provider upsert.

See Asset Events for full details.

docs.title: 🔄 Data Flow: Sync Pipeline
docs.text:
When the user triggers a sync (or the scheduler does), bulk_refresh_prices() executes a 3-phase pipeline:

graph TD
    API["POST /assets/prices/sync"] --> Manager["AssetSourceManager.bulk_refresh_prices()"]

    subgraph "Phase 1 — PREPARE"
        Manager --> Prepare["refresh._prepare_refresh_items"]
        Prepare --> DB1[("Caller AsyncSession<br/>(read-only)")]
        Prepare --> Registry["AssetProviderRegistry"]
    end

    subgraph "Phase 2 — FETCH (parallel)"
        Prepare --> Fetch["refresh._fetch_refresh_items<br/>(no database access)"]
        Fetch --> Thread["core._run_provider_in_thread"]
        Thread --> P1["Provider A"]
        Thread --> P2["Provider B"]
    end

    subgraph "Phase 3 — PERSIST"
        Fetch --> Persist["refresh._persist_refresh_items"]
        Persist --> Store["price_store / event_store operations"]
        Store --> DB2[("One AsyncSession<br/>per asset")]
    end

    Persist -- "FARefreshResult per asset" --> API

    style P1 fill:#e3f2fd,color:#1b1b1b,stroke:#1565c0
    style P2 fill:#e3f2fd,color:#1b1b1b,stroke:#1565c0
    style DB1 fill:#f3e5f5,color:#1b1b1b,stroke:#7b1fa2
    style DB2 fill:#f3e5f5,color:#1b1b1b,stroke:#7b1fa2
  1. PREPARE uses the caller's AsyncSession for reads only. It resolves assets, assignments, provider instances, validated parameters, and resume dates into immutable prepared records. It performs no provider I/O and no writes.
  2. FETCH receives no database session. It uses an asyncio.Semaphore, the core history and current caches, and core._run_provider_in_thread() for provider history/current calls. Price data and best-effort provider events remain in memory.
  3. PERSIST creates a distinct AsyncSession for each asset. It compares fetched points with stored rows, then delegates price writes to price_store.py and event writes to event_store.py.

When the range reaches today, FETCH asks a provider's history only up to yesterday, then calls get_current_value() and adds its value as the close of its as_of_date (today when the provider gives none), replacing any history point of that date; PERSIST stores it with the rest. A provider without history (supports_history = False, such as the CSS Scraper) therefore builds its series one sync at a time, one point per day; outside syncs, the current-quote write-back stores the same day's point.

Before asking a provider's history from a dated start, FETCH reads the core history cache (core._asset_history_cache): it asks from the first day the cached entry misses between the start and history_end, the last day asked as a price (yesterday when the range reaches today), and skips the call when the entry misses none. The walk that looks for the missing days covers at most RANGE_SPAN_LIMIT_DAYS (100 years) before history_end (range_span_floor(), X-R55): an older start counts as missing, so the provider is still asked from it, never for less than before.

Persistence intentionally does not claim one atomic transaction for the whole refresh. bulk_upsert_prices() commits bounded chunks of PRICE_UPSERT_CHUNK_SIZE = 1000; event upserts commit their own bounded chunks; and last_fetch_at is committed separately afterwards. This keeps SQLite writer-lock windows bounded and preserves truthful partial results when one step fails. Provider-generated events remain scoped by provider_assignment_id, so manual events are not replaced.

bulk_upsert_prices() merges each point with the stored row of its date, field by field (the F.4 merge, _merge_field()): for open, high, low and volume, None keeps the stored value, a number is written, and "clear" (CLEAR in backend/app/schemas/prices.py) writes NULL; close is always written. Only a manual write sends "clear" (N92): POST /assets/prices reads its points as FAPriceWritePoint (FAUpsert.prices), whose open, high, low and volume are each a PriceWriteValue ("clear", a number or None, tried in that order, union_mode="left_to_right", so that "clear" is never taken for a number):

  • a number of 0 or more is written; "clear" empties the stored value (NULL); null, or no field at all, leaves the stored value as it is, as before N92, for a provider as for a client;
  • a negative number, -1 included, a text that is neither "clear" nor a number ("d", "Clear", ""), a value that is not finite and a boolean are refused with a 422 located on the field (the open of the first asset's first point: a loc that starts ["body", 0, "prices", 0, "open"]), and so is a close not above 0: nothing of the request is written. Before N92, -1 was the F.4 sentinel that wrote NULL; a client that still sends it gets the 422;
  • "clear" has no digits: the digit check of a manual call, below, skips it (_price_limit_issue());
  • its JSON schema carries enum: ["clear"] beside pydantic's const, so that the generated client reads z.literal('clear'): openapi-zod-client 1.18.3 ignores const, and schemas/signals.py pins its literals the same way.

FAPricePoint, the model of a provider's history, of the query answers and of a sync's changed_points, checks no sign since N92: the refresh decides about a provider's day. Before the change count and the upsert, PERSIST (_persist_refresh_item() in refresh.py) sets aside the points LibreFolio does not keep: a point in another currency than the asset's (#R3-2, N points discarded: currency mismatch (got …, expected …)), and, since N92, a day with a close of 0 or less or a negative open, high, low or volume (_sign_issue()). A zero open or volume is a value, and is kept; a value that is not a finite number is left to _unstorable_provider_point() (W-B58, below). The discarded days are named in one error, N points discarded: a close not above 0 or a negative open, high, low or volume (…), each day with its ISO date and the fields at fault, 2026-01-02 (volume=-10), as W-B58 names a value no column keeps, the first five then (+ N more); and a warning is logged, Provider prices discarded: … with the same rule, with asset_id, provider, the first five days and the count. points_fetched counts only the points kept. With other points left the item is partial, the first of its errors its message; when every point is discarded it is failed, with points_fetched 0 and nothing written, as after a currency mismatch (#R4-1). The points kept reach the upsert through FAUpsert.model_construct(), not validated again as write points: they are FAPricePoint already built and filtered, and FAPriceWritePoint checks no digits (a value no column keeps reaches _unstorable_provider_point() either way), so a full validation of a 45 000-point history would cost about 0.23 s on the event loop for nothing. Before N92, the plugin's own FAPricePoint refused such a day, so its whole history download failed (with no current value either, the item failed with No price data available from provider), and an open, high, low or volume of exactly -1 was stored as an erased value.

bulk_upsert_prices() writes open, high, low and close through truncate_priceHistory() (backend/app/db/precision.py): 12 decimal places, then 15 significant digits, both rounded down — what a RealDecimal(24, 12) column reads back (see Decimal Columns). That truncation is for a provider's long floats. A value that is not finite, or has more digits before the decimal point than its column (12 for a price, 24 for the volume), fits no truncation: a provider's call drops every date holding one before any slice is written (W-B58: a value that raised in the truncation of a later slice left the earlier ones committed). That is a price storable_price() cannot keep (not finite, past 12 digits before the point, or a non-zero close truncated to 0), or a volume past 24 digits (_unstorable_provider_point()). The call logs a warning, writes the other dates, and reports the dropped ones in the asset's result message (rejected N date(s) with a value no price column can keep, the first five dates with the field and value), which the sync adds to the asset's errors as it does the OHLC rejections. The sync's change count, which runs before this (_count_actual_price_changes() in refresh.py), and its fallback take only the points that _unstorable_provider_point() accepts, dated no later than the last storable date (kept_items in _persist_refresh_item(), W-B62; the date check since X-R65): a date skipped for either reason is neither counted in inserted_count / updated_count nor listed in changed_points, from which the asset page's chart would draw a point the database never got; points_fetched still counts it. Before W-B62, the count took every point: truncating the fetched close of a date already stored raised from 1E+48 up, or on a close not finite, and its fallback then announced every fetched point. The current value a refresh adds as today's point, when the range reaches today, goes through the check of the live price, storable_current_value(), in FETCH, before the shared current-value cache: a value no price column can keep, or one of 0 or less (N92), is neither cached nor added as a point, so the sync neither counts nor announces it, but the result names it, as the upsert names a date it skips (unstorable_quote_reason(), X-R51): Current price 1E+60 not saved: a price is above 0, keeps at most 12 digits before the decimal point, and is never 0 once cut to 12 decimal places, the value cut as in the log (Current price -5 not saved: … for a negative one). With other points the item is partial, that reason in its errors after those of the discarded days, if any, and the first of them its message; with no other point, as for a provider without history such as the CSS Scraper, the item is failed, that reason its one error instead of No price data available from provider. The refusal is still logged once. Before N92, a current value of 0 was dropped here in silence, and a negative one made the refresh raise. A kept value is cached as stored, so the live price then comes from the cache already truncated. An open, high, low or volume the F.4 merge keeps from the stored row, written by an older release past its column's digits, is written as NULL (_kept_price(), _kept_volume()) instead of raising mid-slices. A manual call (source_plugin_key="MANUAL", the default, used by POST /assets/prices) is checked first instead: _reject_prices_over_the_limit() refuses the whole call when a price exceeds any of its limits — 12 digits before the decimal point, 12 decimal places, 15 significant digits — or is not finite, or when a volume has more than 24 digits before the point (only its size is limited: a fractional volume is accepted), before anything of it is written — a ValueError, which the route answers with HTTP 400 naming the asset, the maxima (the volume's included) and the dates. Two more checks follow, in this order and still before any write: the dates (X-R65) and the currency of the prices (X-R71).

bulk_upsert_prices() also keeps every date it stores no later than latest_stored_date() (X-R65, night decision N83): latest_range_end(), tomorrow by the server's calendar, included. There is no first date. X-R65 also kept stored dates from 1900-01-01 on; the developer lifted that floor from every price and rate write, a provider's included, on 19/10 (N83's revision), so a date before 1900, 0001-01-01 included, is stored like any other. The helper lives in backend/app/utils/date_range_limits.py, with DateOutOfRangeError and date_out_of_range_detail(), the builder of the 422 detail. The floor's reason was J's SEC8-1b: a price stored at 0001-01-01 made a backward fill or a risk replay walk about 740,000 days per asset. The walks' own limits now carry that protection. The per-day price fill of a full history loads from FULL_HISTORY_LOAD_START (1900-01-01, price_query.py), the start of every provider's history: since Z-30 it reaches back no further, where an older row at most seeds the fill, and never cuts a point-derived warm-up that starts earlier (bulk request limits). The portfolio walks (the engine, the lots and the positions) have no such start: they read their stored dates as steps (D-P4, 26/10/2026; the constant EARLIEST_RANGE_START, once the first day of every replay (R13-SEC8), is gone). A risk range starts no earlier than range_span_floor(), 100 years before its end (bounded_range() in backend/app/services/risk/scope.py, R13-SEC8-1b).

  • Manual call: right after the digit check, _reject_dates_out_of_range() refuses the whole call when any date is after tomorrow, before the call reads or writes anything (a call that fails both gets the digits' 400). The DateOutOfRangeError becomes a 422 {"code": "date_out_of_range", "message", "params": {"max"}, "items", "count"} (message: Dates must lie on or before …: N do not, or 1 does not). items lists, in request order, each asset with such dates as {"asset_id", "dates"}, its first ten dates (at most ten assets); count is every date refused. An earlier date, 0001-01-01 included, passes this check.
  • Provider call: the dates after tomorrow are dropped before any slice is written, like the unstorable ones: the call logs a warning, Provider prices skipped: date out of range, writes the other dates, and reports the dropped ones in the asset's result message (rejected N date(s) after …, the first five dates), which the sync adds to the asset's errors. An older point, before 1900 included, is stored and counted.

The FX rate writes keep to the same last date. Transactions have no first date since D-P4 (26/10/2026; the floor was 1900-01-01 since N74) and keep the same last date (Transaction dates, where the code is dateOutOfRange). The web app's data editors tell these 422s in the interface language, naming the dates refused and the last day a date may carry (N dates are after …, common.writeRefusal.dateOutOfRange; writeRefusalMessage() in frontend/src/lib/api/writeRefusal.ts, X-R46); before, they showed Axios's Request failed with status code 422.

A manual call is all or nothing on the currency of its prices, as on its digits and dates (X-R71). Its third check, _reject_currency_mismatches(), runs right after _reject_dates_out_of_range(), before anything is written; a call that fails several checks gets the refusal of the first, in the order digits (400), dates (422 date_out_of_range), currency. It reads the currency of every asset the request names (SELECT id, currency, in slices of 500 ids, nothing else on the session), then checks every item, in the request's order: a point whose currency, when given, is not its asset's is at fault. The web app never sends a per-point currency, so only an API client meets this check. The PriceCurrencyMismatchError it raises (a plain Exception, like DateOutOfRangeError) becomes a 422 {"code": "price_currency_mismatch", "message", "items", "count"} (message: Prices must be in their asset's currency: N are not), built by price_currency_mismatch_detail() in price_store.py. items lists, in request order, each item at fault as {"asset_id", "expected", "found", "dates"} (at most ten items): expected is the asset's currency, found the currencies given, first seen first, and dates at most ten of the item's dates at fault, in request order; count is every date at fault. Nothing of the request is written. A database error in the middle of a large upload still leaves the slices already committed: that is the price of the slice commits, not a check. Before X-R71, the check ran only inside the per-asset loop, once the earlier assets were written, each in slices of 1,000 dates with a commit after each: a request whose third asset had a price in another currency answered 400 with the first two already saved.

  • Unknown asset: an item whose asset does not exist is left to the loop, which answers it in its own result (Asset N not found, count 0) while the others are written, as before.
  • The loop's check stays: under a provider's key it still raises its ValueError (a refresh writes one asset per call, and drops the points in another currency itself before); for a manual call it is a safety net, for an asset whose currency changed between the read and the write.

Every date an asset's write leaves out is named in that asset's result, results[].rejected (X-R46; FAPriceRejection in backend/app/schemas/prices.py): one {"date", "reason"} per date, in date order, and an empty list when none is (an unknown asset's result, Asset N not found, names none). count counts only the dates written, and the English message keeps its sentences unchanged: the sync still copies it into the item's errors when it holds rejected (_persist_refresh_item() in refresh.py). A manual call meets only ohlc_inconsistent: a date after tomorrow or a value over the limits refuses it whole instead.

reason The date is left out because Met by ohlc_inconsistent Its point carries two real bounds, a low and a high that are not the "clear" erase, and low > high or its close lies outside [low, high], the values compared as sent; its stored row is kept Manual and provider calls date_out_of_range It lies after tomorrow, the last storable date Provider calls; a manual call is refused whole (422 date_out_of_range) value_not_storable It holds a value no price column can keep (_unstorable_provider_point()) Provider calls; a manual call is refused whole (400)

The integrity guard behind ohlc_inconsistent runs in the upsert loop and skips one date, never the call. Only two real incoming bounds are held to the close: a bound sent as "clear" is erased (written as NULL by the F.4 merge) and is no bound, so it is not checked (X-R46; the erase was -1 until N92). A point without two real bounds is never refused: when the merged [low, high] has both, it is widened to include the new close, so that a close-only update (the justETF and scheduled-investment case) does not fail on the bounds an older flat candle left; otherwise the row is written as sent, a single real bound unchecked even on the wrong side of the close. The web app's asset data editor sends a row's Low and High with its close, and "clear" for an erased cell: a close typed outside two real bounds comes back as ohlc_inconsistent, while erasing High, Low or both saves the row with those bounds NULL. Before X-R46, the guard took an erased bound (sent as -1 at the time) for a real bound of -1, so erasing High (with a Low) or both left the date out. The editor counts count as saved and names the refused dates (up to five, then a count) with their reasons in a warning (rejectedMessage() in frontend/src/lib/api/writeRefusal.ts).

docs.title: 🕛 Dates on the Exchange's Own Day
docs.text:
A provider dates each price point and event on its session's day at the exchange, not on the UTC date of a timestamp (Asset Plugin Guide). The refresh stores the dates as the provider gives them: no schema field or column holds an exchange timezone.

The Yahoo plugin (yahoo_finance/plugin.py) keeps that rule since Z-33:

  • History: yfinance stamps a daily bar, a dividend and a split at midnight in the exchange's timezone, so _normalize_yahoo_date() takes the index value's own date. Up to 1.2.1 the plugin converted it to UTC first, which gave the day before the session for every exchange east of UTC: Milan all year, London in summer time, Tokyo.
  • Current value: as_of_date is regularMarketTime read in the timezone of info["exchangeTimezoneName"], UTC when Yahoo gives none or the server does not know it, and the server's today without regularMarketTime.

Rows saved by earlier versions stay as they are, by decision (Z-33r): no migration or refresh re-dates them. A sync writes the session days it fetches, each on its own day; after the update, the scheduler's first history sync fetches its window, the Lookback horizon (14 days by default). So:

  • Prices: in the range a sync fetches, each session day gets its own close; older rows of an exchange east of UTC stay a day early. A day without a session before a session, a Sunday or a holiday, keeps the next session's close: no fetch writes it again.
  • Events: a dividend or a split a sync fetches again is stored twice, the old one a day early and the new one on its day, since the upsert keeps a stored event the provider no longer returns (Dedup Strategy). A split counts only through the ADJUSTMENT rows linked to it, so the new one changes no figure unless the user links it too.

The remedy, for a user who asks: delete both events, then sync their dates again; an event linked to a transaction is deleted only once unlinked (EVENT_IN_USE). A clean price history takes the market-data wipe (the wipe a currency PATCH /api/v1/assets performs), then a sync of the whole history. The wipe also deletes the asset's events that are not SPLITs, manual ones included, and unlinks the transactions from them; the SPLITs stay with their linked transactions, and the wipe is never refused since N68.

Unknown timezone (Z-36). _exchange_zone(), private to the plugin, gives the name's ZoneInfo, or None. On a server whose timezone database lacks the name (Windows outside Docker without the PyPI tzdata package, a minimal container; the Docker image installs one) the current value is dated in UTC: the day before for the part of a session that falls before UTC midnight, such as Sydney's or Auckland's. For an Area/Location name (Europe/Rome) the plugin then logs a warning once per name and process, Exchange timezone unknown to this server's timezone database: the current value is dated in UTC, with timezone; a fixed offset or a name without an area is not logged. Adding tzdata to the dependencies is Z-36, a developer decision.

Tests: the test_z33_* of test_yahoo_finance_errors.py (each bar and event on its exchange day, the current value in the exchange's timezone, the warning once per name and never for a name without an area).

docs.title: 📊 Data Flow: Price Query
docs.text:
POST /assets/prices/query is the primary read endpoint for price data. It reads directly from the database (no provider calls) and applies backward-fill for gaps.

graph LR
    FE["Frontend"] -- "POST /assets/prices/query" --> API["API Endpoint"]
    API --> Manager["AssetSourceManager.get_prices_bulk()"]
    Manager -- "DB-only reads" --> DB[(Database)]
    DB -- "Raw prices" --> Manager
    Manager -- "Backward-fill gaps" --> Manager
    Manager -- "FAPriceQueryResponse" --> FE

    style DB fill:#f3e5f5,color:#1b1b1b,stroke:#7b1fa2

Each query item can request:

  • include_price: true — price history with backward-fill
  • include_events: true — asset events in the date range
  • max_points, resolution or sample_like, at most one of them — the price series sampled for a compact chart, daily, weekly or monthly, and with signals their series reduced to the same dates; key names an item for another item's sample_like (Sampled Price Series)

get_prices_bulk() never invokes a provider. Provider acquisition belongs to refresh.py through POST /assets/prices/sync; the query path remains DB-only while retaining its warm-up, event, FX-conversion, signal-computation, and final response-slicing passes.

Each item's range has a ceiling (X-R55). Before any pass, get_prices_bulk() cuts it to end no later than tomorrow by the server's calendar (datetime_utils.latest_range_end(), the helper R13-SEC7-1 also uses), a day of margin for a user whose today is already the server's tomorrow. The series, the comparison series, the signals and the events see the cut range; an item that starts after it gets an empty result in its place (its asset_id, no price, event, error or signal), and the other items are unaffected. POST /assets/prices/query, the risk preparation and AI Export all read through this method, so a range of theirs that reaches past tomorrow stops there. Before, the last price was carried forward to the end, one point per day: about 2.9 million from a recent price to 9999-12-31, followed by a 500 (OverflowError). Without a seed price (none stored before the range), the series (read by observation) also starts at the first stored price of the range instead of its start, as the native _build_backward_filled_series() does: the days before it cost nothing, and the points emitted are the same. X-R55's own module, backend/app/utils/date_range_limits.py, keeps the span limit: RANGE_SPAN_LIMIT_DAYS (36,525 days, 100 years) back from an end (range_span_floor()), which bounds the history-cache walk of a sync and the FX conversion ranges.

A request also has two caps (Z-25, night decision N77). X-R55 gives each range a ceiling, but no limit on how many ranges one request holds: 1,000 FX conversions of 100 years would build about 36.5 million daily conversions. The caps live in backend/app/utils/date_range_limits.py too, with the builders of their 422 detail, bulk_too_many_items_detail() and bulk_too_many_days_detail(); the modules that read them import them by name, where test_bulk_limits.py lowers the budget. The conversion endpoint has the same two caps.

  • Items: more than MAX_BULK_ITEMS (1,000) items get a 422 {"code": "bulk_too_many_items", "message", "max_items", "items"} from the route, before any work: no database read. Exactly 1,000 pass.
  • Writes (MF-SEC9a): DELETE /assets/prices takes at most MAX_BULK_WRITE_ITEMS (10,000) date ranges, all assets together, the same 422 with that max_items. Each asset's ranges, from every item that names it, are merged into disjoint day intervals (inclusive bounds, end defaulting to start), then counted with one COUNT … GROUP BY asset_id and deleted with one DELETE per chunk of OR_TERMS_PER_QUERY (500) intervals (utils/sql_chunks.py), in one transaction: one DELETE with an OR of every range failed from 1,000 ranges, and one COUNT per range made 10,000 queries at the cap. Each result's deleted_count is the rows its asset lost, a row counted once however many ranges cover it, an asset named by two items counted over both (MF-SEC9e: before, overlaps counted twice and such an asset reported its last item only); the counts add up to total_deleted. An empty request answers an empty result, no longer a 500. A failure of POST, DELETE /assets/prices or POST /assets/prices/sync answers 500 with a fixed message, the error in the log.
