docs.title: 📊 Volatility
docs.text: Volatility measures the dispersion of returns — how much an asset's price fluctuates over time. It is the most fundamental risk measure in finance and the building block for nearly all other risk metrics.

docs.title: 📐 Standard Deviation of Returns
docs.text:
\[ \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N-1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (R_i - \bar{R})^2} \]

where \(R_i\) are individual period returns and \(\bar{R}\) is the mean return.

docs.title: 📈 Annualization
docs.text:
Per-period volatility is annualized by multiplying it by the square root of the number of periods a year contains:

\[ \sigma_{annual} = \sigma_{period} \times \sqrt{f} \]

The factor \(f\) is measured from the observed data, not fixed in advance: it is the number of returns actually used, rescaled to a full calendar year over the span they cover.

\[ f = \frac{N \times 365}{D} \]

where \(N\) is the number of period returns and \(D\) the calendar days they span.

Why a square root?

Returns are assumed to be independent across periods. The variance of a sum of \(f\) independent variables is \(f\) times the individual variance. Therefore:

\[\text{Var}_{annual} = f \times \text{Var}_{period}\] \[\sigma_{annual} = \sqrt{f} \times \sigma_{period}\]

√252 is a result, not a constant

A daily-priced stock contributes roughly 252 returns over a full calendar year, so \(f = 252 \times 365 / 365 = 252\) and the familiar \(\sqrt{252}\) is recovered — as the outcome of the measurement, not as an assumption written into it. An instrument that trades every calendar day, such as crypto, gives \(f \approx 365\) and therefore \(\approx \sqrt{365}\): a hardcoded \(\sqrt{252}\) would understate its annualized volatility. A weekly-priced fund gives \(f \approx 52\).

→ See Observed Annualization for the derivation, the worked examples and what coverage adds to them.

docs.title: 💡 Interpretation
docs.text: Annualized Volatility Typical Assets 1-5% Money market, short-term bonds 5-15% Government bonds, investment-grade corporates 15-25% Large-cap stocks, diversified equity ETFs 25-40% Small-cap stocks, single stocks 40-80%+ Crypto, meme stocks, leveraged products

docs.title: 📈 Realized (Historical) Volatility
docs.text:
Computed from past price data. This is what LibreFolio computes:

\[ \sigma_{realized} = \text{StdDev}(\text{historical returns}) \]

docs.title: 🔮 Implied Volatility
docs.text:
Extracted from options prices using the Black-Scholes model. It represents the market's expectation of future volatility:

\[ C = f(S, K, T, r, \sigma_{implied}) \]

Implied volatility is forward-looking but only available for optionable assets.

docs.title: 🔄 Rolling Window Volatility
docs.text:
Rather than computing a single volatility number for the entire period, rolling window volatility computes \(\sigma\) over a sliding window of \(w\) return observations — one per quote day with a return, e.g., \(w = 30\) — producing a time series that shows how volatility evolves:

\[ \sigma_t^{(w)} = \text{StdDev}(R_{t-w+1}, R_{t-w+2}, \ldots, R_t) \]

This is useful for:

  • Identifying volatility regimes (calm vs turbulent periods)
  • Detecting volatility clustering (high-volatility days tend to follow high-volatility days)
  • Setting dynamic position sizes (reduce exposure during high-volatility periods)

docs.title: 📐 Volatility and Portfolio Theory
docs.text:
Volatility plays a central role in Modern Portfolio Theory:

  • It is the denominator of the Sharpe Ratio
  • It determines the width of Bollinger Bands
  • It is the key input for portfolio optimization (minimizing \(\sigma_p\) for a target \(R_p\))
  • Diversification reduces portfolio volatility when asset correlations are less than 1

docs.title: ⚠️ Limitations
docs.text:
Volatility ≠ Risk

Volatility treats upside and downside movements equally. An asset that frequently spikes upward has high volatility but may be very attractive. For a downside-focused measure, use the Sortino Ratio or Max Drawdown.

Non-normality

Financial returns typically have:

  • Fat tails (more extreme events than a normal distribution predicts)
  • Negative skew (large drops more common than large gains)
  • Volatility clustering (calm and turbulent periods)

Standard deviation alone doesn't capture these features.

docs.text:

  • 📊 Sortino Ratio — Downside-only volatility variant
  • 📏 Bollinger Bands — Volatility envelope on charts
  • 🔀 Diversification — Reducing portfolio volatility

docs.title: 🔻 Worst Realization
docs.text:
Worst realization is simply the least favourable single-period return actually observed in the available history — an observed fact rather than an estimate.

Every other figure in this section is computed from the observations. This one is one of them.

docs.title: 🔢 What It Is
docs.text:
Given the returns of the analysed window, the worst realization is their minimum:

\[ WR = \min_t \; r_t \]

There is no confidence level to choose, no distribution to assume, no averaging. The figure is a return that happened, and it comes with the date it happened on — which is what separates it from every parameter on the surrounding pages. A date can be looked up. It anchors the number to an event the portfolio actually went through, rather than to a statistical construction.

docs.title: 🆚 Against Value at Risk
docs.text:
The natural companion is Value at Risk, and the pair works by contrast rather than repetition:

Says Nature Value at Risk One period in twenty goes worse than this A threshold, estimated Worst realization And the worst one was this, on this date A single point, observed

Value at Risk describes a rate and is silent about magnitude beyond the threshold. Worst realization describes a magnitude and is silent about rate — it happened once, and the figure says nothing about how likely a repeat is. Conditional Value at Risk sits between them, averaging the whole tail rather than reading its boundary or its extreme.

Together they bracket the tail: where it begins, how deep it runs on average, and the deepest single step recorded.

docs.title: 🧭 Distribution or Path
docs.text:
Metrics labelled risk fall into two families that answer different questions, and nothing in a row of eight numbers signals which is which.

Shuffle the returns, and see what moves

Shuffle the order of a portfolio's returns and the Value at Risk does not change by a comma — while the maximum drawdown can double.

Value at Risk, Conditional Value at Risk and worst realization read the distribution: which returns occurred, in any order. Max Drawdown, Current Drawdown and the durations attached to them read the path: the order in which they arrived.

Worst realization belongs firmly to the distribution family, and the distinction is not academic. It answers how bad can a single period be? — while a portfolio is not destroyed by one bad day but by a sequence of them. Three consecutive losses of 5% do more damage than one isolated loss of 12%, and only the path-reading family can tell them apart.

Reading a distributional figure as if it described the worst experience available is the mistake this section is arranged to prevent.

docs.title: 💡 Interpretation
docs.text:
Use it as a reality check on the estimated figures. A Value at Risk far milder than the worst realization is not a contradiction — the quantile is meant to be exceeded sometimes, and this is what exceeding it looked like at its most extreme.

The date matters as much as the value. A worst realization from a well-known market event reads differently from one on an unremarkable day, which often points at something specific to the portfolio: a single holding, a corporate action, or a pricing artefact worth checking in Data Quality.

docs.title: ⚠️ Limitations
docs.text:
It is an extremum, so the window can only make it worse

Lengthening the analysed period can never improve this figure and can only worsen it: a longer window contains every observation the shorter one did, plus more chances to find something worse. Comparing worst realizations across portfolios is therefore meaningless unless they were measured over the same window — a longer history will usually look worse for that reason alone.

One observation carries no frequency

The figure rests on a single period. It says nothing about how often such a period occurs, whether anything close to it happened more than once, or how the rest of the tail behaved. For the shape of the tail rather than its extreme, use Conditional Value at Risk.

It depends on the length of a period

A worst day, a worst week and a worst month are different quantities, and they do not convert into one another. The figure is tied to the observation frequency of the series it was read from — see Observed Annualization for how that frequency is established.

docs.title: 📊 Compound Growth
docs.text: A compound growth benchmark represents compound interest — the value grows exponentially, meaning returns are reinvested.

docs.title: 💡 Financial Meaning
docs.text: This is the natural growth model for most financial assets and the standard assumption in discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis. Compound growth produces an exponential curve that accelerates over time — the foundation of long-term wealth building.

docs.title: 🔢 Mathematical Formula
docs.text:
\[ y(t) = y_0 \cdot (1 + r)^t \]

where:

  • \(y_0\) is the starting value,
  • \(r\) is the annual growth rate (decimal),
  • \(t\) is time in years from the start.

This is equivalent to the compound interest formula \(A = P(1 + r)^t\) with annual compounding. The generalised formula with \(n\) compounding periods per year is:

\[ A = P \cdot \left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{n \cdot t} \]

LibreFolio's backend supports the following compounding frequencies: Annual (\(n=1\)), Semiannual (\(n=2\)), Quarterly (\(n=4\)), Monthly (\(n=12\)), Daily (\(n=365\)), and Continuous (\(n \to \infty\)).

When \(n \to \infty\) (continuous compounding):

\[ A = P \cdot e^{r \cdot t} \]

docs.title: 🔄 Iterative Computation (Daily Stepping)
docs.text:
In LibreFolio the compound curve is computed iteratively rather than calling pow() for each data point. This is both more efficient and instructive:

\[ \text{dailyFactor} = (1 + r)^{1/365} \]

Then, for each successive day:

\[ y_{i+1} = y_i \cdot \text{dailyFactor} \]

This is mathematically equivalent to the closed-form \(y_0(1+r)^t\) but replaces \(N\) expensive power operations with \(N\) simple multiplications — the same principle behind how banks actually accrue daily compound interest.

Rule of 72

A quick mental shortcut: an investment growing at \(r\)% per year will approximately double in \(72 / r\) years. At 7% → ~10.3 years.

docs.title: ⚙️ Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Key Default Description Annual Rate annualRate 8 Compound growth rate in percent per year. Offset offset 0 Vertical shift as % of base value.

docs.title: 🔍 Interpretation
docs.text:
The curve is straight on a logarithmic scale — this is the telltale sign of exponential growth. Overlaying a compound benchmark on a log-scale chart is the cleanest way to judge whether an asset is growing faster or slower than a target rate.

Compound Interest on Wikipedia

docs.title: 🎯 Synthetic Benchmarks
docs.text:
LibreFolio can overlay synthetic benchmark curves on any chart. Unlike technical indicators (which are computed from market data), synthetic benchmarks are generated mathematically, computed locally in the browser, and serve as visual reference lines — "what if the price had followed this ideal trajectory?"

They are invaluable for:

  • Comparing actual returns against a target growth rate.
  • Visualising what a disciplined investment plan would look like.
  • Adding oscillatory or cyclic references for seasonality analysis.

docs.title: 📈 Linear Growth
docs.text: A linear growth benchmark represents simple interest — the value increases by a fixed absolute amount each period.

docs.title: 💡 Financial Meaning
docs.text:
This models the scenario where you do not reinvest earnings (dividends, interest, coupons): cash payouts are received but kept aside, so only the original principal generates returns.

If instead you reinvest those earnings — either manually or automatically through accumulating instruments (e.g., accumulating ETFs, which reinvest dividends internally and benefit from tax deferral) — you should expect compound growth, where returns generate further returns.

In practice, the difference between linear and compound growth widens dramatically over long horizons. This is why the Linear benchmark appears as a straight line while the Compound benchmark curves upward exponentially.

Capital gains & losses

When selling an asset above its purchase price, the difference is a capital gain; below, a capital loss. Each jurisdiction has its own rules regarding tax rates, holding period thresholds, loss carry-forward duration, and matching methods (FIFO, LIFO, specific identification). For a theoretical overview, see Taxation & Tax Efficiency.

docs.title: 🔢 Mathematical Formula
docs.text:
\[ y(t) = y_0 \cdot (1 + r \cdot t) \]

where:

  • \(y_0\) is the starting value (first data point of the chart),
  • \(r\) is the annual growth rate (expressed as a decimal, e.g. 0.07 for 7%),
  • \(t\) is time in years from the start.

This is equivalent to the simple interest formula \(A = P(1 + rt)\), where \(t\) is expressed in years using the applicable Day Count Convention.

docs.title: ⚙️ Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Key Default Description Annual Rate annualRate 2 Growth rate in percent per year. Offset offset 0 Vertical shift as % of base value.

docs.title: 🔍 Interpretation
docs.text:
The line is perfectly straight on a linear scale. Any point where the actual price is above the line means the asset has outperformed the target; any point below means underperformance. Because the growth is additive, the line curves downward on a logarithmic scale — making it easy to visually distinguish from compound growth.

Simple Interest on Wikipedia

docs.title: 🌊 Sine Wave
docs.text: A sine wave benchmark represents periodic oscillation. It is the only non-growth benchmark in LibreFolio.

docs.title: 💡 Financial Meaning
docs.text:
Useful for:

  • Modelling seasonality (e.g. agricultural commodities, tourism-linked currencies).
  • Providing a visual reference for cyclic patterns that traders suspect in the data.
  • Testing the rendering pipeline with a known analytic waveform.

docs.title: 🔢 Mathematical Formula
docs.text:
\[ y(t) = A \cdot \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi t}{T}\right) + y_0 + \text{offset} \]

where:

  • \(A\) is the amplitude (peak-to-peak range as % of base value),
  • \(T\) is the period in days,
  • \(y_0\) is the base value (first data point),
  • \(\text{offset}\) is a vertical shift.

docs.title: ⚙️ Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Key Default Description Amplitude amplitude 15 Peak oscillation range as % of base value. Period period 45 Full cycle length in days. Offset offset 0 Vertical shift as % of base value.

docs.title: 🔍 Interpretation
docs.text:
If the actual price roughly tracks the sine reference, the market exhibits a detectable cyclic component at that frequency. Deviations from the sine suggest non-periodic shocks or trend drift. Adjusting the period parameter lets you scan across different cycle lengths — effectively performing a manual version of spectral analysis.

Sine Wave on Wikipedia

docs.title: 🔐 Connection Security
docs.text:
The connection security indicator in LibreFolio's sidebar tells you whether what you type — your password, your figures — travels encrypted between your device and your server. It shows one of three levels, secure, local network or not secure, depending on the address you opened and the network you are on. Administrators also see there when the security checks of the instance need their attention: see Security Warnings for Administrators.

For maximum security, give LibreFolio an HTTPS address and use it everywhere, even on your home network.

docs.title: 🟢 Connection: secure
docs.text:
What you type is encrypted, or it never leaves the server.

✅ Pro ⚠️ Con Nobody along the way can read or change it, not even on a public Wi-Fi. Nothing, as far as risk goes.

📱 Tailscale over plain HTTP and the app

Through Tailscale with a plain http:// address, such as http://100.110.x.x:6040, your browser will not install LibreFolio as an app. That is why an HTTPS address is still better: as a risk the two are the same, since Tailscale encrypts the traffic too.

👉 What to do: nothing, keep using this address. For the app, switch to an HTTPS address.

🔍 When a connection counts as secure

The details give one of three reasons:

  • HTTPS: any https:// address. Your browser decides alone, whatever the server sees.
  • On the server itself: localhost, names ending in .localhost, and loopback addresses such as 127.0.0.1 and ::1. Your browser decides alone: the traffic does not leave that computer.
  • VPN (Tailscale): a plain http:// address in Tailscale's ranges, 100.64.0.0/10 and fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48, or a name ending in .ts.net. Tailscale encrypts the traffic between your device and the server. If the server sees the request coming from the internet instead, the level is local network, as unclear.

docs.title: 🏠 Connection: local network
docs.text:
You opened LibreFolio over plain http:// inside your home or office network, for example at http://192.168.1.100:6040, the address other devices use after a standard installation.

🤷 You settle for ⚠️ Con A connection that needs no setup, and whose traffic stays inside your network. Nothing is encrypted: anyone on the same network, such as a guest on your Wi-Fi, could read the traffic, password included.

👉 What to do: use the HTTPS address at home too.

The same level appears with a reason starting with Unclear when LibreFolio cannot tell where you really are: the advice does not change.

🔍 When a connection counts as local network

A local address over plain http://: an address in 10.x, 172.16.x to 172.31.x, 192.168.x or 169.254.x, an IPv6 link-local or unique local address, or a name ending in .local, .lan, .home.arpa or .internal, or with no dot at all, such as http://nas:6040. A short Tailscale MagicDNS name, such as http://my-server:6040, has no dot either, so it counts here: the Tailscale IP or the full name ending in .ts.net counts as secure.

Unclear: your browser judges the address you opened, and the server then reports where it sees the request coming from, only the kind of address and never your IP address. The server can confirm the browser's verdict or make it uncertain, but never make a connection count as secure; until it answers, the browser's verdict stands. When the two disagree, the level is local network and the reason starts with Unclear:

  • a public-looking address that the server sees coming from your local network, from Tailscale or from the server itself, for example through split DNS or a local proxy;
  • a local or Tailscale address that the server sees coming from the internet.

The traffic is not encrypted, and LibreFolio cannot tell where you really are.

docs.title: 🔴 Connection: not secure
docs.text:
You reached LibreFolio over plain http:// from the internet, for example through a port opened on your router. On a phone, a red dot on the menu button warns you even while the sidebar is closed.

✅ Pro ⚠️ Con None. Passwords and data travel in clear text over networks you do not control: anyone along the way could read them, or even change them.

👉 What to do: avoid this address. If you run the server, give LibreFolio an HTTPS address and stop exposing plain HTTP. Then change your password: Settings → Profile → Change Password. This also signs out every other device signed in to your account.

🔍 When a connection counts as not secure

A public address over plain http://: an address or name that is not local, not Tailscale and not the server itself, such as a public IP or a domain name like http://myhome.duckdns.org:6040. The level holds when the server also sees the request coming from the internet, or cannot tell. If it sees the request coming from your local network, from Tailscale or from the server itself, the level is local network, as unclear.

docs.title: 🔒 How to Connect Securely
docs.text:
Give LibreFolio an HTTPS address, then use only that one. Whoever runs the server sets it up, in one of two ways:

  • Tailscale, with no port opened on your router: Tailscale Serve gives an HTTPS address to the devices of your tailnet, and Funnel a public one that needs no Tailscale on your devices. See Exposing Securely.
  • A reverse proxy with a TLS certificate, such as Caddy, Traefik or Nginx: see Advanced Docker.

Then follow a few good habits:

  • use the https:// address on every device, at home too;
  • bookmark it, and update the old bookmarks and home-screen shortcuts that still point to http://;
  • if you do not run the server, ask whoever runs it for the address;
  • check the indicator: it should show Connection: secure.

If you run the server, Checking Connection Security shows how to verify the result.

docs.title: 🛡️ Security Warnings for Administrators
docs.text:
If you are an administrator, the same line also tells you, on every page, when the security checks of your instance need your attention: the errors and warnings that Settings → Administration → Security lists, and counts on its tab.

  • A dot on the icon. A small dot sits on the corner of the line's shield, with the sidebar expanded or collapsed: red when at least one check is an error, amber when there are only warnings.
  • A link in the details. Click the line: after the reason, a link gives the count, such as 2 security warnings, errors included. It opens the Security tab, where each finding says what is wrong, and closes the details.
  • The count in words. With the sidebar collapsed, pointing at the shield shows the level and the count, such as Connection: secure — 2 security warnings. A screen reader reads the same, with the sidebar expanded or collapsed.
  • On a phone, the sidebar hides behind the menu button, so the button carries the dot too: red with an error, or when the connection is not secure, amber with warnings only. Open the menu to see the line.

The dot follows the Security tab: information is never counted, so with only information, or nothing at all, there is no dot. LibreFolio reads the checks once, when it opens in your browser: after you fix something on the server and restart it, reload the page, or click Check again on the tab. Other users never see the dot or the link, and their browser never asks for the checks. What each check means, and how to fix it: «Security» in Global Settings.

docs.title: 🧭 What the Indicator Does Not Do
docs.text:
The indicator describes the connection you are using right now, and gives advice. Three things are beyond it.

It blocks nothing. It is advice, not a check. And since it describes the connection of the device you are on, the same LibreFolio can show Connection: secure on your laptop and Connection: not secure on your phone.

It does not check certificates. A self-signed certificate that you accepted in the browser shows Connection: secure. The traffic is encrypted, but nobody vouches that the server is really yours.

It cannot always see where you are. When LibreFolio runs in Docker Desktop and is exposed directly, or sits behind a proxy that does not pass your address in X-Forwarded-For, the server sees every visitor as local. Plain HTTP from the internet then shows Connection: local network, as unclear, instead of Connection: not secure. Docker Engine on Linux keeps your address.

Whatever the indicator shows, the advice stays the same: use the HTTPS address.

docs.title: 🔗 Related
docs.text:
• 🌐 Exposing Securely — Tailscale, from a private VPN to a public HTTPS address
  • 🔍 Checking Connection Security — For administrators: the HTTPS address, the session cookie and the reverse proxy
  • 🐳 Advanced Docker — Compose file, environment variables, reverse proxy
  • 📝 Configuration — Every option of the .env file
  • 📦 Installation with Docker — Local and remote access after installing
  • 📱 Install as App (PWA) — Needs an HTTPS address

docs.title: 🚀 Getting Started
docs.text: Welcome to LibreFolio! In a few steps you create your account, take a quick tour and import your first broker statement — and your dashboard fills up by itself.

docs.title: 📝 1. Register Your Account
docs.text:
Open your LibreFolio address (for example http://localhost:6040): the login page appears. Click Register here to create an account.

If the login page shows no Register here, your administrator lets people in only with an invitation link, or has closed sign-ups: ask them for an invitation, or for an account. With an invitation, follow If You Received an Invitation Link.

Fill in your details:

  • 👤 Username — unique, 3 to 50 characters, without @: you log in with it. Spaces, accented letters and signs such as ., _, - or + are fine. When you log in, LibreFolio reads anything with an @ as an email address, so the form refuses one: The username cannot contain @: to sign in, you can always use your email address.
  • 📧 Email — a valid address; it works for logging in too.
  • 🔑 Password and Confirm Password — the strength indicator tells you when the password is strong enough.

First User = Admin

The very first account to register becomes the administrator: it manages the instance-wide Global Settings and every admin feature.

docs.title: ✉️ If You Received an Invitation Link
docs.text:
An administrator can invite you with a link of your own, by message or by email: the email is You are invited to LibreFolio, and its Create your account button opens the link.

  1. Open the link. LibreFolio checks it, then shows the registration form with a note that you have been invited; a second note tells you when the invitation makes you an administrator.
  2. If the administrator wrote your email address on the invitation, it is already filled in: you can change it.
  3. Choose your username and password, then click Register.

  4. You are back on the login page, with a confirmation: log in with your new account.

  5. ⏱️ An invitation link works once, for 7 days. If the page says the link has expired, has already been used, has been withdrawn or is not valid, ask your administrator for a new one.

  6. 📬 If the instance asks you to confirm your email address, open the link it emails you before you log in: see If LibreFolio Asks You to Confirm Your Email.
  7. 🔒 As soon as the page opens, the address bar loses the secret part of the link: keep the message you received in case you need to open the link again. If the page says the link is incomplete, open it again from that message.
  8. 🚪 If the page says that registration is disabled, the administrator has closed sign-ups for now: ask them.

docs.title: 📬 If LibreFolio Asks You to Confirm Your Email
docs.text:
Some instances ask every new account to confirm its email address before the first sign-in. Then, after Register:

  1. The login page says: Account created. We are sending you an email with a link to activate it: open it within 24 hours, then sign in. No email after a few minutes? Check the spam folder, then sign in with your username and password: you will be offered a new link. You cannot sign in yet.
  2. Open the email Confirm your email address and click Confirm my email address. If the button does not work, copy into your browser the address written under it.

  3. The button opens a LibreFolio page that asks you to confirm. Click Confirm my email address there: LibreFolio then confirms your address and brings you back to the login page, with a confirmation: log in with your username and password.

  4. 🖱️ Why one more click? Some email services open the links of a message by themselves, to check them: the click makes sure that it is you who confirms.

  5. 🙋 If you did not sign up on this instance, just close the page: nothing happens.
  6. ⏱️ The link works once, for 24 hours.
  7. 📭 No email? Look in the spam folder. Then, on the login page, sign in with your username and password: LibreFolio says that your address is not verified yet, and offers Send the link again below. A new link replaces the older ones. If you ask too often, or after too many wrong passwords, the page tells you in how many minutes you can ask again.
  8. 🚦 If the login page says instead that the activation email could not leave now, because there were too many sign-ups from your network in the last hour (or the instance has sent too many emails), no email is on its way. Your account is created all the same: wait the minutes the page names, then sign in with your username and password, and you are offered Send the link again.
  9. ⌛ If the page says that the link has expired, sign in the same way: you are offered a new link. If the instance has no free place left meanwhile, ask your administrator.
  10. ✅ If the page says that the link has already been used, your account is probably active already: sign in.
  11. 🔒 As with an invitation, the address bar loses the secret part of the link as soon as the page opens: keep the email until your account is active.

docs.title: 🔐 2. Log In
docs.text:
After registering, you are back on the login page. Log in with your username (or email) and your password. Type your username exactly as you chose it, capitals included. If your username contains an @, which accounts created before version 1.3 may have, log in with your email address instead. If LibreFolio asked you to confirm your email address, open the link it emailed you first: see If LibreFolio Asks You to Confirm Your Email.

Under the card, as on every sign-in page, one line holds the legal notice of your instance.

Too many login attempts

After 10 wrong passwords in 15 minutes for the same username or email address, or 50 from the same IP address, the login page says Too many login attempts: wait a few minutes and try again. Until the wait is over, even the right password is refused: wait up to 15 minutes, then log in. Your administrator can also let you in at once, by restarting LibreFolio.

docs.title: 📧 If You Forgot Your Password
docs.text:
On the login page, click Forgot Password?. When your instance can send emails, the page has a form at the top:

  1. Type your username or your email address, then click Email me a reset link.
  2. The page answers Email sent: check your spam folder too., the same whether an account matches or not: look in your inbox, and in the spam folder.

  3. Open the email Reset your LibreFolio password and click Choose a new password. The page that opens is the one of a link sent by an administrator: follow If an Administrator Sent You a Password-Reset Link from step 2.

  4. ⏱️ The link works once, for 30 minutes.

  5. 📭 No email after a few minutes? The account may be deactivated or registered with another address, or the requests came too close together: try again later, or ask your administrator.
  6. ⏳ After a request, the button counts down 5 minutes before you can ask again: the server sends at most one email every 5 minutes for the same account. Reloading the page keeps the countdown.
  7. 💻 When your instance cannot send emails, the page shows instead the command your administrator runs on the server to reset a password: ask them.

docs.title: 🔑 If an Administrator Sent You a Password-Reset Link
docs.text:
Your administrator can also send you a link to choose a new password yourself, by message or by email.

  1. Open the link: the page shows the account it belongs to.
  2. Type the new password twice: it must meet the rules shown under the field.

  3. Click Set the new password. You are back on the login page, with a confirmation: log in with the new password.

  4. ⏱️ The link works once, for 30 minutes. If the page says it has expired, has already been used or has been withdrawn, ask for a new one: each new link withdraws the ones sent before it.

  5. 🚪 Setting the new password signs your account out on every device: log in again with the new password on each of them.

docs.title: 🎉 3. Welcome Setup & Quick Tour
docs.text:
The first time you log in, LibreFolio opens a Welcome page before the dashboard:

  • 🌍 Check Language and Default Currency: they start from your administrator's defaults.
  • 🖼️ Add a profile picture if you like — otherwise your initials are shown.
  • ✅ Click Continue to save, or Skip setup permanently to keep the current settings.
  • 🚪 Need to leave? Log out is at the top right.
  • ⚖️ Under the card: the legal notice of your instance.

A short welcome animation follows, then the Quick tour starts by itself — click Start tour to begin right away, or ✕ to skip it. The tour shows where things are: the menu button, then Dashboard, Transactions, Brokers, FX, Assets, Tools and Settings. It only points: it never opens a form or creates data.

👋 Already using LibreFolio? — accounts older than the guides

If your account existed before the guides were added, LibreFolio does not send you through them: the Welcome setup counts as Completed, the tour and every guide as Skipped. You can still replay any of them from Settings → Preferences → Onboarding and guides.

⚠️ Setup does not load — what to do

If your settings or your guide progress cannot be loaded, a We couldn't load onboarding page offers Retry and Log out. If your Welcome setup is already done, you may see the Dashboard instead, with a Retry banner on top.

docs.title: 🧭 Contextual guides
docs.text:
Later, short guides start the first time you reach a place where they help:

Area Contextual guides Transactions Page overview, Add Transaction form, bulk workspace, and Import Wizard Brokers Brokers page, Add Broker form, and broker details FX FX page, Add Pair form, and pair details Assets Assets page, Add Asset form, and asset details
  • They point at real controls and never click, upload, edit or save for you.
  • A pulsing frame marks the area a step talks about; a small cursor marks a button you can try. Clicking it does its normal job and moves the guide on.
  • The message panel fades a little after a moment, so you can see the page behind it; hover it to bring it back.
  • Leave a page mid-guide and its guide picks up at the same step when you come back; closing a form restarts that form's guide.

You can replay any guide from Settings → Preferences → Onboarding and guides.

docs.title: 🏦 4. Import Your First Statement (Create Broker & Assets On-the-Fly)
docs.text:
Your dashboard is still empty — whether you land there directly or after the welcome screens above.

The fastest way to fill it is to import your transaction history. You don't need to set up brokers or assets first: the Import Wizard creates them as it goes.

docs.title: 📋 Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the Import Wizard: on the Transactions page, click Import (). A broker's detail page has the same button, with that broker already selected.

  2. Upload Your Statement: drop your broker's report (.csv, .xlsx or .xls) into the wizard and assign it to its broker — choose Create new if the broker does not exist yet. Every report you upload is kept (you find it in Files & Uploads): next time, skip this step and tick the report in the next one.

  3. Select Files & Parse: tick the reports to import. Each one gets its broker's parser — change it per file if needed, Generic CSV for an unknown layout. LibreFolio then reads every row and sums up what it found: transactions, securities, issues and likely duplicates. Some files then need an extra step or two (see the panel below).

  4. Review & Import: match each security to your asset library, or create it on-the-fly with the details read from the statement. Likely duplicates arrive unticked, and rows dated before the broker's opening date are left out. More in Asset Mapping.

  5. Save from the Bulk Editor: Import N transactions moves the ticked rows into the bulk editor — nothing is saved yet. Give them a last look, then click Save All.

🧩 Extra steps — only when your files need them

The wizard adds a step only when your files call for it; a clean single-file report skips them all:

  • Unify assets — the same security appears under different names or codes.
  • Corrections — some rows could not be fully read.
  • Duplicates — the same movement is in two files you import together.
  • Align with the bank — after Review, for a report set such as Danske Bank, when the bank's figures differ from LibreFolio's.

See Steps that appear only when needed.

The first time you open the wizard, a guide walks you through the steps your files need; it never clicks or saves for you (see Guided First Import). For the full walkthrough see How to Import Transactions; for the supported brokers and file formats see Import from Broker.

docs.title: 📈 5. Back to the Dashboard
docs.text: Go back to the Dashboard: your portfolio value, your allocation (by type, sector and geography) and your performance history are now filled in.

docs.title: 🔮 6. What's Next?
docs.text:
Now that your portfolio is populated, you can:

  • 🤝 Share your broker — Give access to family members or advisors.
  • 💱 Set up FX rates — Configure currency conversion for multi-currency portfolios.
  • ⚙️ Customize your preferences — Adjust your language, default currency, and theme. Administrators also manage the system-wide Global Settings.
  • 🧭 Replay the welcome setup or guided tours — Revisit the welcome screen, quick tour, or import guide any time from Settings → Preferences.
  • 📱 Install LibreFolio as an app — Put it on your phone's home screen or in its own desktop window.

docs.title: 📖 User Manual
docs.text:
Welcome to the LibreFolio User Manual. This section provides guides on how to use the application features.

A header that makes room

The page header slides away while you scroll down and comes back as soon as you scroll up, on desktop and on mobile. It stays in place while the keyboard focus is inside it, while one of its menus, the mobile navigation menu, or a dialog is open, and while a guide is running.

docs.title: 🏁 Getting Started
docs.text:
• 🚀 Getting Started: Register, log in, and create your first broker — a step-by-step onboarding guide.
  • 🐳 Installation: How to deploy LibreFolio using Docker.

docs.title: ⭐ Core Features
docs.text:
• 🏦 Brokers: Create and manage brokerage accounts, upload reports, and share access with other users.
  • 📂 Files & Uploads: Manage static resources and broker reports. Upload files, edit images.
  • 💱 FX Rates: Track currency exchange rates, configure data providers, set up auto-sync, and import CSV data.
  • 🧰 Tools: Standalone calculations that never change your portfolio. The first one, the PAC allocator, plans the purchases that bring a new investment as close as possible to its target allocation, without placing any order.

docs.title: 🧩 Misc
docs.text: • ✂️ Image Crop Tool: How to use the interactive image crop, zoom, rotate, and resize tool.

docs.title: 🐳 Installation with Docker (User)
docs.text:
This guide installs LibreFolio with the official pre-built Docker image: the simplest and recommended way to run it at home.

You only need Docker: no Python, Node.js or Pipenv, and nothing to compile.

🍓 The official image is published for amd64 and arm64, so it runs natively, without emulation, on a Raspberry Pi 4/5 (64-bit OS) and on Apple Silicon Macs (32-bit ARM is not published).

docs.title: ✅ Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install Docker, which includes Docker Compose, on the computer that will run LibreFolio:

LinuxmacOSWindows

Follow Docker's official guide for your distribution: Install Docker Engine. On Debian and Ubuntu, the guide first adds Docker's package repository, then installs:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin

Docker group permissions (Linux)

On Linux, your system user must belong to the docker group to run commands without sudo:

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

Then log out and log back in (or run newgrp docker) to apply the changes to your current terminal session.

Install Docker Desktop:

  • Download Docker Desktop for Mac (Apple Silicon or Intel).
  • Or, with Homebrew:
brew install --cask docker-desktop

Install Docker Desktop:

  • Download and install Docker Desktop for Windows.
  • Enable the WSL 2 backend during installation for the best performance.

docs.title: 📁 1. Create a project folder
docs.text:
Open a terminal, go to the folder where you want to keep LibreFolio (for example your Documents folder), then create a librefolio folder and enter it:

# 🏠 Go to the main folder where you want to place the project (e.g. Documents)
cd /path/to/your/folder

# 📁 Create and enter the LibreFolio folder
mkdir librefolio
cd librefolio

docs.title: 📥 2. Get the base configuration files
docs.text:
LibreFolio needs two files: docker-compose.yml, which describes the container, and .env, which holds your settings. Download both from the official repository with one of these commands:

wgetcurl 
# 📥 Download the official docker-compose.yml file
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Librefolio/LibreFolio/main/docker-compose.prod.yml -O docker-compose.yml

# 🔑 Download the .env.example file and save it as .env
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Librefolio/LibreFolio/main/.env.example -O .env

# 📥 Download the official docker-compose.yml file
curl -L https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Librefolio/LibreFolio/main/docker-compose.prod.yml -o docker-compose.yml

# 🔑 Download the .env.example file and save it as .env
curl -L https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Librefolio/LibreFolio/main/.env.example -o .env

The stack runs the official image from the GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) and keeps all your data in a LibreFolio-data folder next to docker-compose.yml.

✍️ Prefer to write docker-compose.yml by hand?

Create a file named docker-compose.yml and paste this content, the same service as the official file:

services:
  librefolio:
    image: ${LIBREFOLIO_IMAGE:-ghcr.io/librefolio/librefolio:latest}
    container_name: librefolio
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "${PORT:-6040}:6040"
    volumes:
      - ./LibreFolio-data:/app/backend/data/prod-docker
    env_file: .env
    environment:
      - LIBREFOLIO_DATA_DIR=/app/backend/data/prod-docker
      - HOST=0.0.0.0
      - PORT=6040
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "python", "-c", "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:6040/api/v1/system/health')"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      start_period: 15s
      retries: 3

The env_file: .env line needs a .env file in the same folder: download it as shown above, or create an empty one, otherwise Docker stops with an error.

docs.title: ▶️ 3. Start the application
docs.text:
Start LibreFolio in the background:

docker compose up -d

Docker downloads the official image from GHCR and starts LibreFolio. The latest tag is the light variant of the image, the recommended default.

docs.title: 🌐 4. Access LibreFolio
docs.text:
Open your browser at http://localhost:6040.

On your first visit, LibreFolio shows the login page: click Register here to create your account. The first account automatically becomes the administrator; to let other people in, send them an invitation link.

🖥️ Watch the status and the logs (optional)

From the terminal, docker compose logs -f follows LibreFolio's logs (Ctrl+C stops following). For a graphical view of your containers and their logs in real time, try Portainer, a lightweight and widely used Docker management tool.

docs.title: 📶 5. Local and Remote Network Access
docs.text:
Once started, LibreFolio is reachable:

  • 💻 from the host computer, at http://localhost:6040;
  • 📱 from other devices on the same local network (smartphones, tablets, other PCs), at the host computer's local IP address, for example http://192.168.1.100:6040.
🛡️ Firewall — only if other devices cannot connect

Open port 6040 in the host computer's firewall:

Debian / Ubuntu (UFW)RHEL / Rocky Linux / Fedora (Firewalld) 
sudo ufw allow 6040/tcp

sudo firewall-cmd --add-port=6040/tcp --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

🌍 Away from home, use the solution you prefer, such as a reverse proxy with an SSL certificate. For the simplest and safest setup, with no ports opened on your router, we recommend Tailscale: see Exposure with Tailscale.

docs.title: 🏷️ Image Variants: Full and Light
docs.text:
The official image comes in two variants. Both contain the whole application and all documentation text pages, in all four languages; they differ only in the documentation screenshots:

  • 🪶 Light (the recommended default): without the documentation screenshots, which load on demand from the online documentation site. About 450 MB to download.
  • 🗂️ Full: also includes the documentation screenshots (desktop and mobile, in all four languages, in light and dark themes), so the built-in documentation works fully offline. A larger download.

Each release is published with these tags:

Tag Variant Use it to latest 🪶 Light Follow the newest release (the tag used by the docker-compose.yml above) X.Y.Z (e.g. 1.1.0) 🗂️ Full Pin a version, with the documentation fully offline X.Y.Z-light (e.g. 1.1.0-light) 🪶 Light Pin a version and stay on the light variant
  • Version tags have no v: 1.1.0, not v1.1.0 as on the GitHub releases page.
  • There is no latest-light tag: latest already is the light variant.
  • The full variant exists only under a version number. Using it means pinning a version, and a pinned image does not move to newer releases on its own (see Updating LibreFolio).

The light variant needs internet for documentation screenshots

With the light variant (latest or any -light tag), viewing the screenshots inside the built-in documentation (Help menu) requires an internet connection, because they are fetched from the online documentation site. Everything else — the whole application and all documentation text — is served from the image itself.

🗂️ Switch to the full variant

Add this line to your .env file, with the version you want:

LIBREFOLIO_IMAGE=ghcr.io/librefolio/librefolio:1.1.0

Then run docker compose up -d: Docker downloads that image and restarts LibreFolio on it. If your docker-compose.yml has a fixed image: line, without LIBREFOLIO_IMAGE, put the tag on that line instead.

docs.title: ⚙️ Configuration Options
docs.text:
All LibreFolio settings, such as the port and the session security key, live in the .env file as environment variables.

For every option and how its value is resolved, see the Configuration Guide in the Admin Manual.

docs.title: 💾 Data Backup
docs.text:
All your data (the SQLite database, uploaded files, broker reports and logs) lives in the ./LibreFolio-data folder next to docker-compose.yml. Back up that folder, stopping the container first for a consistent copy.

For what to save and how, see the Backup section of the Admin Manual.

docs.title: 🔄 Updating LibreFolio
docs.text:
Database migrations run automatically when the container starts and are designed to keep existing data, while some features, such as the What if…? risk simulation, are still in beta and can change between versions. Take a backup before updating: it is your way back if something goes wrong.

  • With the latest tag you always get the newest release, along with any change it brings.
  • To update only when you decide, pin a version instead of latest: ghcr.io/librefolio/librefolio:1.1.0 (full variant) or ghcr.io/librefolio/librefolio:1.1.0-light (light variant). See Image Variants.
  • After the update, each user sees once what changed since the version they last used: see What's new after an update.

docs.title: 🛠️ 1. Manual Update
docs.text:
To update LibreFolio to the newest image:

# 🛑 Stop the running container
docker compose down

# 📥 Download the newest version of the image from the registry
docker compose pull

# 🚀 Restart LibreFolio using the new image
docker compose up -d

The database migrations run on their own when the container starts.

🧯 LibreFolio does not come back after an update

If a database migration fails, LibreFolio stops and its log (docker compose logs librefolio) shows Failed to apply database migrations with the error; Docker then keeps restarting the container. Stop it with docker compose down, restore your backup of LibreFolio-data, and pin the version you were using until the problem is solved.

docs.title: 🤖 2. Automatic Update (Watchtower)
docs.text:
Watchtower updates containers as soon as a new image is published. We recommend its active and updated fork, nicholas-fedor/watchtower. By default it watches every running container on the system: this command limits it to LibreFolio and checks once a week, on Sunday at 04:00:

docker run -d \
  --name watchtower \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -e TZ=Europe/Rome \
  nickfedor/watchtower \
  --cleanup \
  --schedule "0 0 4 * * 0" \
  librefolio
  • --schedule takes a cron expression with six fields, seconds first; set TZ to your timezone.
  • --cleanup deletes the old images to save space.
  • For every other option, see the project repository.

docs.title: 🔌 3. Other Management Alternatives
docs.text:
For more control over notifications and over when to update:

  • WUD (What's Up Docker): a homelab tool with a convenient web interface and notifications via Telegram, Discord, Gotify and more. It can alert you about new releases without updating, leaving the choice of when to you.
  • Diun (Docker Image Update Notifier): a lightweight notifier that needs no write access to the Docker socket. It watches the image registries read-only and tells you when a new version of LibreFolio is published.

docs.title: 📱 Install as App (PWA)
docs.text: LibreFolio can be installed as a Progressive Web App (PWA) on your phone, tablet or computer: it opens like a native app, from its own icon, without an app store.

docs.title: ✅ What You Get
docs.text:
• 🖥️ Full screen — no address bar and no browser toolbar.
  • 🏠 Home-screen icon — launch LibreFolio like any other app.
  • 👆 No accidental gestures — swipe-back and double-tap zoom are turned off.
  • 🔐 Stay signed in between launches, until your session expires.

Online Only

The app needs a connection to your LibreFolio server: there is no offline mode — your data lives on your server. If you open the app while the server cannot be reached, a Server Unreachable page appears and tries again by itself.

docs.title: 🤖 Android (Chrome / Edge)
docs.text:
1. Open LibreFolio in Chrome or Edge.
  2. Open the Help & Support menu (❓, top right) and tap Install App.
  3. Confirm with Install: LibreFolio appears on your home screen.

No install dialog? Use the browser's ⋮ menu → Install app or Add to Home screen.

docs.title: 🍎 iOS (Safari)
docs.text:
1. Open LibreFolio in Safari.
  2. Tap the Share button (square with arrow).
  3. Scroll down, tap Add to Home Screen, then Add.

iOS has no install dialog: on an iPhone or iPad, Install App in the Help & Support menu shows these instructions instead.

docs.title: 💻 Desktop (Chrome / Edge)
docs.text:
1. Open LibreFolio in Chrome or Edge.
  2. Click Install App in the Help & Support menu, or the install icon (⊕) in the address bar.
  3. LibreFolio opens in its own window.

docs.title: 🌐 HTTP vs HTTPS
docs.text:
Address Install as an app Install dialog from Install App https://… (Tailscale, reverse proxy) ✅ ✅ http://localhost ✅ ✅ http://192.168.x.x (LAN) ❌ HTTPS required ❌ a hint only

HTTPS Connection Requirement for PWA

Browsers install an app only from a secure HTTPS address — localhost and 127.0.0.1 are the only exceptions. Over plain HTTP on your network (for example http://192.168.1.100:6040) LibreFolio still works in the browser, but it cannot be installed.

Any HTTPS setup will do. The simplest, free option is our Tailscale Exposure Guide: a secure HTTPS address without SSL certificates to manage or router ports to open.

On a broker's detail page, select AI Export in the toolbar, next to Refresh: it works from any tab. It first opens on Broker Review.

docs.title: 🧠 AI Export
docs.text: AI Export copies your LibreFolio data as ready-to-paste text, with a focused question if you want one, so you can ask the AI assistant of your choice about your portfolio, a broker, an asset or a currency pair. LibreFolio itself never contacts an AI service.

docs.title: 🎯 What It Is For
docs.text:
• Review with real figures: a broker, a position, a currency pair and your exposure to it.
  • Plan: recurring investments, a rebalancing, or how expiring tax losses might offset gains.
  • Explain: what drove your performance, asset by asset, with dated sources.
  • Keep a snapshot: just the facts, ready for your own question.

What you copy is factual context, not investment advice.

docs.title: 🚀 Open It
docs.text:
Select AI Export () in the toolbar of one of these pages:

Page What the export covers Guide Dashboard Your portfolio, as the Dashboard shows it Portfolio A Broker detail page That broker only Broker An Asset detail page That asset and, if you hold it, your position Asset An FX detail page That currency pair and your direct exposure to it FX

The export is dated on the last day of the page's date range: move that date to export an earlier moment.

docs.title: 🧭 Choose What to Export
docs.text: The panel opens on a ready-to-use choice: change only what you need.

docs.title: 📤 Step 1: Choose the export type
docs.text:
Under Export type:

  • Export Data copies only the facts, to keep as a snapshot or to ask your own question. Paste them alone and the AI only confirms it has received them, in your interface language, perhaps listing the main topics; ask a question in the same message and it answers that question.
  • Request Analysis adds a focused question, rules for checking the figures, and the structure of the expected answer.

docs.title: 🗂️ Step 2: Pick a dataset or an analysis
docs.text: Open Dataset or analysis: each entry has a one-line description. Every page offers a general data export, a detailed market history, and two to four analyses, listed in the guides above.

docs.title: 🔍 Step 3: Set the detail level
docs.text: Choose Compact, Standard (the default) or Full. All three cover the same assets, indicators and period; they only keep more or less history. Full can be very long.

docs.title: 📅 Step 4: Set the AI period
docs.text: Choose 3M (the default), 6M, 1Y or Custom (days, weeks, months or years), ending on the export date. If LibreFolio holds less history, the export flags it as partial: it never invents prices or uses future ones.

docs.title: 📝 Step 5: Add notes (analyses only)
docs.text: With Request Analysis, add context or questions in Notes for the AI: a monthly budget, a target allocation, what worries you. The AI reads them as information, not as new rules.

docs.title: 📋 Step 6: Copy
docs.text:
Select Copy AI Export. After Preparing export…, a message confirms the copy with its estimated size.

📏 Large prompt — when the text is long

The panel first shows the Final prompt size with a warning. Choose Use Compact for a shorter text (not shown on Compact), or Copy Anyway: the same settings then copy without asking for a while.

LibreFolio remembers your last choices on each page for a few minutes; logging out resets them.

docs.title: 🤖 Paste It Into Your AI Assistant
docs.text:
You copy plain text: a short header (what was exported, the date, period, currency and detail level) and your data in compact tables. Request Analysis adds the question and the expected answer structure around them. Every export carries LibreFolio's legal notice near the end, in your interface language and without its links; only a short instruction for the AI follows it: with Export Data, how to reply; with Request Analysis, the line that asks it to answer in your language.

  1. Open a new chat in an AI assistant you trust with financial data.
  2. Paste the text and send it. With Request Analysis, the question is already in it; with Export Data, add your question to the same message, or send the data alone and ask once the AI confirms it has it.
  3. Answer the AI's questions: it is told to ask only for what changes the result (a budget, a goal, your tax situation) and never to guess it.

Good to know:

  • Both export types tell the AI not to repeat the figures you have already seen in LibreFolio, but to use them to answer only the question asked. When your data is not enough, it is asked to also search the web for the latest news and to say which conclusions rely on it.
  • With Request Analysis, the AI is asked to answer in your LibreFolio interface language and to keep your figures apart from its interpretation.
  • The Performance & Market Drivers analyses need an assistant that can search the web; without it, the answer says so instead of inventing sources.
  • Assets, brokers, currency pairs and lots appear as short codes (A1, B1, F1, L1) explained in the text; the AI is asked to answer with the real names.
  • An analysis may suggest one more export under Additional LibreFolio Data, with where to find it. If the AI asks for it, copy that export too and paste it into the same chat.

docs.title: 🔒 Privacy
docs.text:
• LibreFolio sends the export nowhere: it only writes it to your clipboard.
  • The text holds your real figures and the names of your brokers and assets, even while privacy mode is on.
  • Each page exports only its own scope:
    • Dashboard: the brokers you own with a share above 0%, narrowed by the broker filter;
    • Broker: that broker only;
    • Asset and FX: every broker you can open, including brokers shared with you.
  • Review the text before pasting it anywhere; a reminder appears after every copy.

docs.title: 🛠️ When Something Goes Wrong
docs.text:
• AI Export is greyed out: the page is still loading or, on the Dashboard, you own no broker with a share above 0%.
  • This selection is not applicable to the current data.: pick another analysis. Position Review needs a position in the asset; FX Exposure Impact needs cash or a position linked to the pair.
  • A message ending in Refresh and try again.: reload the page.
  • Clipboard access is unavailable. Check browser permissions.: allow clipboard access for LibreFolio in your browser.

docs.text: • 🛠️ How AI Export works — for developers

docs.title: 🧠 Portfolio AI Export
docs.text: Export your whole portfolio, as the Dashboard shows it, to ask an AI about its structure, its performance, a recurring investment plan or your tax losses. The options and how to paste are in the AI Export overview.

docs.title: 📍 Where to Find It
docs.text:
On the Dashboard, select AI Export in the toolbar, next to Refresh. It first opens on Recurring Investment Plan.

The export follows the Dashboard:

  • the brokers you own with a share above 0%, narrowed by the broker filter when it is on; brokers shared with you as an Editor or a Viewer are left out;
  • the Dashboard currency, with the last day of its date range as the export date.

The button turns on once the Dashboard has loaded your brokers, and stays off if you own none with a share above 0%.

docs.title: 📤 Export Data
docs.text: Choice What you get Portfolio Overview & History Positions, cash, allocations, performance, flows, income, recorded costs, an economic FIFO summary, a compact market context per asset, and drawdown Portfolio Asset History Detailed prices, returns, indicators, states and events for each asset you hold, with coverage

docs.title: 🎯 Analyses
docs.text:
Analysis What the AI does Recurring Investment Plan Plans conditional recurring investments from your figures, asking only for what it is missing Portfolio Rebalancing Compares your allocation with the targets you give and frames conditional rebalancing paths Portfolio Performance & Market Drivers Explains your result and researches dated market drivers for every asset you hold: use an AI that can search the web Capital-Loss Offset Strategies Explores how available or expiring tax losses might offset gains, using your FIFO lots 📅 Recurring Investment Plan — what the AI will ask you

The AI starts from your data and asks only what changes the plan: how much you can invest and how often, your goal and horizon, how large a decline you can stand, and practical limits such as liquidity, brokers, minimum orders or assets to avoid. It never guesses these answers, can sketch conditional scenarios in the meantime, and compares investing at once with investing in stages.

🧾 Capital-Loss Offset Strategies — have your tax facts at hand

FIFO lots are LibreFolio's economic calculation, not your legal tax position. Before comparing paths, the AI asks for your tax residence and regime, the account type, and your official tax-loss inventory (for example the Italian cassetto fiscale) with amounts, categories and expiry dates. It never suggests a trade just for tax reasons.

docs.title: 🧪 Correlation Tab
docs.text:
The Correlation tab of the Assets page asks the same questions of a selection of assets you put together — assets you own, assets you only watch, or a broker's holdings. Open it from Assets in the sidebar, then the Correlation tab in the toolbar. A selection has no weights, so the tab shows percentages and ratios, never money: for your own money, see the Dashboard's Risk tab.

Each block below follows one pattern: what it answers, a screenshot, its tools and how to read them.

  • 🧺 Building the Selection — which assets are compared
  • 🕸️ Correlation — which of them move together
  • 📉 How Much Did Each of These Hurt? — the losses of each one
  • ⚖️ What Did Each of These Pay for Its Risk? — risk against return
  • ⏮️ What If…? — a past episode, replayed
  • 🚩 Notices and Missing Data — what the data lacked

docs.title: 🧺 Building the Selection
docs.text:
The card at the top answers which assets are compared? Each chip is one selected asset, and the tab remembers your selection in this browser.

Tools shown

  • Eligibility check — whether an asset has enough prices in the period to be analysed → Data Quality

How to read it

  • Add assets with the +, remove one with its ×, or change many at once with Select all, Deselect all, Invert and My assets — up to 100 assets.
  • The counter — 3 in the analysis, of 42 that can be analysed — counts the selected assets being analysed, out of all those that could be over the period set in the toolbar.
  • A dashed chip cannot be analysed in this period: it stays selected, but out of the results. An amber chip is analysed, with a warning. Hover or tap a chip to read why.
  • If the period leaves some assets without prices, an amber strip offers Use the period in which all have prices, which moves the page's dates to fit them all.

docs.title: 🕸️ Correlation
docs.text:
This section answers which of these move together? — to spot the assets that are really the same bet, and any that cushion the others.

Tools shown

  • Correlation coefficient (ρ) — how closely two assets moved together, from −1 (always opposite) to +1 (always together) → Correlation
  • Order by similarity — the default order: closely linked assets sit side by side, so redundant groups show up as blocks → Correlation

How to read it

  • One square per pair: blue when the two assets move together, red when they move in opposite directions, grey when they move independently. Hover or tap it for the value in words.
  • Start from the two lists: The most alike names the pairs that are almost the same exposure, The ones that offset the pairs that cushion each other. An empty list is a finding. Click a pair to find it in the matrix.
  • A dash is not a zero: the pair could not be measured — too little history, or a price that never moved.
  • The order buttons rearrange the matrix; they never change a value.

docs.title: 📉 How Much Did Each of These Hurt?
docs.text:
This section puts every asset on the same scale of harm: its worst losses in the period, and how far it still stands below its peak.

Tools shown

  • Bad day — the average loss on the worst 5% of days (CVaR at 95%) → Conditional Value at Risk
  • Bad month — the same over real one-month stretches → Conditional Value at Risk
  • Worst fall — the deepest drop from a peak; lasted N d counts the days until the asset was back there, or until the end of the period → Max Drawdown
  • Below peak now — how far it stands below its highest level in the period → Current Drawdown
  • Rise to peak — the gain needed to get back there: 20% below takes +25% → What It Takes to Get Back

How to read it

  • Each column is its own horizon, from a day to the whole period: compare the assets down a column, never add the columns up.
  • Not a ranking: the table opens in your selection's order. Click a column title to sort it, or hover it for what it measures.
  • On a short period, Bad day and Bad month can stay empty while the drawdown columns are filled: they need more history.

docs.title: ⚖️ What Did Each of These Pay for Its Risk?
docs.text:
This section sets risk against reward — how much each asset swung, and what it returned on average per year — in a table and a chart. With a benchmark chosen under Compared with, it also shows how each asset moved with it.

Tools shown

  • Volatility — how much the returns swung, on a yearly basis → Volatility
  • Ann. return — the average annual return: the period's average return, scaled to a year → Observed Annualization
  • Sortino — the return earned per unit of downward swing → Sortino Ratio
  • Sharpe — the return earned per unit of volatility → Sharpe Ratio
  • Beta — with a benchmark: how much the asset moved when the benchmark moved → Beta & Active Return
  • Correlation — with a benchmark: how closely the two moved together → Benchmark Selection
  • Risk/return line — with a benchmark: the dashed line drawn through it on the chart → The Risk/Return Line

How to read it

  • Not a ranking: the table opens with the benchmark's row, then your selection in its own order. Click a column title to sort it.
  • The line under the table gives the exact period behind the figures, and says when it is shorter than yours — usually because of an asset with a shorter history.
  • On the chart, further right means more swing and higher means more average return; the benchmark is the diamond. A circle above the dashed line was better paid for its risk than the benchmark. Click a row or a circle to highlight that asset in both.

The average annual return is not the return you lived through

On a very volatile asset, the return actually lived through is lower: do not read the height of a dot as what the asset earned. It also comes from prices alone — coupons and dividends are not included yet.

docs.title: 🎯 Choosing the Benchmark
docs.text:
• One benchmark for every risk page: your choice under Compared with also applies to the Dashboard, broker and asset risk pages, so that they stay comparable.
  • Its row opens the table, with a dash under Beta and Correlation: the benchmark is not compared with itself. It may also be one of your selected assets.
  • Assets that cannot be measured over the period are listed apart in the picker, read-only. A benchmark among them stays chosen but is not used until you pick a period that suits it.

docs.title: ⏮️ What If…?
docs.text:
This section answers how did each of these come through a real past episode? — a built-in crisis or a period you choose, replayed with real returns. Click its title to open it. Only the historical replay is offered: a hypothetical shock or a simulation would need weights.

Tools shown

  • Historical replay — each asset's real return over a past period → Historical Replay

How to read it

  • Choose a Preset, such as the Global Financial Crisis, or set the Period, then press Run replay. Changing the selection or the page's dates clears the result.
  • The table shows each asset's Return, worst first, with a bar: red for a loss, green for a gain. There is no total: a selection has no weights to add up.
  • Assets without prices at the ends of the period are left out and listed above the table, with the reason. When possible, a button replays the shorter period in which they all have prices.

docs.title: 🚩 Notices and Missing Data
docs.text:
When something is wrong with the data, the tab says so once, right below the selection card, and names the results it affects.

Tools shown

  • Data quality — missing or outdated prices and exchange rates, and the results they make partial → Data Quality

How to read it

  • The data-quality banner lists what to fix, each problem with its action, such as Sync prices or Sync rates. Click it to open the list.
  • A currency pair with no exchange-rate route gets its own button in that banner, one per pair (tooltip Add FX pair): it opens the Add New Currency Pair window right there, already filled in with that pair, and the analysis recalculates by itself once the pair is saved and its rates are downloaded → Adding a Currency Pair
  • The notice below it names the partial results and their cause. A partial result still shows its figures: read them with that cause in mind.
  • A section's own amber banner means a result did not come back at all, often because the period is too short: choose a longer one, or sync the prices.
  • What if…? reports its own problems inside its section.

docs.title: 🔎 Good to Know
docs.text:
• One period for all the assets. Every figure covers the same days for every selected asset, so the rows can be compared. An asset with a shorter history shortens that period for all of them, and their figures change: this is expected → Data Quality
  • One currency. Returns are measured in your Default Currency, set in Preferences (the instance's default if you never chose one), exchange-rate moves included.
  • A dash is not a zero. The figure could not be measured for that asset over this period; hover or tap it to read why.
  • Another page, another figure. Another page or another selection measures over different days: compare figures only when they cover the same period.
